en: Preface to the *Fayi* (Unfolding the Obscure) Commentary on the Meaning of the Bodhisattva Precepts from the "Mind-Ground" Chapter of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*:
I have heard that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are one and the same. Sentient beings are fundamentally the Buddha; the Buddha is fundamentally the mind.

Since the mind is inherently unborn, what need would there be for precepts? It is only because the mind has become deluded that it gives rise to an ocean of afflictions, vast and difficult to fathom. Thus, by means of...
The mind is established through the Dharma-gates; they are vast and immeasurable. Yet, every Dharma must have its order, and every matter its可循 (xún - that which may be followed).
Thus, the immeasurable is condensed into the sands of the Ganges; the sands of the Ganges are condensed into eighty thousand;

further condensing them, one goes from ten thousand to a thousand; further condensing them, one goes from a hundred to ten; and further condensing them, the Six Perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) unfold their framework.

Great Eye (Mahāmaudgalyāyana), furthermore, if one summarizes them, the three trainings encompass their grand framework; yet these three are further integrated and condensed into two, which, being paired together, are called "concentration and wisdom.
When mentioned individually, they are termed *vinaya*. This is truly a tracing back to the current and reaching the source.

All returns to this precept. When one seeks its essence through its name, it is found to be nothing but the single mind; this is the gathering of the mind. When wandering thoughts are withdrawn and profound stillness arises, this is the tranquility of the mind.
When the power of concentration is deepened and the light of wisdom is emitted, the three trainings are complete and the six perfections are naturally cultivated.
The immeasurable Dharma gates have all been set forth. How magnificent is the Precept! Is it not the very source of all dharmas?
Looking back at its categories, there is the Hīnayāna and the Mahāyāna, and their precepts are distinguished accordingly: those of the Śrāvaka and those of the Bodhisattva.

One emphasizes pure cultivation and external caution, such that the body is severed from all that is non-virtuous; the other emphasizes right contemplation and internal diligence, such that the mind...

To have no malevolent thoughts is, first, to guard oneself, which is called being free from transgression. To extend one's compassion beyond oneself is, second, to benefit others, which alone manifests true observance of the precepts.
The Way does not consist of a self; thus, one must establish corrective regulations according to circumstances, gradually perfecting an excellent model.

On one hand, it delineates a unified code for the time, encompassing the entire cycle of wholesome dharmas; on the other hand, it strictly defines boundaries, restricting [the rules] specifically to monks and nuns.
On one hand, it breaks down barriers to universally include both the ordained and the laity;

on the other hand, it follows the prohibitions to be called "prohibitions," clarifying immediate efficacy by adhering to the ancient tracks. On one hand, it takes the Vinaya discipline as the very means to transcend the Vinaya, employing divine ingenuity to...
He established great achievements. Since his physical nature was thus, how could his function not be so? In the extinguishing of evil, it may be like the morning sun dissolving ice:
after a long time, it remains firm and unmoving; yet it may also be like snow cast upon a red furnace: in a single kṣaṇa, not a trace remains.
In the production of goodness, it may be like an infant learning to speak: with a single word, stammering persists for days; yet it may also be like...
The Great Creator brings about a renewal of spring; in a single moment, the myriad plants sprout forth buds.
As for his saving of sentient beings, it may be like a firefly illuminating the ground, its light appearing within a few steps, serving merely as a guide for the path of ants;

or it may be like the bright sun beautifying the heavens, its radiance reflecting through the void, universally providing benefit to the human realm. Heaven and earth are insufficient to evaluate their relative excellence; how could a single day or an entire kalpa [compare]?
This illustrates their relative heights and depths. Therefore, one who wishes to enter the Tathāgata-yāna must first receive the bodhisattva precepts.
By means of these precepts, the myriad practices are brought forth; thus, the King of Samantabhadra’s Vows is realized. By means of these precepts, solitary luminosity is made vast and penetrating.
It is the wisdom-mother of Mañjuśrī, the banner raised in common by all Buddhas, and the broad highway trodden together by the thousand sages.
How magnificent is the Bodhisattva precept! Is it not the very source of all precepts? Therefore, it was transmitted face-to-face by Vairocana.

Miaohai personally heard it: upon a thousand-petaled lotus, the Compassionate Honored One flourished with exquisite beauty branch by branch; from the Seven Buddhas down to the present-day translators, every word has transmitted the sacred sounds.
Alas, although the complete sutra exists, its wondrous commentary has not yet been revealed.

I look back with reverence to the Venerable Zhiyi, who first initiated these subtle words, and extend my thoughts to this humble self, who now once again unveils their hidden meanings. How fortunate that the secret scriptures of the numinous mind have endured through vast kalpas! How blessed am I!
Having personally encountered the fragrant traces of the spiritual shores of several sages, I am deeply ashamed that I have merely followed in their footsteps.

I only hope for the continued circulation of this transmission from teacher to student, so that by polishing the ancient mirror we may restore its brilliance, and by successively upholding the lineage, we may extend the light of the ancestral lamp.

May each person awaken to the Buddha who is but one's own mind, constantly gathering the heart through the precepts; and may every individual realize that this very Buddha is born within, ultimately manifesting through birth.

They shall attain Buddhahood. Whether monk or layperson, human or spirit—without discriminating between those in the evil realms or the dark paths, and regardless of different forms or distinct species—if they but know how to hear the Dharma, they shall all ascend together to the Dharma-gate of the Brahma-net. All who possess a mind shall enter the ground of the heart of Śākyamuni.
Thus it was said at that time.
Recorded on the eighth day of the second month in the year of Dinghai, the fifteenth year of the Wanli era, by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple,
Bhikṣu Zhuhong of Yunqi Temple in Hangzhou.
This is the Preface to the *Fayin* (Unfolding the Hidden), a Commentary on the Meaning of the Bodhisattva Precepts from the "Mind-Ground Chapter" of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
The text written at the top margin of the first fascicle is the commentary (*śāstra*) of Tiantai.
From the second fascicle to the final fascicle, the text written at the top margin is the sūtra text; that indented by one character is the commentary of Tiantai.
"Unveiling the Hidden" (*biao fa yin*) refers to the present exposition.
The topical outlines (*ke*) of various sutras have been compiled into separate volumes; now, I have extracted and abridged them to attach directly to the sutra texts as a distinct method.

While the commentaries and sub-commentaries on various sutras each divide the sutra into sections and the commentary into its own sections, I shall not establish such sectional divisions for this commentary.
In a few instances, I will harmonize and integrate them to avoid excessive detail and complexity.
The characters and phrases in various editions differ from one another and are not uniform; even the Southern and Northern Tripitaka editions do not entirely agree.
To rely solely on the Tibetan text is likewise not appropriate, for every dynasty that underwent a revolution, the Tripitaka was necessarily re-engraved.

There have been instances of inclusion and exclusion. The *Kaiyuan lu* has been transmitted down to the present day; yet there are thirteen or fourteen titles that bear headings but contain no sūtras.
This is especially true for texts outside the canon, some of which may even predate those currently included. How can this be known?
Thus, I have consulted ancient records and weighed them against contemporary sources, considering only the general intent. If there are minor discrepancies, they need not be strictly adhered to.

The current version I rely upon is that which accords with the commentary (*śāstra*). For instance, in the precept against eating the five pungent roots (*pañca-garadha*), the character for *gecong* (wild onion) is written as "茖";
in the precept against setting fire to burn things, the character for "living beings" is written as "生"; in the precept against double-tongued speech, the character for "鬪遘" is written as "遘";

and in the precept against harming sentient beings, the two characters "販賣" (buying and selling) appear at the beginning. Since the scripture and the commentary thus correspond, it is clear that this current version is the authentic one.
During the Sui dynasty, it was not long after the time of the Qin translators; therefore, one should follow [the former] without any doubt.
Since this sutra emphasizes the Bodhisattva precepts, although the commentary extensively enumerates the various stages of a Bodhisattva therein, [its primary intent remains the precepts].
This *Fayi* merely provides a brief explanation. Those who wish to know it in detail should consult the complete works of Tiantai themselves.

Regarding passages within the commentaries where the text or meaning is difficult to comprehend, or where there may be errors due to transcription, I have ventured interpretations based on my own judgment;
yet I do not dare claim these to be correct. I have provisionally preserved them here to await correction by those of superior insight.
The Elucidation of the Profound Meaning of the Bodhisattva Precepts from the "Mind-Ground Chapter" of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*,
Scroll One.
Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Chen and Sui Dynasties.
The Monk Zhuhong of Yunqi Monastery, Ming Dynasty, Reveals the Hidden Meaning:

General Explanation of the Commentary on the Sutra. This main text is divided into two parts: first, the exposition of the meaning prior to the sutra; second, the formal interpretation of the sutra text.
Part One: Exposition of the Meaning Prior to the Sutra (4) 1. General Clarification of the Main Intent; 2. Identification of the Speaker; 3.
Brief Explanation of the Title of the Sutra; 4. Detailed Analysis of the Headings of the Commentary.
First, a general clarification of the main intent.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): In Tiantai’s commentaries on the sutras, there are always five levels of profound meaning (*wuchong xuanyi*). This sutra does not expound them;

although there is an exposition of the meaning prior to the sutra itself, it merely explains the title of the sutra commentary. We shall follow this established precedent here as well, which will present no hindrance.
The original title of this sutra was *Brahmajāla*. It consisted of two volumes, an upper and a lower; what is now published separately is only the lower volume.
The titles carved for it at various times differ: some call it the "Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Mind" (*Pusa Xindi*), thereby omitting the name "Vinaya";

others call it the "Bodhisattva Precept Text" (*Pusa Jieben*), which conflates it with the translations of other masters. To give it the single title *Brahmajāla* makes it resemble a complete sutra. Furthermore...
This is not permissible. Moreover, the commentary text has been added, and its title is distinct.

What we rely upon now is that the commentator first explains the title of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, next explains the title of the "Mind-Ground" chapter, next explains the names of the bodhisattvas, and finally explains the name of the fundamental precepts.
Thus, the sūtra, the chapter, the persons, and the dharma are as clear as looking at one’s own palm. Furthermore, the original title of this commentary is "Bodhi... [The text here is truncated].

The *Pusa jie yi shu* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Bodhisattva Precepts). Now, combining these and titling it the *Fannwang jing xin di pin pusa jie yi shu* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Bodhisattva Precepts from the "Mind-Ground" Chapter of the Brahmajāla Sūtra), the sequence is fully established, leaving no room for dissent.
II. Identifying and indicating the person who expounded [this work]:
"Explication of the Profound Meaning" (Fayin) spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Chen and Sui dynasties.
Chen and Sui are the names of two states. During the Dajian era of the Chen dynasty, the Master propagated the Way at Waguan Temple. Subsequently, he...

The Emperor invited him to reside at Guangzhai Monastery. During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, while the Emperor Yang was still in the Eastern Palace, he requested the Master to confer the Bodhisattva Precepts upon him;
thus, the Way flourished once again. From the sovereigns of the two dynasties—namely Chen and Sui—to their ministers and subjects, there were none who did not revere him.
"Tiantai" is the name of a mountain. The Master received it with his hands as if in response to a dream; auspicious signs were felt as the bells rang, and even the *chimei* (goblins) [were subdued].
His virtue was so sublime that it seemed to dissolve into the void; a Brahman monk descended from the sky to pay him homage. He propagated the sutras at Luoshui and passed away at Shicheng.
Because his spiritual affinity was rooted in this mountain, it was named Tiantai. "Zhizhe" (Wise One) was his title;

Emperor Yang received the precepts from him and consequently adopted this title, for the scriptures state that only one who is a "Wise One" is fit to serve as a precept master. Thus, he was praised for the excellence of his virtue.

He was a man of wisdom. His master’s name was Shangzhi (Upper Wisdom) Xi (Lower Composure). The reason his personal name is not recorded here is that the master’s title is what people delight to hear;

thus, we follow the established convention. As for the title "Great Master" (Dashi): he gathered the essence of the fourfold assembly and was revered by all generations for ten thousand ages, just as a Buddha appears in the world;

therefore, he is called the Great Master. Regarding the terms "expounding" (shuo) and "compiling" (zhuan): they differ slightly. "Compiling" refers to composition with the pen, while "expounding" may issue from the mouth.

This is a record by his disciples. The Master’s magnificent virtue and great achievements, as well as his spiritual responses and auspicious omens, are fully detailed in his primary biography and supplementary records;
here, I have taken only the general outlines, as there was no leisure for extensive citation.
III. A Brief Explanation of the Title of the Sūtra (2) I. Praising the Precepts. II. Explaining the Title. ○ I.
Praising the Precepts (3) 1. The Greatness of the Benefit Bestowed. 2. The Extensiveness of Those for Whom It Is Intended. 3. Concluding with the General Significance.
○ First, it is of great benefit.
The Bodhisattva Precepts are the opening chapter for mobilizing goodness and the vanguard for repelling evil. By returning directly to the Way, the source of birth can be exhausted.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): To initiate a great and vast meritorious undertaking is difficult; to shatter the vanguard of a flourishing evil Māra is difficult.
This Mind-Ground Precept is neither good nor evil, yet its actual function is to practice good and cease evil.
By relying upon this precept, one then possesses the proper method for practicing good and the correct path for ceasing evil. Therefore, it opens up and expands [the way].
Distributing all virtuous merits constitutes the first chapter. Subduing and destroying all evil Māras constitutes the vanguard.
As the Sūtra says: "From precepts arises concentration; from concentration issues wisdom. This is indeed the constant rule for the transformation and guidance of the Buddhas of the three periods.
Throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, one’s births have flowed on without end, precisely because of erroneous conduct and following deviant paths.

It is merely because one is deluded, turning one’s back on the source and forgetting the way home. Now, by following these precepts to cease evil and practice good, one proceeds through the path of rectitude to still delusion and return to the truth.
How could this not dry up the flowing current of the river of craving, parch the vast expanse of the sea of suffering, and lead to the realization and witness of non-arising?
Upon reaching this state, both good and evil are simultaneously extinguished, and the fundamental source is restored.
This is the true precept of the source-ground (cittabhūmi).
Second, regarding the breadth of its application:

even those of the Śrāvaka’s minor practices cherish and revere the Prātimokṣa; how much more so should a Bodhisattva, who possesses a comprehensive heart, not maintain the categories of precepts with meticulous care?
Both the internal and external factions alike revere and uphold [this teaching]. The common people of the royal house offer their allegiance with profound devotion. To reveal its hidden depths:

the precepts possess such great benefit as described above that those who are reached by them are vast in number. Whether internal or external students, whether of noble or lowly birth, there are none who do not follow them.
To cite an analogy for those who hear [the teachings]: it is truly because even the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which seeks only self-benefit, still prioritizes [these principles] first.

If this is so even for those who uphold the precepts, how much more so for the Mahāyāna path that benefits both self and others? It is for this very reason that it is titled the "Bodhisattva Precepts.
As for the term *weizhi* (委質), it means to offer one's person as a pledge; it refers to the act of single-mindedly submitting oneself in service.
III. Expanding the Meaning of the Three Bonds.
This is the supreme cause for hastening toward the ultimate fruit and the wondrous practice for establishing the *maṇḍala*.

To reveal the hidden truth: one attains Buddhahood by means of the precepts; hence they are called the "supreme cause for the ultimate fruit. It is the movement of the good intention. Relying upon the precepts, one subdues [afflictions].

Because it subdues Māra, it is called the "Sublime Practice of the Site of Enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*). It repels evil intentions; its merit is such that it is only fitting that all should follow it.
II. Explaining the Title (in two parts): 1. Clarifying the numerous versions. 2. Explaining the present sutra.
Section One: Clarifying the Various Categories (2). First, the original precepts differ; second, they vary according to the capacities [of practitioners].
Regarding the first point, the original precepts differ:

however, as recorded in the sūtras and śāstras, there are many varieties of precept characteristics (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*); yet, as analyzed in the records and biographies, the methods of receiving them are not without commonality.
Differences.

*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): Although the aforementioned precepts are of great benefit and widely encompassing, the characteristics recorded in the sutras differ, and the methods by which people receive them also vary.
Second, [the distinction arises] from the differences in the capacities of the audience.
This is because the awakening of their faculties may be either partial or complete; accordingly, they require either detailed or concise instruction.

Since two verbal expressions cannot be uttered simultaneously and two matters cannot be enacted together, the *Fayin* (Unveiling the Hidden) explains that this is truly because the awakening of people’s faculties is either partial or complete. Therefore, [the teachings differ].

In these demonstrations to Cien, there are both detailed and concise versions, as the teaching was adapted according to the capacity of the recipient. How could they be presented indiscriminately together or allowed to proceed in parallel?
Part Two: Explanation of the Main Scripture (in two sections): First, stating the title; second, explaining the meaning.
Section One: Listing the Titles (Part Two). First, explaining the major compendium; second, explaining the single-text version.
First, explaining the major compendium:

I now respectfully follow the Dharma-characteristics as set forth by Master Kumārajīva, which originate from the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, specifically the "Section on Vinaya" (*Vinaya-skandha*). Master [Kumārajīva] was of the Qin...
In the third year of Hongshi, he arrived within the borders of Han and brought forth the brilliance of the Mahāyāna, rectifying and upholding the holy teachings.

He translated over three hundred fascicles of sūtras and śāstras, revealing what was hidden. As for Master Shi, he is Master Kumārajīva; this is translated as "Child Longevity" (Tóngshòu), owing to his youthful age and profound virtue.
Shao. Thus, when the Former Fu Qin first invited him, he had barely reached the halfway point when Yao Xing succeeded the Qin dynasty and welcomed the Master back to his own kingdom.
Because he was proficient in both Chinese and Sanskrit and had extensively mastered the various scriptures, he was titled the Tripiṭaka Dharma Master.

It is said that he was a translator of Buddhist scriptures since the time of the seven Buddhas. Regarding what is now described, according to Sengzhao’s preface: in the third year of Hongshi of the Qin, Kumārajīva—

At the Cidang Temple in Chang’an, the Master, together with three thousand śramaṇas specializing in the study of doctrine, held the Sanskrit manuscripts in their hands and orally translated and explained more than fifty sections, totaling three hundred fascicles.
This refers to the fact that among those fifty sections, there were some consisting of three hundred fascicles;
this *Brahmajāla Sūtra* in one hundred and twelve fascicles and sixty-one chapters is one such instance.
This was translated at that time.
Second, regarding the single-text versions:
one copy of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* was recited last. Out of a vow to propagate and proclaim it widely, he was diligent, repeating each word three times over.
*Fayi*: According to Sengzhao’s preface, this "Chapter on the Mind-Ground" (*Xindi pin*) should be the tenth chapter.
At that time, over three hundred people, including Daorong and Daoying, received the Bodhisattva precepts; each of them recited this chapter and subsequently transcribed eighty-one copies.
It was for the sake of broad circulation. What is now called "one fascicle" refers precisely to this single chapter. To "repeat three times" expresses the caution with which one recites it.
As the saying goes: "Nan Rong repeated three times the words of the white jade tablet"—this is what that means.
II. Explanation of the Meaning (in three parts): First, the purpose; second, the title; third, the citation of the chapter. I. The Purpose:

Because the phrasing and meaning are profoundly obscure and the underlying intent is deeply mysterious, this work is intended to point out the palm of the hand for clear instruction, so that future generations may grasp it.

Awakening is easy; yet, the purpose of my diligent and repeated expositions is specifically because [the meaning] is obscure, hidden, profound, and mysterious. Therefore, I have been insistent and exhaustive in my instructions, so that later generations may easily awaken and know the difficulty with which the virtues of the former masters were attained. As for the phrase "pointing at the palm," it means: [The text continues: ...it is like pointing at one’s own palm; it is not something that can be grasped by the mind alone. It is like a person who has never seen an elephant; when they see an elephant for the first time, they ask, "What does an elephant look like? Another person takes a rope and ties it to the elephant's leg, then shows it to them. The person asks, "Is this the elephant? The other replies, "No. They then show them the elephant’s trunk, saying, "This is the elephant. The person asks, "Is this the elephant? The other replies, "No. They then show them the elephant’s ear, saying, "This is the elephant. The person asks, "Is this the elephant? The other replies, "No. They then show them the elephant’s leg, saying, "This is the elephant. The person asks, "Is this the elephant? The other replies, "No. They then show them the elephant’s tail, saying, "This is the elephant. The person asks, "Is this the elephant? The other replies, "No. They then show them the elephant’s belly, saying, "This is the elephant. The person asks, "Is this the elephant? The other replies, "No. They then show them the elephant’s back, saying, "This is the elephant. The person asks, "Is this the elephant? The other replies, "No. They then show them the elephant’s head, saying, "This is the elephant. The person asks, "Is this the elephant? The other replies, "No. They then show them the elephant’s tusks, saying, "This is the elephant. The person asks, "Is this the elephant? The other replies, "No. They then show them the elephant’s entire body, saying, "This is the elephant. The person asks, "Is this the elephant? The other replies, "Yes. Thus, although the person has not yet fully understood the elephant, they have already gained some understanding of its form. This is what is meant by "pointing at the palm. It is not that there is no elephant; rather, it is that the person has not yet fully understood the elephant. This is why the former masters spoke of "pointing at the palm. It is not that there is no awakening; rather, it is that people have not yet fully awakened. This is why the former masters spoke of "pointing at the palm. The Buddha said that he views the great trichiliocosm as if looking at the palm of his hand; the Confucianist says, "It is as if looking at this," pointing to his palm.
Both express the sense of being clearly manifest and easily seen.
II. Explaining the Title.
The scripture is titled *Brahmajāla* because it seeks to clarify that the Buddha-dharmas of the various Buddhas differ from one another, just like the mesh of the net of the Brahma King.
This is explained in detail in the subsequent commentary on the title. While that [text] speaks of both worlds and teachings, this [text] mentions only the teachings.
Because the world arises from the Dharma, and while all Buddhas benefit sentient beings, the Dharma is of primary importance; thus, I shall explain by citing what is most significant.
Third, the citation of the chapter.

Regarding the term "ground of the mind" (*cittabhūmi*) used in this chapter: the Bodhisattva’s ethical discipline (*saṃvara*) universally guards the three karmas. Mind, thought, and consciousness are one in essence though different in name.

Among the three karmas, mental karma is primary, while bodily and vocal karma are secondary. This is discussed from the perspective of what is predominant; therefore, it is called the "ground of the mind."

*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): The precepts universally guard the three karmas and should properly be designated as such collectively. Since both body and speech are subsumed within the single mind, they are mentioned alone;

by citing the superior, the inferior is implied. Thus it is named the "Mind-Ground" chapter (*cittabhūmi-paṭala*). Regarding the statement that "the substance is one while the names differ": initially there is only the single, true, quiescent substance.
From the perspective of gathering and initiating, it receives the name "mind" (*citta*); from the perspective of deliberation and measurement, it receives the name "intellect" (*manas*).
The name [of this consciousness] arises from the designation "discerning consciousness" (*vijñāna*). When one investigates its fundamental source, there is no duality in its essence.
IV. Detailed Explanation of the Commentary’s Headings (3): 1. Explaining the Name; 2. Identifying the Essence; 3. Discernment and Analysis.
I. Initial Explanation of Names (Three sections): 1. Clarifying personal names; 2. Distinguishing dharma titles; 3.
Clarifying stages and positions. A. Initial Clarification of Personal Names (Two sections): 1. Indicating that there are many names; 2. Revealing the grounds for acquiring those names.
○ First, the term has many names.
In the Sanskrit of India, it is *mahābodhisattva*; what is now called "Bodhisattva" is a contraction of the remaining syllables.
Translated, it means "one who accomplishes sentient beings through the mind of the Great Way. It is also called "Opening Being" (Bodhisattva), "Great Courageous Mind," or "Virtuous and Beautiful.
These names are given according to their respective practices.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden). The Sanskrit term for *bodhisattva* is correctly translated as "a sentient being who has perfected the mind of the Great Way" (*daodaxin cheng zhongsheng*).

This means either "a sentient being who has already perfected the mind of the Great Way," or "one who brings those sentient beings to perfection by means of the mind of the Great Way. The name is established according to their practice.
Furthermore, there are many kinds. A "Bodhisattva" (Kāishì) is one who can internally expand their own wisdom and externally guide the minds of others.

One with a "great courageous mind" is one who dons the armor of the great vows, succeeds to and flourishes the lineage of the Buddhas, and quells the armies of Māra; this is the ultimate in valor and strength.
One who is "virtuous and beautiful" is one who accumulates merit and establishes practice, such that they are praised by others. All of the above follow from their conduct.
There is a slight difference, and their names also differ.
Second, as for the designation of these names:

because the application of their minds is vast and universal, they are given such titles. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin) provides the basis for this, as these individuals possess the mind of the Great Way (*mahāyānacitta*).

It is indestructible, like a diamond (*vajra*). From the initial generation of the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*) until the attainment of equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), all are termed *bodhisattvas*.
They are also called "sons of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*), in the sense of succession. All three vehicles (*triyāna*) arise from the understanding born of the Buddha;

thus, they all share the meaning of being "sons. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "If one were like my son," yet the Great Being who succeeds [the lineage] is superior and is called a "true son. Furthermore, the three...

Those who ride upon [the vehicle] alike all cultivate the path; all possess this meaning. The two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) personally attain their own results, which are narrow and short-lived; the Mahāsattva’s [path] is broad and long.
Because he attains enlightenment for himself and leads others to do so, he receives this title. A verse in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says:
"From the first aspiration, one is already a teacher of devas and humans, surpassing both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Therefore, it is called the "Great Mind" (*mahācitta*).

*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): The aforementioned titles all arise from the universal and expansive movement of the mind; this is precisely what is called the "mind of the Great Way" (*mahāyāna-citta*).
Next, a scripture is cited as proof. Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Great Perfection of Wisdom):

it states that from the initial resolve until the attainment of Buddhahood, the great mind is never again obstructed or destroyed. Therefore, although there are differences in depth and stage, they are collectively termed "Bodhisattvas," and are also referred to as "Buddhas."
A "son" (putra) is so called because he possesses the meaning of being one who succeeds to a position; here, it signifies that he shall succeed to the rank of the Buddha.

While the three vehicles equally inherit from a single Buddha, the Bodhisattva alone is uniquely entitled to this title because what he inherits is the direct, supreme lineage of the One Vehicle (ekayāna).
While the three vehicles equally cultivate the same path, the Bodhisattva alone monopolizes its excellence because what he cultivates encompasses both self and others.

This is the Great Way that penetrates all. Therefore, at the very moment one first resolves upon the mind [of enlightenment], one already takes the celestial and human beings as one's teachers and surpasses those of the Two Vehicles;
what need is there to wait for the attainment of Buddhahood? This is what is meant by the "Great Mind."
II. Establishing the Dharma Name (2). First, a general indication of the meaning of the precepts; second, a detailed exposition of the characteristics of the precepts.
Regarding the first, the general indication of the meaning of the precepts:

the dharma name is itself the meaning of the precepts. In the Sanskrit language, it is *śīla*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the language of Qin, it means 'innate goodness' (*xing shan*), and it is also called 'purity' (*qing*)."
"Refreshing. It is so named because it can quench the heat and affliction of breaking the precepts;

thus it is called by its functional name. It is also called *pratimokṣa*, translated as "preserving liberation. It is also called "pure livelihood," or "accomplishing dignified deportment. It entails not accepting or storing anything improper.

Regarding future rebirths, it ensures one leaves the three evil realms and receives a physical form in a pure land. It can suppress wrong livelihood, prevent transgressions, and stop evil. Furthermore—

To speak of "precepts" (*śīla*) is to refer to the meaning of "restraint," the meaning of "training," and further, the meanings of "binding" and "prohibiting. These are all names established according to their respective meanings. As the Great Sūtra says:
"If you still speak of what the Buddha has prohibited regarding impermanence, you violate the Buddha’s prohibition; your tongue shall then fall off. It also says:
"All the prohibitions and precepts possessed by such a person are incomplete; they cannot even attain the enlightenment of the Two Vehicles, let alone [the higher]."
The Unsurpassed Way.

"Revealing the Hidden. *Śīla* in Sanskrit; in the language of Qin, it means "innate goodness. This was translated by Master Kumārajīva from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, hence it is called "the language of Qin.
"Innate goodness" means that the nature is fundamentally good and inherently undefiled; such is the essence of the precepts (*śīla*).
Names are established according to their respective meanings. Furthermore, there are many kinds of "coolness" (*śīta*):

for one who has broken the precepts, the fire of desire burns fiercely, yet the precepts can extinguish it. "Preserving liberation" means maintaining the three karmas and remaining free from all bonds.
"Pure livelihood" means sustaining oneself through purity. "Accomplishing dignified deportment" means possessing a majestic and awe-inspiring presence, as well as proper ritual conduct.
This is the principle. "Not receiving or accumulating" means not greedily seeking and accepting what is improper, nor being stingy and hoarding much.
"Regarding future places of birth," it means that when one's retribution is exhausted, one will certainly leave the evil realms and be born in a Pure Land. "Ceasing wrong livelihoods" means...
It means being able to cease impure livelihood and not sustaining oneself through wrong occupations.

"Preventing the non-righteous and ceasing evil" means guarding against transgressions so they do not intrude, and bringing sinful evils to rest so they are not committed. "Restraint" (*yue*) has the meaning of binding oneself so as not to be licentious.
"Instruction" (*xun*) has the meaning of teaching and providing virtuous counsel. "Discipline" (*le*) is like a horse accepting its bridle; it means self-taming and submission.

Regarding the meaning of "prohibition" (*jin*): it is like a royal prohibition or decree, which no one dares to violate. Alternatively, it is said that *le* should be read as *qin* (diligence); thus, diligently cultivating the three karmas is also a valid interpretation. The character *le*, however, is superior.

Just as with the Buddha’s prohibitions—whereby if you speak [what is forbidden], you will incur the retribution of a tongue; or as with a king’s prohibitions—whereby if you commit an offense, you bring destruction upon yourself—here we have merely explained the character "prohibition" to serve as an analogy for the rest.
The Buddha prohibits you from speaking [certain things]; if you do so, you will receive the retribution of a tongue, just as if you were to violate a king's prohibition, you would suffer execution.
It means to destroy. The above all contain the meaning of "precept" (śīla). Therefore, it is said that the names are established according to their respective meanings.

○ Second, a detailed exposition of the characteristics of the precepts (in three parts): First, a brief indication of the various types; second, the summary and return to the three clusters (triskandha);
third, the harmonious integration with the three truths (trisatya).
○ First, various types were briefly indicated.

Now, regarding what is called "precepts" (śīla), there are the precepts of restraint (saṃvara-śīla), the precepts co-existent with meditative concentration (samādhi-sahaja-śīla), and the precepts co-existent with the Path (mārga-sahaja-śīla). These names originally derive from the Tripiṭaka.

*Vinaya* (the precepts) is that which prohibits; *īryāpatha* (proper deportment) refers to physical demeanor. Because it can restrain various evils within one's physical form, it is called *śīla* (morality), and is also termed "majestic deportment" (*vinaya*).
"Majesty" (*vi*) means pure, solemn, and awe-inspiring; "deportment" (*naya*) means a model for practitioners, being dignified and inspiring reverence.

It is also called "taming and controlling," which brings the mental activities into a state of harmony and goodness. *Samādhi* (concentration) is stillness and gathering. At the time of entering concentration, one naturally becomes harmonious and good.

It prevents all evils. The Path (mārga) is that which enables penetration. After the realization of truth, one naturally refrains from transgressions. At the stage of the first fruit (srotāpanna), insects are kept four inches away from the plow;
this is the power of the "concomitant with the path" (mārga-sahabhū). Since these two types of precept-dharma are superior functions of the mind, they have the power to give rise to the precepts.
Because the path-concentration and the restraint (saṃvara) arise simultaneously, they are termed "concomitant."
*Fayi*: Regarding the three meanings of *vinaya* (discipline): "Restraint" (*saṃvara*) refers to rectifying the body; "dignified deportment" (*īryāpatha*) refers to transforming sentient beings;

and "self-mastery" (*damana*) refers to controlling the emotions. As for "concomitant with concentration" (*samādhi-sahaja*): when the mind is tranquil, all evils do not arise. As for "concomitant with the Path" (*mārga-sahaja*):

when the mind is enlightened, the multitude of delusions naturally ceases. By merely cultivating the concentration of the Path, the precepts are spontaneously perfected. Therefore, it is said that they arise together with the monastic discipline (*śīla*). Together.
This refers to the common [classification].

The Sarvāstivādins state that there are three types of restraint: the restraint of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*), the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*), and the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*).

Although these names originate from the Tripiṭaka, the wholesome bodhisattva precepts likewise possess these three. That which is obtained through formal vows is called the restraint of the precepts; that which pertains to a bodhisattva’s meditative absorption...
"Common to the Path" (sādhāraṇa-mārga) means that all [practices] are brought to rest within the three karmas;

they are collectively termed "precepts" (*śīla*). *Fayi* [Commentary]: The discipline (*vinaya-saṃvara*) is as previously explained. "Meditative concentration" (*dhyāna*) has the meaning of "definition" (*niyama*). "Taintless" (*anāsrava*) has the meaning of "the Path" (*mārga*). Regarding "vows" (*praṇidhāna*):
whenever one undertakes a great matter, one must first establish a vow. A "vow" (*yao*) signifies a "deadline" (*kāla*) or an "aspiration" (*praṇidhi*).

If one observes the restraint of ethical discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*), the restraint of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the restraint of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla*)—these three categories of precepts are known as the *Vaipulya-bhūmi-vyavasthāna* (the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*) and do not pertain to the Tripiṭaka.

This is the restraint of the Mahāsattva, which encompasses the cessation of the three types of action (*trividha-karma*). Here, they are designated as "restraint" (*saṃvara*) because they are manifested through body and speech.
Regarding the gathering of wholesome dharmas: based upon the restraint of ethical discipline, one gives rise to the great bodhicitta, which is able to cease all unwholesome [actions].

"Cultivating wholesome deeds" means diligently practicing all forms of goodness to fulfill the vow for enlightenment. "Gathering in beings" refers to the eleven ways in which a bodhisattva benefits sentient beings;
these are all acts of benefiting others that bring extensive welfare to living beings.

*Fayi*: The precepts encompass the three types of action. That the present *vinaya* discipline appears to belong primarily to body and speech is because it is explained according to their manifest characteristics.

Since the meaning of "precept" (*śīla*) is the cessation of evil, to say that it "encompasses wholesome qualities" (*kuśala-saṃgrāhaka*) implies that if one merely avoids evil, there is as yet no "wholesome" to be designated.
An said: "Bodhi is the Great Mind. It consists of ceasing evil and practicing all that is good;

therefore, it is said that one should give rise to the Bodhicitta upon the basis of the Vinaya-śīla. Regarding the eleven matters: first, to benefit sentient beings by engaging in the same activities as they do;

second, to tend to the sick; third, to preach the Dharma; fourth, to repay kindness; fifth, to rescue those in distress and hardship, and to provide solace to those afflicted by grief and affliction; sixth..."
1. Providing for the poor; 2. Gathering the assembly through virtue; 3. Comforting sentient beings; 4. Praising those with virtue; 5.
Subduing faults and evils to effect reform; 6. Manifesting faults and evils through supernormal powers to cause people to fear and avoid them.
II. Concluding by returning to the three aggregates:
Having extensively enumerated all the bodhisattva precepts in the Chapter on Ethics, [the text] concludes that these nine types of precepts are all subsumed within the three categories of ethics.

Restraint (saṃvara) enables the mind to abide; gathering wholesome qualities (kuśalasaṃgrāhaka) brings the Buddha-dharma to fruition for oneself; and gathering sentient beings (sattvārthakriyā) accomplishes the welfare of others. This...
These three encompass all the precepts of the Great Beings (*mahāsattva*). The *Ratnavyūha-sūtra* states: "The morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) refers to the ten *pārājika* offenses;

the morality of gathering what is wholesome (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) refers to the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates; and the morality of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*) refers to loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, through which one transforms and reaches all sentient beings."
"May they attain peace and happiness. *Fayi* (Unfolding the Obscurities) states:

The tenth chapter of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* clarifies nine kinds of precepts. The first is called the "precept of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-śīla*). The second is the "all-encompassing precept" (*sarva-śīla*).
Within the all-encompassing precept, the names of the three clusters (*tri-skandha*) emerge. It concludes at the end by stating: "As above, the nine beginning with the precept of intrinsic nature..."
Regarding the various types of precepts, one should know that they are subsumed within the three categories of precepts; these "three precepts" refer to the three clusters (*tripiṭaka*).

Furthermore, citing the *Ratnavyuha-sūtra* (Yingluo jing), that scripture designates the ten grave prohibitions as the code of discipline (*vinaya*), the myriad practices as wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), and the immeasurable four immeasurable minds as the means for delivering sentient beings;

thus, it likewise does not transcend the three clusters. Observing this, [one sees that] the various [precepts], such as those of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the path (*mārga*), and the untainted (*anāsrava*), are all included therein.
There are no precepts that are not encompassed.
○ Third, the integration of the three truths.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in its chapter on the precepts (*śīla-varga*), enumerates ten kinds of precepts: first, unimpaired; second, unbroken; third, unpierced; fourth, unmixed.
Five: following the path; six: non-attachment; seven: praised by the wise; eight: mastery; nine: following meditative concentration; ten: fulfillment.
Inferring the meaning of these ten, one who is "without deficiency" maintains the natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*), whose nature is profoundly pure, like guarding a bright jewel.

If one violates them, it is like a vessel that has been broken; such a person is a mere peripheral follower of the Buddha-dharma. One who is "without breach" maintains the thirteen [precepts] and possesses no...

"Broken" means [the precepts] are damaged. "Not pierced" refers to *pāyattika* offenses and the like; if one commits such transgressions, it is like a vessel with holes or leaks, incapable of receiving the Way.

"Unmixed" means maintaining the *samādhi-saṃvara* (precepts co-arising with concentration). Although one maintains the *vinaya-saṃvara*, if one dwells on thoughts of breaking the precepts, it is called "mixed.

When the mind is maintained through the power of concentration, sensual desires do not arise. As the Great Sūtra says: "Even if there is flirtatious speech or the sound of bracelets outside the wall..."

"Sound" refers to men and women pursuing one another; both defile the pure precepts. "Following the Path" means following the principle of the Truths (*satya*), whereby one can destroy the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*).
"Non-attachment" means that having seen the Truth and become a sage, one is unstained by the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-āsrava*).

These two [categories] concern the observance of the precepts according to the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). "Precepts praised by the Wise" and "Precepts of Sovereignty" concern the Bodhisattva’s transformation of others and being [praised] by the Buddha.
Praise: To attain mastery within the world is what is discussed here regarding the precept of upholding morality according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

"Following concentration" means being fully endowed with both types of precepts; that is, following the *Śūraṅgama* [Samādhi]. Without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), one manifests various dignified demeanors (*īryāpatha*) and displays the forms of the ten dharma-realms to guide and benefit sentient beings.
Although these dignified demeanors involve movement and activity, they are spontaneously and constantly pure; therefore, it is called the "precept of following concentration."

The various precepts mentioned previously, which involve restraint through discipline (*vinaya*), are called "incomplete. The precepts of the Middle Way, however, possess no precept that is not complete;
therefore, they are called "complete. By employing the wisdom of the Middle Way, one universally enters into all phenomena; therefore, they are called "complete.
This is the upholding of the precepts of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the Middle Way.

*Fayin* (Unveiling the Hidden): That which is "deficient" (*que*) has already become completely ruined; therefore, it belongs to the *mūla-pārājika* (offenses involving expulsion). That which is "broken" (*po*) is damaged but not yet ruined;

therefore, it belongs to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offenses requiring suspension and confession before the community). That which is "pierced" (*chuan*) is leaking but not yet damaged; therefore, it belongs to the *pāyattika* (offenses requiring expiation).

This proceeds from the coarse to the subtle. When both body and mind are fully encompassed, it is called "unmixed"; thus, one avoids all three types of transgressions. Entering into principle and shattering false views is the state of pure truth.

The cessation of thought is the precept of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). To accord with the Buddha-mind while traversing the worldly dharmas is the precept of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

When meditative concentration manifests the cessation [of thought], it is the conventional within the ultimate; when movement arises in constant purity, it is the ultimate within the conventional—this is the precept that follows concentration.
Such a precept encompasses all precepts and further enters into all phenomena, leaving nothing unpenetrated.
All things are fully present; there is nothing that is not perfectly interfused. Therefore, it is called "complete" (*ju-tsuk*), and therefore it is called the "Middle Way precept.
**III. Clarifying the Stages and Ranks (2)** 1. A brief indication of the four teachings. 2. A detailed explanation of the four teachings.
First, the four teachings are briefly indicated.

If one examines the various teaching gates expounded throughout the Buddha Śākyamuni’s single career of transformation according to their underlying principles, they are clearly seen to comprise the four teachings: namely, the Tripitaka (Zàng), the Shared (Tōng), the Distinct (Bié), and the Perfect (Yuán).

As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites Kātyāyanīputra’s explanation of the limits of the six perfections: when the Bodhisattva gave his own flesh to replace the pigeon, this was the fulfillment of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
King Sumati did not speak falsely; this was the fulfillment of his ethical discipline (*śīla*). When the seer Kṣāntivādin had his limbs severed by King Kali, his mind remained unmoved;

this was the fulfillment of his patience (*kṣānti*). He performed great acts of giving to drain the ocean; this was the fulfillment of his vigor (*vīrya*). He sheltered the bird's nest in his hair; this was the fulfillment of his meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
The *Gupin* (劬嬪) and the Great Ministers divided the lands to settle disputes; these are the Bodhisattvas of perfected wisdom (*jñāna-pūrṇa*), who are exclusively Bodhisattvas.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that there are Bodhisattvas who resolve to attain the mind [of awakening] in correspondence with *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge); these are the Bodhisattvas of universal penetration.

There are also Bodhisattvas who resolve to attain the mind [of awakening] and sport with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), purify Buddha-lands, and—according to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*—manifest inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*), transforming their bodies to ascend the Dharma-seat. And...

Furthermore, those who again undergo humiliation and reproach are distinct bodhisattvas. Those who, upon generating the aspiration for enlightenment, immediately sit at the site of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), achieve perfect enlightenment, turn the wheel of Dharma, and deliver sentient beings, are perfected bodhisattvas.

*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): The details are contained within the doctrinal teachings (*jiaoyi*). The general meaning is that what is achieved through diligent cultivation of the six *pāramitās*, accumulated bit by bit and inch by inch, constitutes the *piṭaka*.
Why is it called "partial bodhisattva" (*bian pusa*) rather than simply "piṭaka"? It is because the *piṭaka* contains both the two gates of the *śrāvaka* and the bodhisattva;
since this sutra belongs to the bodhisattva precepts, it specifically represents the bodhisattva. This refers to the bodhisattva of the *piṭaka* teachings.

Being partial rather than complete, they are called "partial bodhisattvas. The former [category] pertains to the Shared (Sādhāraṇa) treasury, while the latter pertains to the Distinct (Pratyekabuddha) and Perfect (Samantabhadra) treasuries.

Some, being of dull faculties, perceive only partial emptiness; others, being of sharp faculties, give rise to a resolve that accords with the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatā). These are those who penetrate both the upper and the lower.

This refers to the Shared [Teaching]. Below, it distinguishes the Separate from the Shared; above, it distinguishes the Perfect from them. Because it is distinct from these two, one transforms the body and ascends the seat;
yet because it is not yet perfect, one suffers humiliation and is rebuked. That which is "separate" constitutes a distinct teaching.

That at the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one is able to become a Buddha and save sentient beings—this is the Perfect. Question: Regarding the marks of fulfilling the Six Perfections, performing what is difficult to perform, and possessing such merit as this...

In what sense are they categorized as "small"? Answer: These are the six perfections of the phenomenal realm (*vastu-ṣaṭpāramitā*). Because they are practiced and fulfilled gradually, they possess limits.
For instance, when Śibi cut his own flesh to feed the hawk, his practice of giving reached its ultimate point in the offering of his own body’s flesh and blood; this was the limit of *dāna*.
When Pūrmā regarded death as returning home in order to preserve her integrity, she sacrificed her life but did not abandon her precepts; this was the limit of *śīla*. As for *kṣānti*...
The Rishi endured having his limbs severed, yet his mind remained unshaken; his forbearance reached its ultimate limit.

Prince Mahātyāga, because he had lost a jewel, sought to drain the ocean until it was dry, his heart never faltering or weary; his perseverance reached its ultimate limit. Śāṇakavāsin entered into meditative concentration.
A magpie nested atop his head; only upon emerging from meditative absorption did he realize this, and thus his dhyāna was at its ultimate limit.

He and his consort divided the cities, mountains, and rivers of Jambudvīpa into seven portions, so that the various kingdoms ceased their strife; through such clever skillful means, he reached this state, and thus his wisdom was at its ultimate limit.
Nevertheless, as it did not transcend the laws of cause and effect, arising and ceasing, it is categorized as Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
II. Detailed Explanation of the Four Teachings (4): First, the Tripitaka Teaching; second, the Shared Teaching; third, the Distinct Teaching;
fourth, the Perfect Teaching. I. The Tripitaka Teaching (2): First, briefly citing the Śrāvakas; second, discussing the Bodhisattvas.
First, let us briefly take up the śrāvakas.

Regarding the depth and shallowness of the stages and positions among the four types of bodhisattvas, we shall now explain them. Initially, the Three Piṭakas were primarily intended for the Hīnayāna. Among the śrāvakas, there are seven noble stages (ārya-pudgala).

Of these, there are three external ordinary beings (bāla-pṛthagjana): first, those practicing the five stabilizing meditations; second, those practicing the distinct-characteristics mindfulness establishments (smṛtyupasthāna); and third, those practicing the general-characteristics mindfulness establishments.

The foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Next, one enters the stage of the ordinary person within (*antarapṛthagjana*), where there are four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*): fourth, the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*); fifth, the stage of "Summits" (*mūrdhan*); sixth, the stage of "Patience" (*kṣānti*); and seventh, the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).

Beyond this, one enters the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*): first, the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*); second, the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*); third, the one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*); fourth, the one attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*);
fifth, the bodily witness (*kāyasākṣin*); sixth, the one liberated by time (*samayavimukta*); and seventh, the one liberated at all times (*asamayavimukta*). Such is the case for the śrāvakas.
*Fayi*: Those whose bodies dwell within the outflows (*āsrava*) and in whom the Noble Path has not yet arisen are all termed "ordinary persons" (*pṛthagjana*).

External ordinary persons have not yet seen the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and still remain outside the realm of principle; internal ordinary persons gradually perceive the nature of phenomena, for their minds roam within that realm of principle.
Regarding the three types of external ordinary persons (*bāhyapṛthagjana*): the five cessations (*pañca-sthiti*) have the meaning of subduing [the afflictions].

For example, impurity ceases greed; counting the breath ceases distraction; loving-kindness and compassion cease hatred; dependent origination ceases delusion; and mindfulness of the Buddha ceases hindrances. As for specific mindfulness: mindfulness of the body is its impurity;
mindfulness of sensation is that it is suffering; mindfulness of the mind is its impermanence; and mindfulness of phenomena is their selflessness. As for collective mindfulness: mindfulness of...
The body is impure; one likewise contemplates the impurity of sensation, the impurity of the mind, and the impurity of phenomena. The next three recollections follow this same pattern.
Regarding the four internal stages of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), these are the four preparatory practices, also known as the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*).

"Heat" (*uṣmagata*) refers to the arising of the root of goodness of heat from the mindfulness of general characteristics. It fully contemplates the Four Noble Truths, cultivates the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*), gives rise to a concordant understanding, and subdues [the afflictions].

The afflictions and delusions [are suppressed], and one attains a portion of the Buddha-dharma’s essence. It is like the heat generated when drilling wood, or the first signs of harmony at the onset of spring; this is called *ūṣmagata* (Heat). As for *mūrdhan* (Summit):

the application of contemplation is the same as before, but it becomes even more lucid, like looking from a high vantage point over a great distance; this is called *mūrdhan*. As for *kṣānti* (Patience):
it means to endure, and also carries the sense of acceptance. It is divided into lower, middle, and upper levels. Lower patience involves observing all eight [realms] universally.

Regarding the Truths, one cultivates thirty-two aspects. As the stage of medium patience gradually diminishes, it reaches the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), where only one aspect remains for two moments;
this is called "patience" (*kṣānti*). As for the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*):

from the mind of the two moments of superior patience, when one moment has ended and the remaining one moment still persists within the stage of patience, the next moment of mind ends, and one immediately enters [the Path of Seeing].

The "Supreme Worldly" (*laukikāgradharma*): that which is contaminated (*sāsrava*) is called "worldly" (*loka*). Being the most excellent within the world, it is termed "supreme. These seven stages of skillful means (*upāya*) are the steps for entering the state of a noble one (*ārya*).

Once these are transcended, one enters the stage of the noble ones. Regarding the meaning of the teachings, the stage of the noble ones is divided into three: namely, the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).
Now, they are divided into seven; these are the "follower by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*) up to the "one liberated at any time" (*asamayavimukta*). To correlate them: the follower by faith...

Those who follow the Dharma (dharmanusārin) belong to the path of seeing (darśanamārga). Those who are resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta), those who have attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), and those who have realized through the body (kāyasākṣin) belong to the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).

Those who are liberated by time (samayavimukta) and those who are not liberated by time (asamayavimukta) belong to the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa). In brief, those who follow faith (śraddhānusārin) are of dull faculties because they arise in dependence upon others.

Those who follow the Dharma are of sharp faculties because they enter [the path] by means of their own wisdom. Because they follow faith, they are resolved through faith; because they follow the Dharma, they are resolved through vision.

One attains non-periodic liberation (*asamaya-vimukti*). Only those who are "body-witnesses" (*kāyasākṣin*) possess both the sharp and dull faculties; thus, their realization is distinct for each. Question:
This concerns the depth and shallowness of the stages within the practice of a Bodhisattva; why then is the Śrāvaka cited? Answer:

The Tripiṭaka is primarily intended for the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), while it is secondary for the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, as stated below, the depth and shallowness are established by comparison with the Small Vehicle; therefore, it must be so.
First, the preliminary exposition.
Second, the discussion of the Bodhisattva.

Regarding the Bodhisattva, one does not distinguish between stages or levels; they do not sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), but practice solely the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). If one were to discuss stages and positions, it would only be appropriate [to speak of them] as follows:

This is merely a matter of relative depth and shallowness when compared to the Hīnayāna. From the initial generation of the bodhicitta, one gives rise to vows of compassion and observes the Four Noble Truths, taking the Truth of the Path as the primary gateway.
One single-mindedly cultivates the six pāramitās: generosity (dāna) liberates hungry ghosts; ethical discipline (śīla) saves those in hell;

patience (kṣānti) relieves animals; vigor (vīrya) uproots the asuras; meditative concentration (dhyāna) brings peace to humans; and wisdom (prajñā) illuminates the celestial hosts. From the time of Śākyamuni until [the period of] Kaśmīra...
That Śikhin is called the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*. One attains five kinds of merit: first, not being born in the three evil realms; second, not being born in a borderland;
third, having all sense faculties complete; fourth, not receiving a female body; and fifth, constantly knowing past lives, yet not knowing for oneself whether one will become a Buddha or not.
By comparison, his status corresponds to the five *sthāpanīya* [foundations] and the specific and general foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). From Śikhin...

From the time he abandoned [the world] until he met Dīpaṃkara, this period is called the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa. At that time, although he knew within himself that he would become a Buddha, he did not speak of it.

According to the standard, his stage was that of the *uṣmagata* (Heat) within the *gotrabhūmi* (Stage of the Spiritual Lineage). Since he possessed the faith that realizes the Dharma, he certainly knew he would become a Buddha;
yet, while practicing the six perfections, his realization was not yet clear, and thus he did not speak of it to others. From Dīpaṃkara back to Vipaśyin constitutes the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa.

[The stage of] "Just Fulfilled" (*kevala-pūrṇa*). At this time, the inner mind is clearly aware that one will become a Buddha; one speaks these words spontaneously, anticipating that one stands within the stage of the Dharma-peak (*mūrdha-dharma*).

One practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and clarifies the understanding of the Four Truths (*catvāri satyāni*), just as when climbing a mountain peak, one sees clearly in all four directions.

Therefore, one speaks to others: "If [the path] exceeds three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one plants the karma for the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśan-mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*). Anticipating this, it is considered the lower [stage].

Regarding the stage of patience (*kṣānti*): if one sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one’s position is in the "Supreme Patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*). Subsequently, in a single *kṣaṇa*, one enters into reality;

through thirty-four moments of mind, one severs the fetters and attains *sambodhi*, thereby becoming a Buddha. (Note: *Kie-na* [罽那] is recorded as *Kie-na* [罽那] in the *Sijiao yi*; this remains for further investigation.)
*Fayi* (Unveiling the Hidden): The Dharma of the Śrāvakas involves fearing birth and death and seeking liberation with haste;
they are preoccupied with calculating stages and positions, and anxiously weary of afflictions (*kleśa*). Bodhisattvas do not long for stages and positions, nor do they grieve over afflictions.
They broaden their minds and magnanimously resolve their wills; they focus resolutely only on practicing the Six Perfections (*ṣat-pāramitā*) to save [sentient beings].
It is solely for the purpose of saving sentient beings. Furthermore, there are natural stages that correspond to those of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

Taking the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya) as the first is because one does not merely seek to avoid suffering for oneself; thus, the Truth of the Path comes first, which refers to diligently practicing the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).

As for *dāna* (generosity) belonging to the hungry ghosts (*preta*), it is because they are stingy and greedy, eating alone and refusing to give. *Śīla* (ethical discipline) belongs to the hells (*naraka*).

As for the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes, these belong to the realm of non-restraint because one does not uphold the precepts. Affiliation with the animals means being subject to the devouring of the strong by the weak, for one is unable to endure.
Affiliation with the asuras means being arrogant and self-important, for one does not cultivate diligence.

Even humans habitually cling to external objects, for they have lost the concentrated mind. The devas are deluded by sensual pleasures, for they have squandered their wisdom-mind. Thus, each is characterized by these six [qualities].

"Crossing over" means to cross over the stages. During the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, one does not know that one will become a Buddha because one has not yet attained the conviction (*śraddhā*) regarding the realization of the Dharma;

this stage corresponds to the level of an ordinary person (*bāla-pṛthagjana*). Because the gap between the holy and the ordinary is still too great, during the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, one knows in one's mind that one will become a Buddha, though one does not speak of it verbally;

one already possesses the conviction regarding the realization of the Dharma and believes oneself to be a Buddha. This stage corresponds to the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) level; although one has conviction, it is not yet fully realized.

Because it is not yet determinate, one knows through the mind that one will become a Buddha after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. One who verbally declares, "I shall become a Buddha," has reached the ultimate limit of the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhāga*) and corresponds to the level of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).

Their vision is extremely clear and they possess no further doubt. Regarding "lower patience" (*adhimātra-ksānti*) and "upper patience" (*uttama-ksānti*), these constitute the three divisions of the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*);

the "middle patience" is not mentioned because its meaning is already included within the lower and upper. These six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are the seeds and causes for the marks and signs of physical excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).

The stage from the lower level of patience (*kṣānti*) up to ascending to the position of the future Buddha and sitting at the site of enlightenment corresponds to the middle level of patience. One moment (*kṣaṇa*) corresponds to the upper level of patience;
furthermore, in another moment, one enters the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*), giving rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*).
Through thirty-four moments of mind, one suddenly severs the fetters of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) along with their residual habits (*vāsanā*), attaining *sambodhi*.
II. The Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).

Regarding the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching, this refers to the ten stages common to the three vehicles (*triyāna*). First, the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*): while its phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) share names with those of the Tripitaka teaching, its contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) and mental state (*citta*) are distinct.

It takes the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) as its substance, viewing them as like illusions and transformations; it comprehensively destroys the eight inversions (*aṣṭa-viparyāsa*) of views and attachments. This is called... [the Stage of Dry Wisdom].

The foundation of mindfulness of the body; the foundations of mindfulness of mind, sensation, and phenomena are likewise. Abiding in this contemplation, one cultivates right effort, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and the factors of enlightenment and the path.

Although one has not yet attained the "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) dharma—the water-like stage that accords with the principle—because the wisdom of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is profound and sharp, it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavipaśyanā-bhūmi*).
Second, the Stage of Nature (*gotra-bhūmi*): having passed beyond the Stage of Dry Wisdom and attained the warmth dharma, one is able to advance in the initial [stages].

The subsequent mind, from the entry into the stage of the Peak (*mūrdhan*) up to the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), is all termed the "Stage of Nature" (*dharmatā-bhūmi*). Because one attains the water of the untainted nature (*anāsrava-dharmatā*), it is called the "Stage of Nature."

*Fayi*: "The names are identical, but the observations differ, because their substances are analyzed separately. Since substance and form are identical with emptiness, the five aggregates (*skandha*), eighteen realms (*dhātu*), and six bases (*āyatana*) are all like illusions and transformations.

Regarding the general refutation: this is contrasted with the specific refutations that follow. "Views and attachments" refers to the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* and *vitarka-saṃyojana*).
These two delusions together comprise the eight inversions (*viparyāsa*), all of which are generally refuted here. Thus, the eight inversions do not arise.

This is the correct practice of the four foundations of mindfulness; therefore, it is said that one dwells within this contemplation. From this, one fully cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that assist the path.

This constitutes having already perfected wisdom, yet one has not yet entered the waters of the principle of nature (dharmatā). Possessing wisdom alone while lacking its realization is called the "Stage of Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*).
It is like a dragon that has already mastered the power of transformation but has not yet mounted the clouds and rain, remaining still upon the earth. For this reason—

The aforementioned is designated as the stage of the outer ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*). It corresponds to the five meditative cessations (*pañca-sthāpana*) and the general and specific [contemplations] of the Tripitaka teachings. Progressing from this, one enters the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).

By practicing with unceasing diligence, one attains entry into the water of the untainted nature (*anāsrava-dhātu*); therefore, it is called the "Stage of Nature" (*dharmatā-bhūmi*). From the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) up to the "First Dharma" (*prathama-dharma*), all belong to the Stage of Nature, differing only in their degree of depth.
The aforementioned is designated as the stage of the inner ordinary person (*adhyātma-pṛthagjana*). This corresponds to the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*) of the Tripitaka teachings.

Furthermore, regarding the "Stage of the Eight Persons" (aṣṭamaka-bhūmi): those of the three vehicles who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) or follow by dharma (dharmānusārin), whose realization of the body [of reality] and vision gives rise to the conventional and eliminates delusions, are within the *anantarya-samādhi*.
When they possess the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) in full but lack one part of the wisdoms (*jñāna*), it is called the Stage of the Eight Persons. Fourth is the Stage of Vision (darśana-bhūmi).

Those [of the three vehicles] equally perceive the principle of the first meaning—the non-arising of the Four Noble Truths—and equally sever the delusions of view, exhausting all eighty-eight *kleśas*.

The fifth stage, the Stage of Thinning (*tanubhūmi*): the provisional manifestation of the essence-love becomes true; one severs the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and realizes the sixth liberation.

Thus, the afflictions are thinned. The sixth stage, the Stage of Freedom from Desire (*vītarāgabhūmi*): for those of the three vehicles, the provisional manifestation of the essence-love is immediately the truth; one severs the [afflictions] of the desire realm...

The five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*) are the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), and ill-will (*vyāpāda*); therefore, it is called the stage of detachment from desire (*vītarāga-bhūmi*). Regarding the seven stages of those who have already accomplished their task (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*):

for those of the three vehicles, by realizing the essence of form and the formless realms as emptiness, they give rise to the outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) to sever the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*).

Having exhausted the seventy-two types of defilements—namely, restlessness (*auddhatya*), conceit (*māna*), ignorance (*moha*), attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*), and attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*)—they reach the ultimate end of all phenomenal delusions within the three realms. Thus [it is so called].
This refers to the Stage of Having Accomplished [the Path] (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*).
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden) states: "Person" (*pudgala*) means patience (*kṣānti*). The "Eight Persons" are the eight patiences.

"Realizing the conventional and giving rise to the ultimate" means that by realizing the emptiness of the conventional, one gives rise to the ultimate truth. Regarding the "uninterrupted samādhi": this pertains to the second and third stages.
The initial and final portions of the abandonment of views are difficult to separate, as the two stages are interconnected; thus, it is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*).

Regarding the categories and methods of abandonment through patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), each has eight divisions. Now, while patience is complete, knowledge is deficient; therefore, knowledge lacks one portion.

The "Stage of the Eight Patiences" (*aṣṭakṣānti-bhūmi*) is a single name. The "Stage of Seeing" (*darśana-bhūmi*) encompasses the preceding stage of the eight persons; when the eighty-eight delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are exhausted, it is called the Stage of Seeing.

This corresponds to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) of the Tripiṭaka Teachings (*āgama*). The "Thin Stage" (*tanu-bhūmi*) refers to realizing that the essence of craving is empty and thereby giving rise to the truth;

by severing six grades of the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*), it corresponds to the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*) of the Tripiṭaka Teachings. The "Stage of Freedom from Desire" (*vītarāga-bhūmi*) refers to the essence of the desire realm...
Sensation is itself reality. Because one has severed the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) and the ninety grades of afflictions of thought, it is called "detachment from desire.

This corresponds to the third fruit of the Hīnayāna teachings. As for the "Stage of Having Accomplished What Was to Be Done" (*kṛtāvibhūmi*): its essence is that the craving for the realms of form and formlessness is itself reality.

One severs the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) and the seventy-two grades of afflictions; here, the delusions of views and thought are utterly exhausted. That which was to be done has been accomplished, and there is nothing more to do.
The stage of having already accomplished [the elimination of] afflictions (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*) corresponds to the four fruits of the Tripiṭaka teachings.

Regarding the eighth, the stage of the *pratyekabuddha*: because the power of the true, untainted merit produced by the *pratyekabuddha* is great, they are able to eliminate habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Regarding the ninth, the stage of the *bodhisattva*: entering the provisional from emptiness, the contemplation of the path and the contemplation of phenomena flow together; they deeply contemplate the two truths and proceed to sever [afflictions].
Regarding habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*): when form and mind are devoid of cognition, one attains the Dharma-eye and the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*).

One sports with the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), purifies Buddha-lands, brings sentient beings to maturity, and studies the ten powers (*daśabala*) and four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*) of a Buddha; at this point, the habitual tendencies are about to be exhausted.

As for the ten Buddha-stages (*daśa-buddhabhūmi*): through the power of great merit, one provides sustenance for wisdom, and in a single thought-moment of corresponding insight, one contemplates the ultimate truth to its final conclusion.

Habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are likewise exhausted without remainder, like wood consumed by the kalpa-fire, leaving no ash or charcoal behind; or like a fragrant elephant crossing a river, reaching its very bottom and far shore.
