Furthermore, it is like a sword, a caustic solution, feet, or a bridge. If the mind itself were the precept, why would one need to state that it has no form, color, or tactile contact?

Therefore, we know that there exists separately an "unmanifest" (avijñapti) capable of upholding the mind that intends to keep the precepts, which constitutes true precept. This is the Noble Practice.

In the *Śālistamba-sūtra*, it does not state that one contemplates and analyzes the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*); rather, it directly mentions matter and mind because these are easier to contemplate.
Nor does it say that the unconditioned does not exist. While the Hīnayāna speaks of the four fruits of the path, the Mahāyāna opens this up as a provisional teaching (*upāya-dharma*).

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* explains the dharmas of ordinary beings; Guṇavarman clarifies that they do not truly exist. Furthermore, there is no Mahāyāna sūtra that opens up the unconditioned as being merely provisional. Moreover...

That the nature of stubbornness (*dausthulya*) serves as the cause for Buddhahood is not inherently contradictory; it is analogous to how impermanent virtue also serves as the cause for permanent virtue.

This clarifies that the Mahāyāna possesses "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) [virtue]. Regarding the claim that the precepts are material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), although the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* raises this point...

Regarding "mental factors" (*caitta*): since the mind (*citta*) is directed toward material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), it is said that what is neither matter nor mind, as well as the mental factors, are both currently indeterminate.
Why is this? That which is neither matter nor mind still belongs to the Hīnayāna; the mental factors themselves belong to the school of mental factors. Now, however, we are in the Mahāyāna.
What concern do the mental factors have with that which is feared to reside within matter? Indeed, in the Mahāyāna, it is taught that the precepts are material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*).

It is not said that the precepts are merely numerical phenomena (*saṃkhyā-dharma*). As for the statement that "the words are the same but the minds differ": even if the Mahāyāna were to speak of them as numbers, what harm would there be in the minds being different?
How much more so when the Mahāyāna itself clarifies that the precepts are an aggregate of matter (*rūpa-skandha*)?

Regarding the mirror: it is a metaphor for how an image arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions. An image does not arise without a cause; the precepts are likewise. They must necessarily depend on...

If there is "active" (kṛta) karma, then "unmanifest" (avijñapti) karma is clearly established. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* first states that neither sin nor non-sin can be apprehended, which seems to suggest there is no unmanifest karma;
yet it later states that one receives the cessation of evil dharmas through mind and speech, whereby the mind and speech become the agents of upholding.
When the cessation of unwholesome dharmas is maintained, how could there not be non-action (*avijñapti*)? Regarding those who are inferior, weak, or superior:

in the case of one who violates the precepts, the offense committed may be small while the mind capable of committing it is great; thus, if one commits a minor precept with a heavy mind, the offense is grave, whereas if one commits a major precept with a light mind, the offense is light.
Furthermore, one may relinquish the precepts but not the great vow; even if one breaks the precepts...
Those who destroy right view will ultimately attain restoration to purity.
That which is without contact is not like the categories of eye-and-form, ear-and-sound, and so forth. Nevertheless, people still gaze upon the formless and listen to the soundless.

If one skillfully cultivates expedient means (*upāya*), how could one not cause the essence of the precepts (*śīla-ātman*) to be fully perfected? Consider, for example, the various metaphors in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
a sword can sever things; lye can thereby wash away filth; feet rely upon them to travel; and bridges enable one to cross over.
Even worldly affairs depend upon expedient means; why should the essence of the precepts alone be no different? How could it be otherwise?

There is no such thing as "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*). As for why the "Chapter on the Holy Practices" (*Āryacaryā-parivarta*) and the "Chapter on King Ajātaśatru" do not speak of the contemplation and analysis of the unconditioned, it is merely because they mention those aspects of form and mind that are easy to contemplate;

it does not mean that the unconditioned does not exist. Regarding the "provisional dharmas of the four fruits," this means that in the Mahāyāna, the opening up of the four fruits is considered provisional.
Therefore, Guṇavarman said that they do not truly exist. Furthermore, how could there be an opening [of what does not exist]?
Is non-action (anabhisamskāra) not the principle of skillful means? Regarding "insentient things as the cause for Buddhahood":

if one says that impermanent goodness can serve as the cause for permanent goodness, then it would follow that material dharmas (*rūpadharma*), being insentient, could also serve as the cause for Buddhahood—what obstacle would there be to this?
III. Resolving the Controversy Regarding the Term "Non-existence" (wu).

Now, regarding these two interpretations, which have been subjects of debate since ancient times: the interpretation that [the term] "non-existence" (wu) does not exist [in the original] accords perfectly with the principle, yet it is difficult to reconcile with the text; whereas the interpretation that [the term] "existence" (you) exists [in the original] is more readily acceptable.

In principle, this is difficult to determine; in terms of the textual record, it is extremely convenient. Since both have textual authority, which one accords with principle? Now, principle is neither "appropriate" nor "inappropriate";
whether one takes it as appropriate or inappropriate, both are permissible. When discussing the meaning of the principles and the teachings:

if one says they do not exist, that is appropriate to the principle; if one says they do exist, that is appropriate to the teaching. Principle is the reality (*tattva*); the teaching is the expedient (*upāya*). As for the reality...
Although it does not [exist as a substantial entity], it exists within the gates of the teaching (*śāsana*).

That which is employed here is the "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*). *Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): This passage definitively distinguishes and settles the debate, determining that the unmanifest must necessarily exist. As for "principle" (*li*), it transcends emotion and is free from views;

thus, there is no "is-ness" (*asti*) within principle, and so it is not "appropriate" (*yuan*). Since there is no "non-is-ness" (*nāsti*) within principle, it is not "inappropriate. It may be appropriate, yet it is also without appropriateness.

This is also acceptable; therefore, it is said that "both are attained. Since this is the principle (*li*), when one speaks solely of principle, existence and non-existence are not subjects for discussion.

When one speaks of both principle and teaching (*jiao*), "non-existence" accords with principle, while "existence" accords with teaching. Principle is unconditioned (*wuwei*), whereas teaching has traces.

In reality, one must rely upon the provisional (*quan*) to practice, and the ultimate (*wu*) must manifest by means of the conventional (*you*). To propagate the Dharma and benefit [sentient beings]...
To manifest the Way and transform sentient beings, how could one simply end with non-existence? Therefore, what is employed now is "non-action" (anabhisaṃskāra) that is nonetheless "existent.
It is not a case of non-existence being non-action. Question: Since it is already non-action, why speak further of existence?

If there is an existent non-action, does it not become identical to action? Answer: Although the mind is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and the precepts are formless, yet by means of this unconditioned mind—

One receives the precept of non-manifestation (*avijñapti*); how could it be said that this does not exist? However, as previously stated, once such an action is performed, there arises non-manifestation;
thus, after the single act has been done, one spontaneously ceases from evil and spontaneously maintains goodness, and merit naturally increases.
Non-action is action; action is truly non-action.

Furthermore, regarding the "concomitant with the path" (*mārga-sahagata*) non-informative action (*avijñapti*): it refers to the non-informative action generated within the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), which arises together with the superior path of the mind;
therefore, it is called "concomitant with the path. Master Zhi Guan explains that not all non-informative action generated by the Path of Seeing constitutes the "precept concomitant with the path.

Rather, one takes only that non-informative action generated within the mind of the Middle Way’s correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) as such, because it possesses the sense of preventing what is improper and ceasing evil.
It is called "concomitant with the Path" (*mārga-sahaja*). The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "First is the dharma-precept of the mind; second is the precept received through worldly instruction.

When a Bodhisattva attains the dharma-precept of the mind, it is called the precept concomitant with the Path. One who attains this precept never commits evil; because it is not received from a teacher, it is termed "attained.
This precept is generated and attained within the mind of the Middle Way. As for the precept received through worldly instruction, it refers to the formal ritual of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

It is only later that one attains it; this necessarily relies upon a teacher, and is therefore termed "receiving" (upasaṃpad). As for the distinctions regarding its manifestation, it is called "worldly instruction" (laukika-śāsana).

The concentration-concomitant (samādhi-saṃvara) path is common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles. Regarding the Mahāyāna path, concentration is subsumed within the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas). Some masters state:

Only by entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) can one give rise to non-informative action (*avijñapti*). Within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), meditative concentration does not give rise to non-informative action.

Only by relying on the understanding of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) can one give rise to non-informative action. Some say that as long as one realizes this path of concentration, and according to one's ability suppresses coarse categories [of afflictions], one then gives rise to non-informative action;
thus, even within the realm of desire, prior to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one is able to give rise to the precepts.

*Fayi*: Regarding "concomitant with meditative concentration" (*samādhi-sahagata*): because one enters meditative concentration, this unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*) arises simultaneously with the mental state of tranquil dhyāna.

Regarding "concomitant with the Path" (*mārga-sahagata*): because one realizes the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), this unmanifest precept arises simultaneously with the mental state of wisdom (*prajñā*).
The phrase "not necessarily upon seeing the Path" means that it does not necessarily refer to the unmanifest precept produced by the Path of Seeing.

The practice of the method is called "concomitant with the Path" (*mārga-sahagata*). However, when the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) arises from the contemplation of the mind through the Middle Way, it is simply termed "concomitant with the Path.
This is because, although one has not yet seen the Path while practicing the preparatory contemplation, the mind is focused upon the Path, and thus the Path is present therein.

Within correct contemplation, being neither separated from nor attached to evil is precisely what is meant by "concomitant with the Path. It is like an archer who, though not yet hitting the bullseye, [is already practicing the art].

The focus of the mind is precisely on this; it is precisely here that it resides. It is just like this. Nevertheless, between the two—[the dharma-consecrated (*dharmasamvṛta*) and the path-consecrated (*mārgasamvṛta*)]—the path-consecrated is superior.
Therefore, when weighing the mental factors against worldly teachings, the path-consecrated is categorized as belonging to the mental factors.

However, for one who realizes this concentration of the Path, it is said that based on what precedes it, the beginning of the non-informative (*avijñapti*) arises in the higher realms, whereas it cannot arise in the desire realm.
Some say that one must first attain the understanding of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) before the non-informative (*avijñapti*) can arise; without such understanding, it cannot.

Others say that merely realizing this meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the path (*mārga*) together is sufficient to suppress the coarse categories [of afflictions] and achieve [the state], whereby the non-informative arises.

Within the realm of the desire-dhyāna (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*) and prior to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), what obstacle could there be? Why must it necessarily wait for the higher dhyānas and the understanding of emptiness before arising?
According to the sūtras, there are eight recollections (*aṣṭānusmṛti*). The first recollection is of the Triple Gem; the fourth is of the precepts (*śīla*).

Commentators explain that "precepts" refers to the *saṃvara* (restraint), the *samādhi-sahaja* (concomitant with concentration), and the *mārga-sahaja* (concomitant with the Path). Restraint purifies body and speech; concentration obstructs the afflictions (*kleśa*);
and the Path destroys ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, the precepts encompass both concentration and wisdom; by training in one, one obtains all three. The significance of the precepts is truly great.
V. On the Flourishing and Decline of the Precepts.
Initially, when one seeks to receive the bodhisattva vows through skillful means, their substance flourishes.

However, if one abandons the aspiration for enlightenment, or if one commits the ten grave offenses due to predominant afflictions, their substance declines. If neither of these two conditions occurs, they remain until Buddhahood, at which point they naturally cease. This is certain.

Regarding the two types of precepts: when one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or the Path (*mārga*), these serve as the cause. At the first moment of concentration or the Path, the precepts have not yet arisen together with them;
rather, it is the perfection of the preceding mental state that serves as the cause. It is only at the second moment of mind that the precepts arise together with it; at that time, they truly emerge.

When emerging from concentration or the Path, at the very last moment, they are immediately abandoned. As for the phrase "entering concentration or entering the Path," it refers to the time when the precepts arise together with the mind. At that time—

It is called "arising. When one emerges from meditative absorption or the Path, the precepts and the intentional mind both cease together; at that time, it is called "ceasing. Both are said to be "co-arising with the mind.

Once the three [types of] precepts have been once generated, they are constantly present during entry into and emergence from [meditation]. Later, when entering superior absorptions or the superior Path, they follow along with the name of the superior restraint (*saṃvara*);

at that time, they are constantly arising. When one withdraws from absorption or the Path, the three collections [of precepts] last for the duration of one's life; for a Bodhisattva, this continues until reaching enlightenment.

[The term] "Ti" [indicates that] at that time, it is immediately suspended. The gathering of wholesome qualities and the gathering of living beings are identical to the *vinaya* (precepts); they arise according to their reception and are suspended due to two conditions.
[From] *Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden):

Based on the preceding discussion that the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*) consists of non-manifest action (*avijñapti*), yet possesses states of arising and suspension, there are many such matters. When seeking to receive [the precepts],...

When [the meditative state] arises, the transgression is abandoned; thus it ceases. This is the primary principle regarding the arising and ceasing of the essence of the restraint of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*).

If we discuss the two restraints of the Path and Meditative Concentration (*mārga* and *samādhi*) based on this: after attaining concentration or the Path, both restraints are said to "arise. After emerging from concentration or the Path, it is not the case that both are said to "cease.

This is because their arising is difficult and their ceasing is difficult; thus, arising and ceasing are discussed in terms of this difficulty. Regarding the mind of the restraint that enters concentration or the Path...

To say that both are called "arising," yet when one emerges from meditative absorption (*samādhi*) or the path of cultivation (*mārga-śīla*), the mind immediately ceases and is thus called "declining"—this is a discussion of arising and declining based on what is easily aroused and easily abandoned.
However, once it has been initiated, it is constantly present whether entering or emerging; as it is when entering the path of absorption, so it is when emerging from the path of absorption.
In the interim, there is no further cause for decline, and one certainly does not retreat from the path of absorption or the [path of] sound.

"Throughout one's entire life" means that after a bodhisattva has attained Buddhahood, [the precepts] may be suspended; this refers to the discourse on their constant arising and rare suspension regarding their arising and ceasing.

Furthermore, above we have merely cited the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint); if it concerns the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering wholesome dharmas) or the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings), the principles of their arising and ceasing are the same as this example.
As previously stated, they arise when one seeks to receive them, and they cease due to the two conditions of abandoning or violating them. Regarding the two characters for "cause" (*hetu*), above...
It is said that concentration and the path serve as the causes for morality. To clarify why they serve as the causes for morality:
because the initial moment of cessation is concentration and the path, yet it has not yet conjoined with morality; since we are referring here to that initial moment, it is called the "cause."
○ Six: The Three Aggregates.
Next, regarding the essence of the three aggregates of precepts: *Vinaya* (discipline) refers to the rules and regulations of the Dharma that guide the practitioner and cause them to enter the Path.
It is also said: *Vinaya* means "to level" (*liè*). Just as a worldly horse-race track (*liè*) is used to make a horse well-trained and straight, so too is *vinaya*; it disciplines [the mind].
The practitioner of straightforward conduct does not allow evil to arise. The vow of the Mahāsattva does not exceed the cessation of evil and the promotion of good.

If one does not move body or speech, this is the cessation of evil and the arousal of the precepts (*śīla*). To prevent movement and maintain stillness is the *saṃvara-śīla* (the morality of restraint). If one should move body or speech, this is the promotion of good.

Now, by arousing these precepts and preventing that which would remain unmoving, one gathers what is wholesome and gathers sentient beings; this is [the morality of gathering wholesome dharmas and benefiting sentient beings].

One should engage in activities that involve movement; therefore, [the path] is opened into two. Taking up the encouragement of various virtues, one relies on the gateway of the Six Perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) and is called "cultivating wholesome dharmas" (*kuśaladharma*).
Arising with a mind that encompasses all beings, one relies on the gateway of the Four Great Vows and is called "gathering in sentient beings. This is precisely movement for the sake of others:

transforming sentient beings below, cultivating myriad virtues in the middle, and returning to the fruit of Buddhahood above. The Vinaya discipline primarily governs internal virtue, while gathering in beings pertains to the external.
[The text] explains: "Transformation" encompasses both internal and external virtues; therefore, the three clusters of precepts (*tri-saṃvara-śīla*) are established.

[The *Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden) states: Following the preceding discussion on the non-manifested essence of the precepts (*avijñapti-śīla-tattva*), we now precisely clarify the dharma of the three clusters of precepts.

Herein, "that which is immovable should be moved" refers to cessation (*śamatha*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*). As for "horse track" (*mala*): a short, level enclosure for horses is called a *mala*, as in the Vinaya.
It means to guard the body and mind, ensuring that one does not become negligent. The *Fengsu tong* states: "Yù Shùn created the *lǜ* (vinaya).

*Lǜ* is explained as *xuán* (explanation); *xuán* means the law. The *Guxiang* says: "*Lǜ* is *xuán*; it explains and weighs matters such as lightness or gravity, transgression or non-transgression, and so forth, just like secular laws.
Regarding "preventing movement and non-movement," this means preventing movement so that one remains unmoving. This is the *lǜyí* (prātimokṣa/vinaya discipline).

The Master ceases evil; therefore, he is called "Immovable. If he were to gather virtue or gather sentient beings, he would have to be "moved" in one sense because he would be exhorting all manner of goodness, and in another sense because he would have to arouse the mind to encompass others. Now, encompassing others constitutes transformation from below, while exhorting goodness constitutes cultivation from within.
When all evils are purified and exhausted, how could this not lead upward to the fruit of Buddhahood? Gathering virtue encompasses both the internal and the external.
This means: internally cultivating oneself well, and externally guiding others well.
○ Second, explaining the practice of cessation (four parts): first, good and evil; second, the Way and concentration; third, small and great; fourth, the detailed analysis.
First, good and evil are discussed;
next, the two types of goodness—cessation (*śamatha*) and practice (*bhāvanā*)—are treated, as in the *Śata-śāstra*. To cease evil and refrain from committing it is called cessation;

to believe, accept, and cultivate [the good] is called practice. Although the Buddha’s teachings are manifold, they are fully encompassed by cessation and practice. "Commit no evil" is the admonition.
This is the "Gate. That the multitude practices it is the "Gate of Exhortation. The meaning of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) encompasses both good and evil.

The non-action of good and evil subsumes the meanings of cessation (*śamatha*) and practice (*prayoga*). Now, we first clarify the good. In the case of good precepts, it is simply the non-arising [of evil].

If they do arise, they then strike down evil; all of this is the meaning of cessation. All possess progression; all are the meaning of practice. Depending on their relative strength or weakness, there is thus the distinction between cessation and practice.

The non-manifestation (*avijñapti*) that arises from the intention to cease evil is the non-manifestation of abstaining from unwholesome conduct. The non-manifestation that arises from the intention to cultivate wholesome conduct is the non-manifestation of performing wholesome conduct.

For example, constructing wells or bridges, or prostrating to the Buddha and practicing giving, constitutes the non-manifestation of wholesome conduct. Conversely, constructing nets for fishing or hunting constitutes the non-manifestation of unwholesome conduct.

*Fayi*: Ceasing evil and practicing good are the primary principles of the precepts. However, the meaning of "non-action" (*wu zuo*) encompasses both good and evil; for both good and evil, there are respectively the principles of cessation and practice.

Speaking in terms of the good, as for the essence of the good precepts: if they do not arise, that is one matter; once they arise, they immediately strike down [the seeds of] evil destinies and cultivate goodness.
Within this goodness, there are the two meanings of cessation and practice. By analogy, striking down [the seeds of] good destinies and cultivating evil is considered "evil."

This refers to the two meanings of "cessation" (*saṃvara*) and "action" (*pravṛtti*). The reason for this is as follows: when the wholesome is strong and the unwholesome is weak, one practices the wholesome and ceases the unwholesome;

when the unwholesome is strong and the wholesome is weak, one ceases the wholesome and practices the unwholesome. Such is the nature of their respective forces. Consequently, there is a distinction between the cessation and practice of the wholesome and the unwholesome.

The non-action (*akriyā*) of ceasing evil and the non-action of cultivating goodness are precisely the correct practice of the wholesome. As for the cessation and practice of evil: [...]* *Note: The original text appears to be an excerpt from a commentary on Buddhist ethics, likely discussing the dynamics of moral cultivation.*
The above examples illustrate this. Regarding bridges, fishing, and hunting, I have cited one or two instances to exemplify the rest.
○ Second, the determination of the path (*mārga-viniścaya*).

The determination of the path consists of two types of non-action (*avijñapti*): that which involves activity and that which involves cessation. Of these two aspects of the determination of the path, the precepts (*śīla*) are judged by their meaning to belong to the category of cessation. The determination of the path consists of two... [text ends]

The mind is defined in meaning as "activity" (*caryā*). When seeking ceases from conditions, "non-action" (*avijñapti*) arises; following the cessation of conditions through tranquility (*śamatha*), non-action arises—this is the goodness of tranquility.
Following the cessation of conditions through activity (*caryā*), non-action arises—this is called the goodness of activity.

Furthermore, the gate of admonition is the goodness of tranquility, while the gate of encouragement belongs entirely to the goodness of activity. Moreover, it is explained that activity is exclusively "action" (*vijñapti*), whereas tranquility is exclusively "non-action. It is further said: "Tranquility..."
"Both types of wholesome conduct possess non-informative action (*avijñapti*). [This] reveals the hidden meaning.

This passage states that the path (*mārga*) definitely possesses both the meanings of cessation (*śamatha*) and practice (*pratipatti*). Precepts are categorized as cessation because they are capable of restraint;
the mind is categorized as practice because it is capable of application. "To investigate" means to thoroughly examine. One thoroughly examines on what conditions this non-informative action arises.
After cessation (*śamatha*), there arises that which is born; there is no agent. When evil is exhausted, the unmoving essence is revealed.
After cultivation (*vipaśyanā*), there arises that which is born; there is no agent. When goodness reaches its ultimate limit, the Way of non-action (*wuwei*) is perfected.

To say that cultivation is solely "action" while cessation is solely "non-action" is a distinct interpretation; it is not the fundamental meaning of "non-action. Both cessation and cultivation possess it.
"Non-action. This further clarifies that the aforementioned meaning is the correct one.
III. Small and Great:

The precepts of the seven assemblies of Śrāvakas all constitute the substance of the restraint-precept (*saṃvara-śīla*); they merely cease the two evils of body and speech. The Bodhisattva restraint...

The ritual observances fully guard the three karmas. This is further extended up to the Buddha, differing only in length, brevity, breadth, and narrowness. The principle of non-action (*avijñapti*) arises from conditions:
it is produced by a superior mind, but not by an inferior one. A neutral (*avyākṛta*) mind is too weak to produce non-action.

For example, in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) of the desire realm, there are nine grades of afflictions; the first six grades produce non-action, while the final three do not. Therefore, it is said: "This..."

The Sakṛdāgāmin manifests the non-active (anabhisaṃskāra) informative [action]; the Anāgāmin manifests the unwholesome (akuśala) informative action; the Arhat manifests the neutral (avyākṛta) informative action.
This statement refers to the two meanings of "stopping" (śamatha) and "practice" (vipaśyanā) regarding the small and the great.

The body and speech of the Śrāvaka possess stopping but lack practice; at best, they only realize the small fruit. The three karmas of the Bodhisattva are fully equipped with both stopping and practice, extending even to...
The Buddha Vehicle. This refers to the differences in length, breadth, and narrowness between the precepts of the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas.

Those who give rise to this unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) superior mind do so because their aspirations are lofty and excellent, and their wisdom and understanding are sharp and clear. Those of inferior capacity do not give rise to it because they are weak.
Those who are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) do not give rise to it because they are dull. [This applies to] the first six grades of afflictions of desire within the realm of desire.
"Arising" refers to the upper and middle grades of afflictions. When afflictions are strong, the mind that cuts them off is fierce;
it is like elite troops fighting a powerful enemy, which must achieve great victory. Therefore, there is no "arising" [of the path] for these. The latter three grades belong to the lower afflictions.
When afflictions are subtle, the mind that cuts them off is weak; it is like Tian Dan being unable to subdue the city of Di, or the descendants of Shendiao being unable [to overcome their enemies].
To take Hebei by means of the whole world is precisely what this refers to. Regarding the three fruits [of the path]:

some say that the *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner) has already severed the final three grades of delusion and thus transcends the stage of non-action (*avijñapti*). As for the *anāgāmin* (non-returner) and the *arhat*, they transcend it even further.
According to the textual context, the arising of non-action should occur at the first fruit. Others say that the *sakṛdāgāmin* does not give rise to non-action; later...
The two fruits also arise. While this appears to be consistent with the literal text, it does not accord with the underlying principle.
○ Fourth, the fourfold analysis:

regarding the unmanifest (avijñapti) of good and evil, when discussed in relation to the mind, there are four propositions for each. As for the four propositions of the good: first, that which is precept but not...
1. Non-manifest (avijñapti) that is cessation through the mind’s restraint from evil; this is called *śīla* (precept). 2. Non-manifest that is not *śīla*;

this refers to such acts as digging wells or building bridges, which produce non-manifest karma according to the specific action and its utility, yet cannot restrain evil and are therefore not *śīla*. 3. That which is both *śīla* and non-manifest;
this refers to virtuous restraints (*kuśala-saṃvara*) and the like. 4. That which is neither *śīla* nor non-manifest; this refers to other virtuous states of mind.

Furthermore, there are four propositions regarding unwholesome [actions]. First, that which is a precept but not non-informative (*avijñapti*); this refers to the intention to desist from evil. Second, that which is non-informative but not a precept;

this refers to acts such as killing or stealing, which involve non-informative action according to their application. Third, that which is both a precept and non-informative; this refers to the unwholesome vows (*akuśala-saṃvara*) and so forth.
Fourth, that which is neither a precept nor non-informative; this refers to other unwholesome mental states. There are two types of unwholesome precepts: first, the ten...
The six types of bad discipline (*akuśala-saṃvara*): second, the bad discipline of the heterodox precepts of external paths (*tīrthika-mithyā-śīla*).

As stated in the *Mahā-sūtra*, there are ninety-five kinds of heterodox bad precepts, each with its own system of rules; some take asceticism as their precept, such as keeping cattle, horses, and so forth, serving fire, or inhaling wind.
Constantly standing on one leg, leaping into fire, throwing oneself off cliffs, and so forth—taking these as precepts constitutes heterodox discipline (*mithyā-śīla*).
Whether the mental application is long or short, all such acts are evil discipline (*pāpa-śīla*).
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden). Above, it was clarified that precepts possess non-manifestation (*avijñapti*). Now, the two characteristics of precepts and non-manifestation are distinguished;

each is divided into four propositions based on their being either wholesome or unwholesome. Regarding the four wholesome propositions: this is because the cessation of unwholesome conduct constitutes the precept.
To perform good deeds without any expectation of reward is "non-action" (*anabhisamskāra*). Therefore, the first two phrases each emphasize one of these two aspects.

The third phrase, "virtuous discipline" (*kuśala-saṃvara*), refers to the temporary cessation of evil and the spontaneous engagement in goodness. The fourth phrase refers to other scattered wholesome states of mind;

since these are neither primarily focused on the cessation of evil nor are they wholesome acts performed without expectation, they are excluded from the fourfold classification. (End of section on the four types of evil).
Regarding the phrases: the first is defined as abstaining from performing wholesome deeds; the second is defined as committing evil without any sense of restraint or hesitation.

Thus, each of the first two phrases is dedicated exclusively to one of these aspects. As for the third phrase, "those with evil discipline" (*akuśala-saṃvara*), they both abstain from wholesome deeds and spontaneously engage in evil.
The fourth phrase refers to other distracted states of unwholesome mind; since these are neither focused nor primary in their abstention, they are excluded.
It is well. Furthermore, it is not a lack of moral restraint that constitutes evil. Regarding the sixteen types of evil disciplines (*akuśala-saṃvara*):
first, the butcher; second, the executioner; third, the rearer of pigs and sheep; fourth, the fisherman; fifth, the hunter; sixth, the bird-catcher using nets; seventh, the snake-catcher.
Eighth, raising chickens and dogs; ninth, exorcising dragons; tenth, committing robbery; eleventh, apprehending robbers; twelfth, serving as a jailer;
thirteenth, the house of a prostitute; fourteenth, the house of a wine-seller; fifteenth, the house of a dyer; sixteenth, the house of an oil-presser.
This is called manifesting evil, which people can easily perceive. As for the ninety-five kinds of heterodox practitioners and their deviant precepts:
some maintain the vows of oxen and horses because they consume water and grass; some maintain the vows of chickens and dogs because they delight in eating filth;
some serve fire, taking fire as their teacher, such as Kāśyapa who served the fire-dragon; some practice wind, inhaling external air; and some stand on one foot.

Because they consider themselves diligent, some scorch their bodies with the five heats or sit upon burning wood to burn their limbs, believing that by such suffering they will exhaust affliction and attain bliss.
Because they consider themselves to have cast off the defiled body and attained a pure body, some throw themselves from cliffs;
such practices as smearing oneself with ashes, lying on thorns, or going naked are too numerous to enumerate. Even in these latter days, there are those who observe water-fasts, claiming—
In order to wash away the five turbidities, some go hungry for seven days;

because they claim their four elements are empty and quiescent, others go barefoot in midwinter or carry their hair in a sack during the height of summer, claiming that cold and heat cannot invade them.

These are called "concealing evil"—they appear to be good but are actually evil, and are difficult for people to perceive. Regarding these two types of evil precepts, although the duration of their mental application may vary slightly...
Whether superior or inferior, all are termed "evil precepts.
III. Analysis (three points): First, one must have faith; second, one must be free from the three obstructions; third, there must be the conditions of person and dharma.
First, one must have faith.

Regarding faith, three types are briefly set forth according to the gateway of the Tripiṭaka: first, faith that causes and effects—whether good or evil—necessarily bring about their respective results;

second, faith that by contemplating the Truths one attains the Way, and that because one is capable of contemplating the Truths, one will certainly attain the Noble Path; third, faith that there exists the precepts.

Contemplating the Truths is the primary gateway for entering the Path. Relying upon the *Vaipulya* precepts, one should therefore be fully equipped with these three kinds of faith, further augmented by three more:
first, faith that the Buddha-nature exists within the mental consciousness of both oneself and others; second, faith that diligent practice of supreme goodness will inevitably yield its fruit.
The fruit obtained through the three kinds of faith is permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
[From] *Fayi* (Exposition of the Hidden): "To summon good fruits, one must contemplate the Truths and attain the Way; to contemplate the Truths and attain the Way, one must maintain the precepts.

Therefore, one should maintain the mind of faith through the precepts. Furthermore, the three kinds [of faith] are: first, faith that the fundamental nature is the Buddha; second, faith arising from the mind...
This is the Buddha; therefore, because the cause necessarily attains the fruit, one must have the threefold faith that the mind is the Buddha.
Because the fruit necessarily realizes Buddhahood, and without this correct faith precepts cannot be attained, it is said that one requires the mind of faith.

II. The Absence of the Three Obstructions (3). First, the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); second, the obstruction of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*); third, the obstruction of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the first, the obstruction of afflictions:
sentient beings have three kinds of obstructions. Because afflictions are ever-present, they are not designated as "obstructions."

*Fayi*: It is not said that [afflictions] constitute an obstruction because, although they are obstructions, they are not [ultimate] obstructions; this is because afflictions are ever-present within sentient beings.
The sky is constantly filled with clouds and mist, yet the realm of space remains unmoved; the sea is constantly filled with waves and billows, yet the nature of water remains unmoved;
humans are constantly possessed of afflictions, yet the essence of awakening remains unmoved. Thus we know that although afflictions are obstructions, their obstructive power...
Because they are minor, they are not said to constitute obstacles; this clarifies that the affliction-obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) does not obstruct the precepts.

Second, the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*). The obstacle of karma has both light and heavy degrees. Heavy karma obstructs the precepts in the sense of preventing the cause [of liberation]; this refers to the seven heinous acts (*saptānantarya*) and the ten grave offenses (*daśātyaya*). Manifestly...
If one possesses these in this life, they constitute an obstruction. In such cases, the previous body can no longer be known, as the events of a different lifetime are remote.

Regarding the seven heinous offenses (*ānantarya*): first, some say that through repentance they are extinguished and do not constitute an obstruction; second, others say that if even one is committed, whether repented or not, all are obstructions. Regarding the ten grave precepts (*daśa-guru-dharma*):

first, some say that the first four are natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) whose gravity is equal to the seven heinous offenses; thus, whether repented or not, they all constitute obstructions. As for the latter six, if repented, they are not [obstructions].

[The first view] holds that they are obstacles; if one does not repent, they constitute obstacles. The second [view] states that for the first four, repentance is required, whereas seeing the signs (*nimitta*) is not an obstacle; for the latter six, even if one does not repent, they do not constitute obstacles.
The third [view] states that if one does not repent, all ten grave offenses (*daśa-guru-dharma*) are obstacles; once repented, none of them are obstacles.
*Fayi*: Regarding "preventing the cause," this means that heavy karma obstructs the precepts; because they do not arise at the stage of the ground (*bhūmi*), one must prevent them.

Regarding "matters of distant lives," this explains the reason why one is unaware of previous existences. That one is unaware of previous existences manifests as an obstruction for the present existence.
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are, by their very nature, precepts; they are fundamental offenses, and are therefore called "inherent offenses" (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

These differ from the six [cases] below, where the Buddha’s prescription constitutes the precept itself. Some say that repentance is not an obstacle; some say that non-repentance is also not an obstacle;
some say that both repentance and non-repentance are obstacles; others say that non-repentance constitutes an obstacle while repentance is no longer an obstacle once it has occurred.
Though the expressions differ, each possesses its own specific meaning. As for what is called an "obstacle," it is intended to chill the gall of the indolent.

"Venerable suppression" (awe) has the meaning of subduing; saying that [anger] is not an obstacle serves to broaden the gateway for the transformation toward goodness. "Compassionate inclusion" has the meaning of gathering [beings] through kindness.
To discuss these comprehensively, the latter meaning is the correct one.
Third, the obstacle of retribution (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*).

Regarding the obstacle of retribution: those in the two realms of hell-beings and hungry ghosts are separated by their own heavy suffering; based on general precedent, they are not said to be [capable of] causes [for ordination].
Non-humans and animals, provided they can understand speech, are all able to receive the precepts. "Non-humans" refers to ghosts, spirits, and asuras.

Dragons are among the animals; humans include males, females, eunuchs, and those with dual sexual organs; and there are devas, from the six heavens of the desire realm up to the eighteen Brahma heavens—all these are said to be causes [for receiving the precepts].

Since those in the four formless attainments can also hear the Dharma, they too should be able to obtain the precepts; however, because their karmic retribution is subtle and ethereal, they are omitted here.

As for those in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, although they hold inverted attachments, if they were to turn their minds toward the good, they would also be able to obtain the precepts.

The Sūtras state that the three miserable realms (*durgati*), the long-lived heavens, and the borderlands (*pratyanta*) constitute "difficult places" (*kṛcchra-bhūmi*). This is based solely on the sense that one cannot cultivate the Path there. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā* states:

"When dragons and others receive the eightfold fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*), they merely obtain wholesome merit; it cannot be called 'fasting' (*upavāsa*). Now, following the text and inferring from the principle:

since the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*) are the root of the Bodhisattva precepts and do not specifically represent the Dharma of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the five precepts and the Bodhisattva... [text fragment]
Regarding the *śīla* of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), it is permitted that all four paths [of rebirth] may attain it; this applies from the eight precepts up to the full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Since these constitute the outward manifestation of the settled majestic demeanor of one who has left the household life, they can only be induced among humans in the three continents; for the other paths, none are suitable causes.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, even dragons can obtain the eightfold fast-day precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-śīla*).

*Fayi*: This clarifies that among the obstacles to retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*), only those of the hells and hungry ghosts constitute such obstacles; seeing others as such is not the case. The four formless heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*) are empty and subtle;

even if one were to come and receive birth there, one would have no awareness [of the Dharma]. Although the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is submerged [in ignorance], if one turns the mind [toward awakening], one may still attain it.

When the sutras do not permit long lifespans for the three miserable realms (*apāya*) and so forth, how could they truly mean to prohibit them? It is simply based on the fact that those beings are unable to cultivate the Path.
This is all that is being said. If one can give rise to the mind of practicing the Way, what obstacle could there be to obtaining the precepts?

Therefore, what is taught in that sutra is not the meaning of the present sutra. As for the claim that dragons and other beings cannot be called "observers of the fast" (zhāi), this is the position of the Sarvāstivādins; we now refute it.
It is said that the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*) is not uniform. There are those determined by manifest action (*vijñapti*), and those not determined by manifest action.

Regarding those determined by manifest action, they involve formal procedures and strict prohibitions; they are not conferred indiscriminately. Thus, according to the constant dharma of the Buddhas, the five precepts and the bodhisattva precepts are compatible with all four realms of existence.
The eight precepts and the bhikṣu discipline are permitted only among human beings. Since this present case pertains to the bodhisattva precepts, how is it so?
Dragons do not receive the precepts. A sutra states that there was once a garuḍa who entered the sea to seize a dragon but was unable to do so;

this is because the dragon had received the precepts—this is the proof thereof. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Five hundred merchants sailed across the ocean to gather treasures."
As they were about to enter the mouth of the King of Makara fish, they cried out in terror and called upon the Buddha, saying, "Namo Buddha.

This fish had previously received the Buddha’s precepts in a former life; it immediately repented and reproached itself, closing its mouth and ceasing to swallow them. Thus, the multitude was spared from the calamity.
Since the fish could recollect the precepts, how could the dragons not receive them? Furthermore, the *Sāgara-nāgarāja-sūtra* states: "Thereupon, the World-Honored One removed..."
The body-kāṣāya addressed the Dragon King, saying: "Distribute this kāṣāya among the various dragons.
Even those who receive but a single thread shall not be able to be harmed or touched by the Golden-Winged Bird King (Garuda). As the dragons divided the Buddha’s robe, they could never exhaust it.
All the dragons were greatly delighted and said with one voice: 'Today we respectfully accept the prohibitive precepts and shall forever protect the Buddha-Dharma. How so?"

A dragon cannot receive the full precepts; however, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites that a dragon may indeed receive the eightfold fast-precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*). This directly refutes the doctrine of the Sarvāstivāda school.

Bowl. He was granted the name Zhenbiao and soon thereafter developed the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Furthermore, the *Jiguinei fachen* (Account of the Inner Dharma Sent from Abroad) states:
"The nun Huimù’s mother was elderly and toothless; she would chew her food and feed it to him. Because her mouth was impure, he did not dare to receive the precepts.
Weeping bitterly day and night, he repented and begged for ordination. Suddenly, he saw that the ordination platform and the heavens were all golden in color. He raised his head—"
Looking upward, he saw a person to the south, whose robes were likewise golden. This person said to the wood, "I have already conferred the precepts upon you.
Considering these two instances, they are similar to the case of [the monk] Jin; in both, the utmost sincerity was able to evoke the precepts, rather than being a matter of mere coincidence.
People today, however, retreat at a single rebuke and turn their heads to walk away forever. How can they endure such a thing? To abandon them!
In seeking [the Dharma] with his own body, he severed his arm to find peace of mind. Looking back to the ancient style with far-reaching thought, how could one not shed tears of pain?
Is it not weighty that one has attained the precepts? When speaking of the eminent disciples of Hexi, Daolang was also a disciple of Tanwuchan;

this is just as Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra were called the World-Honored One’s disciples of divine power, or as Yan Hui and Zeng Shen were called the eminent disciples of the Confucian school. (Juzhi)
"Qu Mengxun" is the name of the King of Hexi. As for "Jing Huan," it was translated as "Hexi" (River West), yet his original title was Gaochang;
this is because Huan moved his seat to Gaochang and offered [the scriptures] from that land. As for "Xuan Chang," there is a separate version of Chang himself;
the current version is because it was produced by the Master Chen (Chanshi). "Jingzhu" has no [corresponding] production; perhaps it is a place name.
As for what is called the *Slightly Expanded Ground-Holding Sūtra* (*Dìchí jīng*), it is based on the original text of the *Ground-Holding Sūtra* while slightly expanding its wording.
○ Fifth, the *Maṇḍala-Necklace Original*:

the *Maṇḍala-Necklace Sūtra’s* Method for Receiving the Bodhisattva Precepts first involves prostrating to the Three Jewels of the three periods of time, followed by receiving the four unbreakable faiths.
I take refuge in the Buddha. I take refuge in the Dharma. I take refuge in the Sangha. (Recite three times. Next, repent of the ten evil deeds, the five heinous crimes, and so forth.
(Recite three times. Next, the ten grave precepts are proclaimed: one who violates them loses the forty-two dharmas of the worthy and holy ones. Question: Are you able to uphold them?
Answer: "I am able. Thereupon, the Three Refuges are formally administered. The ten heavy precepts mentioned previously are recited once more, followed by praises and the making of vows.

It is said that one who receives the Bodhisattva precepts shall transcend the four māras and overcome the suffering of the three realms; they shall never be lost throughout successive lifetimes and shall always follow the practitioner.

Until one attains Buddhahood, if one does not receive the precepts, one cannot be called a person of consciousness; such a person is no different from an animal. They are perpetually separated from the ocean of the Triple Gem and are not Bodhisattvas;
they are heterodox practitioners of false views who do not accord with human sentiment. Therefore, one should exhort and transform others to receive the precepts, for this brings great merit.
It is better to construct eighty-four thousand jeweled stupas than for one who possesses the precepts to violate them; it is better to have no precepts and not violate them.

If one receives them in the true presence of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, it is called the superior grade of precepts. If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there is no Dharma master within a thousand li, and one receives them by making a self-vow before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, it is called the inferior grade of precepts.

*Fayi*: Regarding the four māras—namely, the māra of desire, the māra of the body, the māra of death, and the celestial māra (devaputra-māra)—it is by relying on these precepts that one eternally severs desire.
Without desire, there is no body; without a body, there is no death. When these three are absent, Pāpīyān finds no opportunity.
This is what is meant by "transcending the four māras. As for "surpassing the three realms," some may doubt whether the goodness of the precepts merely leads to rebirth [within those realms].

O Celestial One, how could one suddenly transcend the three realms? As previously stated, the Bodhisattva’s Great Precepts encompass both meditative concentration and wisdom; by studying one, all three are attained.
By severing afflictions and shattering ignorance, why worry about being unable to transcend the three realms? Regarding the statement that "through successive births one does not lose them":
when the Great Precepts sustain the mind, past causes remain unobscured, and one constantly follows pure practitioners until cultivation reaches its consummation.

This is the stage of Buddhahood. Therefore, one should know that if practitioners of the path do not attain liberation in this present life, then in future lives within the ocean of birth and death, it is upon the precepts alone that they rely for maintaining the primary cause of leaving the household life and cultivating the sacred fruit of Bodhi.
How can the precepts be treated lightly? To say that one does not possess consciousness while claiming that even animals possess consciousness is [a contradiction].

Regarding the statement that they are no different from animals: it is precisely because they do not receive the Buddha’s precepts and are thus stubborn, ignorant, and lacking spiritual sensitivity, like animals who, though possessing consciousness, lack true awareness.
As for those who violate the precepts being superior to those who do not: this was because they previously received them;

now, having violated them, they recognize their transgression and thereby develop a sense of shame. For a brief moment, the holy teaching perfumes their minds, ultimately leading them toward virtuous action.
The seed of the Buddha. Indeed, how could receiving the precepts be a minor cause or condition? The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states:
"Although the son of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada received the precepts for the sake of five hundred pieces of gold, he nonetheless attained immeasurable merit."

How much more so for one who has personally attained a sincere mind for the sake of liberation: having precepts yet committing transgressions is superior to having no precepts at all and not committing them;
it cannot be called a fault. Nevertheless, this rhetorical exaggeration merely serves to emphasize that the precepts ought to be received.

To rely on these [precepts] while intentionally committing offenses, boasting of one's superiority over others, and being devoid of shame or remorse, is to become an object of derision for the world; such a person turns the finest essence of ghee (*sarpis*) into poison.
This is truly self-inflicted harm; why should the Buddha be blamed?
○ Sixth, the Newly Compiled Edition.
The Newly Compiled Edition was assembled by various masters of recent times and consists of eighteen sections. First, when the Master first entered...

First, one prostrates to the Buddha at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and takes a seat beside the Buddha. Second, the disciple enters the site of enlightenment, prostrates to the Buddha, and kneels with the right knee on the ground.
Third, the teacher holds the Three Jewels. Fourth, he causes [the disciple] to arouse the thought that the Three Jewels are as if present before their eyes.
Fifth, they repent of the ten unwholesome karmas. Sixth, they invite the various sages to serve as teachers. Seventh, they invite the teacher present before them.

Eighth, the teacher praises the disciple for being able to give rise to the supreme resolve (*adhyāśaya*). Ninth, the formal request for this precept. Tenth, the instruction to give rise to the bodhisattva mind (*bodhicitta*).
Eleventh, the inquiry regarding obstructing factors (consisting of fifteen questions). Twelfth, the mental visualization of attaining the precepts.

Thirteenth, the taking of an oath at the time of generating the precepts. Fourteenth, receiving the three refuges of a bodhisattva (also generating the precepts by means of the three refuges). Fifteenth...
5. The Preceptor rises and recites the *karmavācanā* (the formal act; it is also by this *karmavācanā* that the precept is generated). 16. The conclusion of the binding [of the precepts]. 17.

The Preceptor returns to his seat and exhorts [the candidate] to study. 18. He explains the characteristics of the ten grave offenses, summarizes them, offers praise, performs a prostration, and departs.
*Fayi*: To sit beside the Buddha means that one does not turn one’s back on the Buddha’s radiance.
○ Regarding the *Zhizhi ben*:
the *Zhizhi* ordination fully contains the methods for both lay and monastic practitioners; they are not listed here in detail.
*Fayi*: "The 'Imperial Decree' (*zhizhi*) refers to the purport of an imperial edict. It is the ritual law established by the King so that the fourfold assembly may all receive the precepts;
it is like the present-day Wanshan Precept Platform (*jietan*). Thus one should know that the state originally possesses great benevolence, and the monastic community ought to repay this virtue.
Yet some willfully violate the sacred instructions, acting with unrestrained impropriety and defiling their own conduct."

When good deeds are brought to light, they are thwarted and overturned; when a single evil act occurs, it defiles its entire class. As transgressions accumulate, the calamity extends to the Dharma-gate.
This is for the state not to fail the Sangha, but for the Sangha itself to fail the state—how truly lamentable!

Question: It was previously stated that there are five levels of profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*), yet this scripture does not mention them. Is there no contradiction? How can there be no contradiction? Answer:
There are three reasons for this intention: first, because the principles of the meaning are clearly evident; second, because it harmonizes with other schools of thought.

Third, because it is fundamentally beyond words, it is said that "the principles and categories are clearly manifest. If one relies on the aspects of name, essence, principle, function, and teaching, then this [text] takes the person, the dharma, and the analogy as its "name";
the true mark (*tathatā*) and the ground of the mind as its "essence"; the upholding of the precepts of the mind as its "principle";
the extinction of evil and the production of good as its "function"; and the initial flavor of milk as its "teaching aspect. Such is its meaning.
It is made manifest; it does not need to be spoken of for it to be seen. Therefore, there is no impediment even if it is not discussed here.

Regarding the "harmonization of other schools," this is based on Xianshou’s five gates of the *Prajñāpāramitā*: namely, the arising of the teaching, its inclusion within the Piṭakas, its essential tenets, the explanation of the title, and the interpretation of the text.
There are ten points concerning the arising of the teaching: first, because it proclaims the constant Dharma transmitted from one Buddha to another; second, because it establishes [the teaching]...
1. Because it is the fundamental basis for sentient beings to enter the Path; 2. Because the threefold illumination clarifies the mind-ground, giving rise to the Great Precepts;
3. Because it briefly opens up the vast practices and vows of Bodhisattvas; 4. Because it extensively reveals the gateway of the precepts to universally embrace all living beings;
5. Because it protects and sustains Bodhisattvas so that they certainly do not fall back; 6. Because it inspires those of the Lesser Vehicle to study the Mahāyāna.
Eighth, because it directly points out that ordinary beings are themselves Buddhas. Ninth, because it anticipates the final dharma age to act as a great guide.

Tenth, because it circulates the holy precepts so that they may be transmitted endlessly. Regarding its inclusion within the collections (*piṭaka*): among the three collections, it is included in the Vinaya Piṭaka;
among the two collections, it is included in the Bodhisattva Piṭaka; and among the provisional and ultimate teachings, it is subsumed under the ultimate teaching.
Regarding the fundamental aim (*abhiprāya*): in its general sense, the Great Precepts of the Mind-Ground take the cessation of evil and the practice of good as their fundamental aim;

in its specific sense, the characteristics of the Vinaya teachings constitute the fundamental aim, while the purpose is to cause one to realize the wondrous meaning of the Mind-Ground—this is the correspondence between teaching and meaning.

Furthermore, taking the true realm of the Mind-Ground as the fundamental aim, the purpose is to skillfully maintain it through wisdom—this is the correspondence between realm and wisdom. Moreover, with respect to...
Upholding the precepts of the mind is the cause; attaining the fruit of Buddhahood is the goal. This is the correspondence between cause and effect. Regarding the explanation of the title:
"Bodhisattva Precepts" refers to the meaning expressed (*lakṣya*), while "Sūtra" refers to the teaching that expresses it (*lākṣaṇa*). This is the correspondence between teaching and meaning.

The precepts are the dharma; the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and others serve as the analogy. This is the correspondence between dharma and analogy. The precepts of the mind constitute the essence; they consist of the cessation of evil.

Practicing the good is the function; this constitutes the correspondence between essence and function. According to the present commentary, within the central tenets (*zongqiu*), the essence and function are fully embodied:

the tenet (*zong*) encompasses the essence, while the purpose (*qiu*) encompasses the function. As for names and characteristics following the tenet, there is no need for further discussion. Now, let us explain the text.
Thus, I shall explain each passage according to its respective scripture. It should be understood that although the names of these two schools differ, their essential intent is one;

both may be employed interchangeably. Therefore, there is no contradiction in not discussing them here. As for the phrase "originally beyond words," it refers to the Middle Way of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which transcends existence and non-existence.
The single truth of the Dharma-realm is utterly quiescent and free from all dependencies; when unfolded, it manifests as the myriad phenomena.
There is that which is inexhaustible; how could the five [aggregates] ever exhaust it? If one rolls them up, even "one" cannot be established—how much less the five?
The mind cannot be conceived, and speech cannot be deliberated upon; therefore, not speaking of it now is likewise unimpeded.

To reach the ultimate unity of the source while neglecting the divergent categories of the branches and details leads only to the sudden emergence of points of contention, all of which become mere frivolous discourse.
The Exegesis on the Meaning of the Bodhisattva Precepts from the "Mind-Ground Chapter" of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, Fascicle One:
The Ritual for Reciting the Precepts by Half-Moon;
Preface to the Precepts.
All you sons of the Buddha, join your palms and listen with a sincere mind. I now wish to recite the Preface to the Great Precepts of all Buddhas.

As the assembly gathers, listen in silence. Those who know they have committed an offense should confess; through confession, there is peace and happiness, whereas without confession, the offense deepens.
Those without offense should remain silent. By your silence, it shall be known that the assembly is pure. Venerable sirs, [this is for] the upāsakas.
"Upāsikās, listen attentively! After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, you should revere the Prātimokṣa.

The Prātimokṣa is precisely these precepts. When upholding these precepts, it is like encountering light in the darkness, like a poor person finding treasure, like a sick person recovering from illness, like one released from prison, or like a long-distance traveler [reaching his destination]."
We have found refuge. You should know that this person is the Great Teacher of this assembly; he is no different from the Buddha remaining in the world.

It is difficult for a sense of dread to arise, and it is difficult for a virtuous mind to be stirred. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Do not treat even a small offense lightly, thinking there will be no calamity.

Though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel. To commit a sin in a single kṣaṇa brings the calamity of falling into the Avīci Hell. Once one loses the human body, ten thousand kalpas pass."
It will not return. The vigor of youth does not remain; it is like a galloping horse. Human life is impermanent, passing away faster than water flowing over mountains.

Though one exists today, tomorrow is difficult to guarantee. Each of you must single-mindedly cultivate diligence and exert yourselves. Be careful not to be indolent or lazy, nor to indulge yourself in sleep.
At night, collect the mind and maintain mindfulness of the Triple Gem; do not let time pass in vain, setting up [practices] only to have them be fruitless.

Weary and fatigued, those of later generations will deeply regret this. May each and every person among the assembly single-mindedly and reverently rely upon these precepts, practicing according to the Dharma;
this is how you should train.
I take refuge in Rocana and the Vajra Buddhas of the ten directions. I also pay homage to the former Master of the Treatise and shall awaken to the Honored One Maitreya.
Now I shall explain the three clusters of precepts; may all bodhisattvas listen together. The precepts are like a great bright lamp, able to dispel the darkness of the long night.
The precepts are like a true jewel mirror, illuminating all phenomena without omission. The precepts are like a *maṇi* gem, raining down objects to relieve poverty.
One leaves the world and swiftly attains Buddhahood; this Dharma alone is supreme. Therefore, all Bodhisattvas should diligently protect and uphold it.

Venerable sirs, the four months of the spring equinox constitute one season (this follows the system of the Western Regions, where a year is divided into three seasons, each consisting of four months: from the sixteenth day of the twelfth month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month is the spring season;

from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month is the summer season; from the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month is the winter season. For now, we shall designate the spring season; you should follow accordingly).

Adjust it according to the three periods [of the year]. When half a month has passed (the end of the twelfth month constitutes half a month; the fifteenth of the first month constitutes one month; the end of the first month constitutes one and a half months;

the fifteenth of the second month constitutes two months; the end of the second month constitutes two and a half months; the fifteenth of the third month constitutes three months; the end of the third month constitutes three and a half months; the fifteenth of the fourth month constitutes four months; the remaining summer and winter periods are adjusted accordingly). If one night is missing, there remains one night;
three and a half months remain (i.e., three months remain, two and a half months remain, two months remain, one and a half months remain, one month remains, or half a month remains).
The sun is setting. Old age and death have drawn near; the Buddha-dharma is about to perish.

For the sake of attaining the Way, O Venerable Ones, laymen, and laywomen, you must with single-mindedness and diligent effort seek progress. Why is this? Because all Buddhas, with single-mindedness and diligent effort, sought progress.
Thus, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; how much more so other dharmas of the wholesome path!
Each of you, hearing this while you are strong and healthy, should strive diligently to cultivate the good. Why do you not seek the Way? How can you wait until old age? What joy could there be then?
This day has already passed, and life likewise diminishes accordingly; like a fish in shallow water, what joy is there in this?

"Is the Saṃgha assembled? (Answer: "The Saṃgha is assembled. "Are you in harmony? (Answer: "We are in harmony. "The Saṃgha being assembled and in harmony, what shall we perform? (Answer: "We shall recite the precepts for the Poṣadha.

"Among those present, have any who have not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts, or those who are impure, departed? (There are two such categories: first, those who have not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts; second, those who previously received them but have committed offenses and have not yet repented.

These two types should not participate in the Poṣadha together. If there are any, they should be sent away; if there are none, answer "none"). "Those who did not come—have they entrusted their consent for the Poṣadha? (Answer: "They have. ...the entrustment of the Bodhisattva [precepts].

How many people are there who must declare their *chanda* (consent) and *pārisuddhi* (purity)? It is said that among those present, if anyone is unable to attend due to circumstances such as serving the Three Jewels, one’s parents, or illness, they should entrust their declaration to the *karmadāna* (officer in charge) or to a companion at the place of the *sthavira* (elder).

Regarding the declaration of *chanda*, the one receiving the entrustment says: "There is [so-and-so] whose *chanda* and purity have come for the *poṣadha*. Due to certain business matters, he cannot come in person; he has sent me to speak on his behalf. Regarding the declaration of *pārisuddhi*, it means:
"That [person], so-and-so, is free from any offense regarding the Dharma-based affairs of the Saṃgha, whether seen, heard, or suspected. The assembly should listen with a single mind.

Maintaining the precepts purifies body and speech; gathering the mind and maintaining right mindfulness, as well as extensive learning that gives rise to true wisdom—all these have the precepts as their foundation.
The precepts are the treasury of the sublime Dharma and also the wealth for transcending the world. The precepts are a great vessel capable of crossing the ocean of birth and death.
Precepts are a pool of coolness, wherein one bathes away all feverish afflictions. Precepts are a spell of fearlessness, which subdues and eliminates the harm of perverse poisons.
Precepts are an ultimate companion, capable of leading one across perilous and evil paths. Precepts are the gateway to the nectar of immortality, where all the noble sages roam.

Maintaining the precepts with a mind free from arrogance, being single-mindedly diligent and without negligence, not grasping at the characteristics of right precepts, and likewise having no thoughts of deviance—this is called pure precept-keeping, which is praised by all Buddhas.
Maintaining the precepts with a mind free from regret, one’s aspirations shall likewise be fulfilled.
Precepts are the moat of the Dharma-city, capable of warding off the thieves of affliction. Precepts are the valiant general, who crushes and subdues the hosts of Māra’s army.
Precepts are the wish-fulfilling jewel, which can bestow treasures upon merchants. Precepts are the sublime pavilion, wherein one sports in all samādhis.
Observing the precepts serves as level ground; meditative concentration serves as a dwelling place. It can give rise to the light of wisdom, which gradually attains clear illumination.
Adorned by the power of concentration and wisdom, the myriad practices are brought to fulfillment. Even until the attainment of the Buddha-way, all depends upon the precepts as its foundation.
Therefore, the wise person with firm resolve guards the precepts; even at the cost of losing body and life, they must carefully avoid transgressing them.
With palms joined, pay homage to the Lion of the Śākyas. I now wish to recite the precepts; the assembly should listen with one mind.
Even regarding minor transgressions, one’s mind should feel great dread; having committed a fault, one should repent with single-mindedness and never commit it again.
The horse of the mind gallops down evil paths, and its heedlessness is difficult to restrain; the Buddha taught urgent admonitions for practice, which are like sharp reins and bits.

The Buddha speaks the teachings and precepts with his own mouth; those who are virtuous are able to believe and accept them. Such a person is like a well-trained horse that can defeat the army of afflictions.
If one does not receive these instructions nor cherish the precepts, such a person is like an untrained horse, submerged in the army of birth and death.
If a person guards the precepts as a yak loves its tail, binds their mind to heedfulness as a monkey is bound by chains,
and always exerts themselves day and night for the sake of seeking true wisdom— such a person, within the Buddha’s Dharma, is able to attain a pure livelihood.
Venerable sirs, today, on the fifteenth day of the [waxing or waning] moon, we shall perform the *poṣadha* and recite the Bodhisattva precepts. The assembly should listen with a single mind.

Those who have committed offenses should confess them; those without offenses should remain silent. By remaining silent, it should be known that the venerable ones are pure and fit to receive the recitation of the Bodhisattva precepts.
The introduction to the Bodhisattva precepts has now been concluded. (Proceed below to inquire regarding offenses: those who have them should repent; those who do not should remain silent.)
Now I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter? (The question is asked three times; the answer is given three times. Venerable ones, because you are silent, you are pure in this matter.
Thus shall this matter be held.
Before reciting the precepts, the presiding master ascends the seat and addresses the assembly, saying: "I, [Name], prostrate myself in salutation and respectfully address the great assembly.
Having been appointed by the Sangha to recite the precepts, I fear there may be errors; I pray that those who recite with me will compassionately point out my mistakes."

Having finished reciting the precepts, he descends from his seat and expresses gratitude to the assembly, saying: "I, [Name], respectfully thank the great assembly. Appointed by the Sangha to recite the precepts, my three karmas were not diligent;
the wording of the precepts was stiff and dry, and I sat for too long, causing delay and distress to sentient beings. I hope the assembly will look upon me with compassion."
Rejoicing in Generosity.
