The *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, "Mind-Ground Chapter," with the *Commentary on the Meaning of the Bodhisattva Precepts* (*Fayi*), Fascicle Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty;
Commentary by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Chen and Sui Dynasties;
Exposition of the Hidden Meaning by the Śramaṇa Zhuhong of Yunqi Temple.
II. Correctly Explaining the Text (in three parts): First, re-explaining the title; second, identifying the translator; third, explaining the meaning of the scripture.
○ First, re-explaining the title.

The title of this sutra is *Brahmajāla*. The text of the first fascicle states that the Buddha observed the Indra’s net of the Great Brahma Heaven King, where its thousandfold layers of variegated patterns do not obstruct one another; he then taught that the infinite worlds are like the meshes of that net.
Each and every world is distinct from the others; the various gates of the Buddhas' teachings are likewise so.

Adorning the Brahma-body, they are without any obstruction. These names are established through metaphors, serving as general analogies for what is realized within each respective section; thus, they differ in their specific details.
It is like the net of Brahmā. The title of this chapter, "The Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Mind," is also a metaphorical name.
The essential functions of the Great Being elucidated within this chapter are like the heart within a human body; it can govern all affairs and give rise to supreme fruits.
It is that upon which the Great Beings rely; in meaning, it is like the earth. *Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden) asks:

Why is there this re-explanation? In the previous [section], the intent of the various versions of the *Mahāvaipulya* was predominant, while the intent of the "Earth-Mind" (*cittabhūmi*) of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* was not fully addressed;
therefore, it is re-explained here. As for the *Brahmajāla*, it is named after its metaphorical subject: Indra.

This refers to what is called the "Celestial King" (Devendra), also known as the "Red Jewel of Heaven. Now, both terms are used together to describe the red-jewel net of the Great Brahmā Heavenly King.
Its crimson light radiates back and forth, its precious colors intermingle and shine, and its patterns form a thousand layers without obstructing one another.
This is cited to clarify that the establishment of the worlds in the ten directions is likewise immeasurable; it is also thus. Ten.
The various arrangements established within the gateways of the Buddha's teachings are likewise thus.
The diverse ways in which the bodhisattvas of the ten directions practice and realize these teachings according to the instructions are likewise thus. As for "adorned Brahma-bodies":
the pure essence of the fundamental source of all Buddhas is called the Brahma-body; this is arrayed as immeasurable worlds and opened out as—
The immeasurable gates of teaching serve as immeasurable means of cultivation and realization for the purpose of transformation and guidance;
thus they adorn this body, just as the Brahma King uses a net of jewels as floral ornamentation. As for the "mind-ground," it is also a metaphorical expression:

just as when the hundred skeletal members of a human body assemble, there must necessarily be a governing mind, so too when the various virtues of a Bodhisattva are cultivated in conjunction, there must necessarily be that which is essential and wondrous.
As for its function: that which is essential is precisely the precept of the fundamental source-mind-body (*mūla-citta-tattva*).
All phenomena are governed by it, just as the earth supports all things. Supreme fruits arise because of it, just as the earth nurtures and grows all things.
It is for this reason that the sutra is titled *Brahmajāla* and the chapter is titled "The Mind-Ground" (*citta-bhūmi*).
II. The Translator’s Colophon.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
[The phrase] "Fayi" (Unfolding the Hidden) indicates that the Yao Qin differs from the Chen and Sui dynasties. "Yao" is the surname and "Qin" is the state; this distinguishes it from the Fu Qin.
III. Explaining the Meaning of the Sūtra (Part 2) First, the introductory preface at the beginning of the first sūtra. Second, the threefold classification of the sections.
*Fayin*: From "At that time, Vairocana Buddha" up to "the fundamental source, the self-nature is pure," this single passage of prose originally had no divisions.
One version, however, contains a division, because the *Zeshanxian* [commentary] following the sūtra...
The Dharma Master spoke several words, whereupon people began to suspect that all [the preceding] were his own arrangements. Now, I shall slightly revise those arrangements.

The reason for doing so is that, according to the general structure of various sutras, the text naturally falls into the sections of Introduction (nidāna), Main Body (dharmadeśanā), and Dissemination (parīndanā). However, the commentator of this sutra’s sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) has judged that the verse portion alone constitutes the Introductory Section;
consequently, the prose section (*gadya*) listed at the beginning would have no place to be situated. Alternatively, it may be that the original version of the sub-commentary...
There is none; or perhaps it has been lost through scribal error, so that it cannot yet be known.

However, upon examining the meaning of the preceding and following contexts, it appears that the prose section constitutes the introduction (*nidāna*), while the verses merely restate it. For this reason, I have not altered the old text of Tiantai;

rather, I have treated both the prose and the verses as the introduction, which is unobjectionable on both counts and may even be logically consistent. As for the commentary (*śāstra*), there are instances where it is either missing or abbreviated.

I have nevertheless provided supplementary explanations. To supplement the scriptural text is to reveal what was not yet commented upon in the sutra; to supplement the commentary is to reveal what was not yet excerpted in the sub-commentary.
Thus it is titled *Fayi* (Revealing the Hidden). "Hidden" refers to that which is contained but not yet manifest; I have merely brought it forth for the sake of elucidation.
I do not presume to say that I have added anything to it.
I. The Preface to the First Sūtra (2) A. General Presentation of the Extensive and Abridged Versions. B. Specific Clarification of the Real and the Manifested. I.
General Presentation of the Extensive and Abridged Versions (2) 1. Direct Explanation. 2. Citation of Scriptural Evidence.
First, the actual clarification:

At that time, Vairocana Buddha, for the sake of this great assembly, briefly opened up the *cittabhūmi* (mind-ground) from among the dharma-gates of ineffable teachings as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of *gaṅgā* rivers, to an extent only the size of a palm.
As for Vairocana, the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* translates it as "Pure and Full. It is called "pure" because all afflictions have been completely exhausted;
it is called "full" because all virtues are perfectly complete.
*Fayi*: When all afflictions are exhausted, there is no delusion that is not eliminated; this is the fruit of ceasing evil.
When all virtues are perfected, there is no excellence that does not gather; this is the fruit of practicing good. These "great assemblies" refer to the Buddhas upon the thousand-petaled lotuses.
As infinite as the sands of the Ganges, even down to the most minute hair-tip, within these inexhaustible Dharma-gates, one opens a mind as small as a single filament.
The "Earth" [Sutra] extensively enumerates and briefly summarizes [the teachings], like picking up a handful of soil from Mount Tai or using a single drop from the vast ocean;
by means of the small to illustrate the great, it speaks to the ultimate extent of the vastness of this Dharma-gate.
II. Manifesting the Verification.
This has been taught by all Buddhas of the past, will be taught by the Buddhas of the future, and is being taught now by the Buddhas of the present.
It has been studied, will be studied, and is being studied now by Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time.

*Fayi*: Following upon the above, although the Dharma now being taught is said to be but a small portion, it is in fact that which all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have taught together and that which Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time have studied together.
Ten thousand sages have transmitted it without differing words; a thousand worthies have received it as a non-dual Dharma. How could one not follow it?
II. Specific Explanation of the True and the Manifested (2) A. First, explaining the true Buddha’s bestowal of instructions. B. Second, explaining the transmission by the manifested Buddha. A.
First, explaining the true Buddha’s bestowal of instructions (2) 1. First, citing his own cultivation and realization. 2. Second, commanding him to instruct others.
First, he raises the subject of his own cultivation and realization:
"I have cultivated this mind-ground for a hundred kalpas; thus I am named Vairocana.
[This is] the revelation of the hidden. First, it indicates that this Dharma-gate of the mind-ground is a perfected method already tested by oneself, clearly manifest.
This is faith.
○ Second, instructing others to turn [the Dharma] toward them (in two parts): First, a brief indication; second, a detailed exposition.
○ First, the brief indication.
"You all Buddhas, turn what I have spoken to open the path of the mind-ground for all sentient beings and reveal that which is hidden.
Regarding "turning": it means transmitting the Buddha’s words to reach sentient beings; it refers to receiving them from above and disseminating them below.

The "joyful earth" refers to the fundamental mind-ground, which is inherently level, upright, empty, and pervasive. Since beginningless time, it has been obstructed and hindered by deluded attachments;
yet when these are regulated by the precepts (*śīla*), the obstructions are removed and the hindrances eliminated. It becomes vast, level, and upright, and expansive, empty, and pervasive.
All the planting of manifold virtues and the bearing of responsibility for sentient beings arise from this, and thus it is likened to the earth. This...
This is the essential purport of the sutra. Question: It is said that "gathering the mind constitutes precepts. What is meant by "opening"? Answer:
The precepts of the Hīnayāna merely involve gathering and maintaining [the mind] for oneself; the precepts of the Mahāyāna additionally involve opening and benefiting sentient beings.
Therefore, the meaning of "gathering" is narrow, while the meaning of "opening" is broad.
II. Extensive Exposition.
At that time, in the Lotus-Womb World (*Padmagarbha-lokadhātu*), the Buddha Vairocana, seated upon a majestic lion throne amidst celestial radiance, emitted light.
This light addressed the Buddhas upon the thousand petals, saying: "Take this 'Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground' and depart. Thereupon, it was further transformed into...
The thousands of billions of Śākyamunis, together with all sentient beings, shall sequentially expound for you this chapter on the Dharma-gate of the Superior Grounds of the Mind.
You should receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and practice it with single-minded devotion.
Regarding Śākyamuni: the *Śūnyatā-sūtra* (瑞應經) translates this as "Capable Sage" (能儒), also called "Capable Benevolent One" (能仁), or "Capable of Endurance" (能忍), and also "Straight Forest" (直林).
As for Muni, it refers to body, speech, and mind; some say it means "Crossing the Wat-chiao" (度沃焦), which is a divergent interpretation.

In the "Chapter on Names" (*Nāma-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka*, he is sometimes named Rocana and sometimes named Śākya. Here, we clarify that these names are neither identical nor different, according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Please lend an ear to this revelation of the hidden meaning.

As for the "Lotus Flower Terrace Treasury," it refers to the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*). As for "the light’s proclamation," it means that the Flower Adornment Cloud Terrace and other such realms all preach the Dharma.
Regarding the "hundreds, thousands, and ten-thousands of millions," there are four types of *koṭi* (million) in the Western Regions: one million, ten million, a hundred million, and so forth.
"Ten million times ten thousand times ten thousand" refers to the present "hundreds of thousands of millions," meaning ten billion upon a thousand petals;

taking "ten million" as "one hundred million," it expresses the number of the Great Trichiliocosm. This phrase then connects with the following sentence, stating that [the merit] is also for the sake of all Buddhas and sentient beings.
The Confucian is gentle and harmonious; the benevolent one is compassionate and wise; the patient one is tolerant and enduring.

"Forest-dweller" (Lin) refers to one who dwells in a grove of straight trees and takes that forest as his surname; furthermore, "forest" (Lin) signifies growth and flourishing—all of which carry the meaning of Śākya.
"Body, speech, and mind" refers to the tranquility of the three karmas; this is the meaning of Muni. "Crossing the Wujiao (Wojiao) [Shoal]"—the "scorching stones" (jiao-shi) dry up all waters, yet...
"Overflowing" (*yi*) is a metaphor for ordinary beings who thirst after the five desires without satiety; that one can now deliver them also incorporates the meaning of Śākyamuni.

According to the *Avataṃsaka*, Vairocana is identical to Śākyamuni; yet they are not one because their superior and inferior aspects are distinguished, nor are they different because their fundamental and manifested traces are integrated.
Now, following capacities and responding to conditions, it is logically appropriate to open [this teaching] within the gateway of transformative deliverance.
II. Explaining the Transmission of the Emanated Buddhas (in two parts): 1. A general enumeration of the many Buddhas in all realms.
2. A specific manifestation of the one Buddha in this realm. I.
General Enumeration of the Many Buddhas in All Realms (in two parts): 1. Clarifying only a single realm. 2. Distinguishing and explaining the others.
Category.
○ First, Clarifying a Single Realm (3): 1. Receiving the Dharma and Preparing to Depart; 2. Returning to One’s Original Realm; 3.
Benefiting Sentient Beings in Accordance with the Imperial Decree.

○ At the beginning, when the Dharma General was about to take his leave, at that time, the Buddha of the Thousand-Petaled Lotus and the hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis rose from their majestic lion thrones within the World of the Lotus Treasury.
Each of them withdrew, emitting inconceivable light from every part of their bodies; this light all transformed into...
The Buddhas, at one time, offered immeasurable blue, yellow, and white flowers as an offering to Vairocana Buddha.
Having completed the reception and upholding of the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" as explained above.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): The thousand Buddhas transform into a thousand billion, and these thousand billion further transform into the infinite.
This represents how the Dharma of the Mind-Ground Precepts gives rise to [beings] without end. As for the body emitting light and the light transforming into Buddhas:

this represents that the *dharmakāya* possesses immeasurable wisdom; the Buddhas thus manifested are all the Buddha-wisdom itself. With immeasurable exquisite flowers, one makes offerings to the Buddhas.
This signifies that immeasurable sublime dharmas emerge from the ground of the mind of Samantabhadra;
now, by offering exquisite flowers back to the original Buddha, it signifies returning with these sublime dharmas to adorn one's own fundamental nature.
Second, returning to their original realms:
each of them vanished from this Lotus-Womb World (*padmagarbha-lokadhātu*).

Having vanished, they entered the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of Essential Nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā-kusumaprabhā-samādhi*) and returned to their original source-world, beneath the Bodhi tree in Jambudvīpa.

*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): Regarding the Samādhi of Essential Nature (*tixing sanmei*): the essential nature has been fundamentally empty from the beginning; the radiant light manifests spontaneously and naturally.

It is like the vast expanse of the great void, wherein clouds, mist, the sun, and the moon, as well as running creatures, flying birds, grasses, and trees—ten thousand diverse categories—are in constant flux.

Their arising and ceasing, their concealment and manifestation, proceed side by side without contradiction. Therefore, the Buddha, within this samādhi, may enter or emerge at will, exercising mastery according to his mind.
Also. ○ Third, Benefiting Sentient Beings in Accordance with the Imperial Decree (2): First, emerging from samādhi; second, expounding the Dharma-gate.
○ First, emerging from samādhi.
Emerging from the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of the Void Nature. [Commentary:
This refers to "emerging" (chū), following the previous mention of "entering" (nyū).
○ Second, the teaching of the Dharma-gate.
Having emerged, he sat upon the Vajra-Thousand-Rays King Throne in the Hall of Sublime Light and taught the Ten Ocean-like World Realms.
Rising again from his seat, he went to the palace of Śakra and taught the Ten Abodes. Rising again from his seat, he went among the Yāma devas and taught the Ten Practices.
Rising again from his seat, he went to the Fourth Heaven and taught the Ten Dedications. Rising again from his seat, he went to the Nirmāṇarati...
The Deva spoke of the ten dhyānas. Rising again from his seat, he went to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven and spoke of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Then, going into the first dhyāna, he spoke of the ten vajras. Going into the second dhyāna, he spoke of the ten patiences (*kṣānti*). Going into the third dhyāna, he spoke of the ten vows (*praṇidhāna*).
Finally, going into the fourth dhyāna, to the palace of Maheśvara, the King of Devas, he spoke of the Lotus Throne, the source of my own origin.
The Chapter on the Dharma-Door of the Mind-Ground as Taught by Vairocana Buddha in the Lushena-Buddha World.
Śākyamuni preached this Chapter on the Mind-Ground in the Palace of Mahesvara in the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven.

Examining the beginning and end of the text, there are a thousand Śākyamunis, together with a hundred billion Śākyamunis, each connecting with those with whom they have a karmic affinity; all of them reach Vairocana.
Having received the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, they each sat upon their respective sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and manifested the attainment of perfect awakening.
They subsequently recounted and expounded the Dharma in ten locations: first, in the Hall of Sublime Light, they taught the Ten Ocean-like Worlds;
second, in the palace of Śakra, they taught the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*); third, in the Yāma heaven, they taught the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*); fourth, in the Tuṣita heaven, they taught...

10. The Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). 5. In the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, he taught the Ten Meditative Absorptions (*daśa-dhyāna*). 6. In the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, he taught the Ten Grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*).

7. In the First Dhyāna, he taught the Ten Vajras (*daśa-vajra*). 8. In the Second Dhyāna, he taught the Ten Patiences (*daśa-kṣānti*). 9. In the Third Dhyāna, he taught the Ten Vows (*daśa-praṇidhāna*). 10.
In the Fourth Dhyāna, he taught the "Chapter on the Mind-Ground" (*citta-bhūmi-paṭala*). The Tenth Assembly: In total, he further expounded upon the aforementioned [teachings].
The thirty minds and ten stages are all explained according to the principle of signlessness (*animitta*).

[This is from] *Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden). This clarifies that the hundreds of thousands of myriads of bodies of Śākyamuni all first received the precepts before Vairocana, and subsequently preached the Dharma in ten locations;
yet this Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground (*cittabhūmi*) was preached last, signifying that among all phenomena...

This is the ultimate state of wholeheartedness. All these points concern the signless (*animitta*). Having previously enumerated various names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), I fear that people might cling to appearances and obscure the mind;
therefore, I clarify that appearances are fundamentally empty by nature, yet exist due to causes and conditions—this is precisely "appearance as non-appearance."
Second, the explanation of other categories:
the remaining billions of Śākyamunis are likewise thus; they are non-dual and without distinction, as explained in the "Chapter on the Worthy Eon" (Bhadrakalpika-parivarta).

*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): "The Buddhas of one hundred billion worlds thus repeat and expound the Dharma in this manner. By extending this principle as an analogy, it is the same for the thousands and hundreds of billions.
This is seen in the *Xianjie pin* (Chapter on the Worthy Kalpa) of the *Daben* (Great Text). Hereafter, follow this pattern."
II. Specifically Revealing the One Buddha of This Realm (4): 1. Subduing Māras when descending from the heavens; 2. Benefiting sentient beings while in the human realm; 3.
Universally exhorting others to receive and uphold [the teaching]; 4. Reiterating the exposition and concluding the section.
First, the subduing of Māra by the celestial [deities].
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, having first appeared from the Lotus-Flower-Pedestal Treasury World in the east and entered the palace of the Heavenly King,
finished preaching the *Māra-parivarta-sūtra*.
*Fayi*: The Dharma previously taught refers generally to a single Buddha in all worlds; the Dharma now taught refers specifically to a single Buddha in this world.
Therefore, while the wording may seem repetitive, in reality there is no redundancy. As for "the East":

It is said that this realm is located to the east of the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*). Question: The *Sūtra on the Demon Receiving Transformation* and the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* were both preached in the celestial palace;
why is one transmitted while the other has vanished? Answer: The demon’s disturbance was but a single-period event; once he received transformation, it ceased.
The precepts have been transmitted by a thousand Buddhas; their propagation shall be inexhaustible. That each transmission is followed by a dissolution is nothing to be wondered at.

II. Benefiting Beings in the Human Realm (3 sections): 1. Descending to Birth and Attaining Enlightenment; 2. Transmitting the Dharma to Benefit Living Beings; 3. The Benefits Derived from Such Births.
First, regarding my descent and attainment of the Way:
I descended into the world in the kingdom of Kapilavastu in Jambudvīpa. My mother’s name was Māyā; my father’s name was Śuddhodana. My name is Siddhārtha.
At the age of seven, I left the household life; at thirty, I attained the Way. I am titled Śākyamuni Buddha.

*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden). This is a general account of the world, kingdom, and town where Śākyamuni descended to be born; his parents’ surnames and clans; his renunciation of the world to practice the Way;
and his attainment of Buddhahood and the saving of sentient beings. Regarding "descending to be born," the *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha-sūtra* states:
The Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra resided in the Tuṣita Heaven for a full four thousand years, manifesting the characteristics of the Dharma for those devas.
Furthermore, observing the lower realms with his divine eye, he saw them creating karma and suffering the oppression and affliction thereof.

Desiring to rescue and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings, and to teach and transform them, he descended to the human world, left the household life, and attained the Way; thus, he descended to be born.
Furthermore, Jambudvīpa—here translated as "Superior Gold"—is where rivers yield golden sand and trees exude liquid gold; it is the continent of the southern world.
Among the four continents, this one alone possesses these three superior qualities; therefore, the Buddha appears in the Southern Continent.
Kāpilavastu—here translated as "Yellow-Haired"—is where yellow-haired sages of old practiced the Way. [This is within] the Great Trichiliocosm.
This is the most central [land]. Therefore, the Buddha was born in Jambudvīpa in the Kāpiśī region. Māyā means "Great Illusion" (Mahāmāyā);
she is the mother of all Buddhas by virtue of her great illusory arts. Śuddhodana is the Sanskrit name; it means "Pure.
Siddhārtha means "Sudden Auspiciousness" or "Accomplishment of All Aims"; he was auspicious from birth, possessing all virtues in their entirety. (7)
He was thirty years of age. The meaning of this is extremely difficult to discern.

Indeed, that he left the palace at nineteen, practiced asceticism for six years, married a consort while still in his home, and fathered a son named Rāhula, is transmitted by both the ancients and the moderns and is fully recorded in the Sūtras and Vinayas. To claim now that he left home at seven years of age contradicts these accounts.
If he were a mere youth, it would not have been appropriate for him to take a wife; yet he attained enlightenment at thirty. His ascetic practices lasted for many years.

According to the *Samantapāsādikā Sūtra*, it is also stated that he attained enlightenment at thirty. Some maintain that after his ascetic practices, there was still a five-year period of wandering, which precisely totals thirty years.
Furthermore, the *Hetupratyaya Sūtra* mentions the cowherd girl offering him milk-rice, while the *Lalitavistara Sūtra* records...
The deities offered him a bath; this all occurred after the sixth year. There is no textual record of his traveling about prior to that time.

Furthermore, according to the *Benxing jing* (Sūtra on Past Deeds), he studied writing and treatises at the age of eight, and according to the *Puyao jing* (Lalitavistara Sūtra), he observed the plowing of fields when he had grown up.
Thus, it is evident that leaving home at seven years of age is even more inconsistent with these accounts. Moreover, the *Adbhutadharmaparyāya-sūtra* states that the Buddha...
Maudgalyāyana was sent to ordain Rāhula. Yaśodharā replied, "When the Tathāgata was a crown prince, he took me as his wife.
Before nine years had passed, he fled into the mountains and marshes. After six years, he attained Buddhahood.
Now he comes again to seek my son for ordination; how cruel this is! Thus, it is also improper for him to have left home at nineteen. It does not stop here."
I have heard that even regarding the time of his birth, many accounts are given. Some say it was during the reign of Jie of Xia; some say it was at the end of the Shang dynasty;
and some say it was during the eras of Kings Zhao, Mu, Ping, Huan, or Hui of Zhou.
This is just like the question posed by Vinaya Master Xuán to a celestial being, which ultimately resulted in an indefinite conclusion. It is also like Lín’s response when Liu Déwēi consulted him.

Regarding old age, it occurs only during the two periods of birth and death. Now, since the texts and commentaries within the Great Canon (Tripitaka) each differ slightly, and the Master of the Commentary has not provided a clear explanation for this point, some may argue that when a Great Sage manifests in the world, how could there be fixed rules?

That the manifested characteristics vary is nothing to doubt. However, they fail to realize that once he has manifested in a body identical to that of an ordinary person, how could he possibly avoid undergoing such transformations and illusions?
First: Within a single trichiliocosm, those who leave the household life on the same day attain Buddhahood simultaneously in ten billion lands—is there ever even a slight difference [between them]?
One should know that this passage is likely a scribal error. Question:

If it is an error, why did the sages of old continue to transmit it, and why did Tiantai never correct or determine its true meaning? Answer: The ancients were cautious and reserved, leaving points of uncertainty unresolved. They did not...

I dare not take such liberties. If everyone were allowed to arbitrarily edit and revise [the classics] according to their own whims, before even a century has passed, the ancient scriptures and laws would have entirely departed from their original models.
At fifty, I studied the *Yi* (Book of Changes); I did not dare further alter its text, yet I have set forth its subtle meanings in my commentaries.
The *Aṣṭottaraśata-puṣpa-sūtra* does not dare to increase the number [of years], yet it refers to Samantabhadra as a "distinct practitioner" (*bīexingzhě*).

If so, who ultimately follows? If one relies on the facts, nineteen or sixteen years are closer to the historical reality. However, I follow the principle that sentient capacities (*jī*) are not uniform;
the occasions for seeing the Buddha, leaving home, and attaining enlightenment are likewise not uniform. Therefore, I follow the capacity.
II. Transmitting the Dharma to Benefit Sentient Beings (in two parts): A. Responding to Capabilities to Manifest Transformation. B. Returning Again by Virtue of Great Vows. I.
Responding to Capabilities to Manifest Transformation (in two parts): 1. Horizontally Indicating the Place and Assembly. 2. Vertically Clarifying the Succession of Events.
First, the section on the horizontal pointing:

At the Site of Tranquil Extinction, seated upon the Vajra Flower-Light King Throne, and so forth up to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara—this is what was taught sequentially at those ten successive dwelling places. At that time, the Buddha contemplated the net of the Great Brahma Kings.
Dhvaja. This is because it is taught that immeasurable worlds are like the mesh of a net; each individual world is distinct and different, being immeasurably diverse.
The gateways of the Buddha’s teaching are likewise so.
Śākyamuni originally descended from the Lotus Treasury World into a celestial palace, then came down to Jambudvīpa to attain enlightenment and was named Śākyamuni;
beginning with his preaching at the site of enlightenment, he proceeded through ten locations.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden). This clarifies the sequential and universal nature of preaching the Dharma and transforming beings; one Buddha is identical to the many Buddhas mentioned previously.

The "Ten Abodes" (*daśavihāra*) do not refer to a dharma of ten abodes, but rather to the ten locations wherein one dwells. As for "Contemplating the Brahma-net," this is the reason for the title of the primary scripture.
One contemplates the myriad meshes of the Brahma-net, layer upon layer, each distinct and immeasurable; through this, one comes to know the world of the Buddha.
The realms are likewise each distinct and immeasurable. Knowing this, one understands that the Buddha’s transformation through teaching is also thus, each distinct and immeasurable.
Within the hundreds of thousands of millions of lands, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis proclaiming the Buddha’s transformation;
therefore, it is named the Brahma Net.
II. Second, the vertical clarification of coming and going:

I have now come to this world eight thousand times. For the sake of this Sahā world, I have sat upon the Vajra-flower-light-king throne, and even in the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara, briefly expounding [the Dharma] for all the great assemblies therein.
The Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground is concluded.
*Fayin* (Unfolding the Hidden): As for the Vajra-seat, it is where the Buddhas of the three periods sit to attain enlightenment; it undergoes no slight change or decay.

This is precisely the mind-ground of the true mark (*dharmatā*). For this reason, it is that for which the sentient beings of this realm sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to achieve perfect realization.
This is the awakening to the propagation of the Dharma. This is a general exposition of the teachings throughout the various periods of the Buddha’s life.
Within the palace of Maheśvara, for the sake of the great assembly therein, he specifically taught these precepts of the Mind-Ground. Alas!

Reflecting upon the World-Honored One’s deeds for the sake of sentient beings, his compassionate vows were vast and profound, delivering them without end. Tracing back from this point, eight thousand [aeons] have passed. And as for humanity...

When a minister has an audience with his sovereign, though it may be but a few inches away, there is still a fixed schedule. Even when a sagacious ruler tours his own kingdom, he still delays for years and decades.
Now, [the Buddha] traverses immeasurable worlds and undergoes the toil of ten thousand round trips, not for his own sake, but out of compassion for us.
How can we, beholding such great kindness, remain complacent and fail to repay it? Truly, this is lamentable!
II. The Second Great Vow for Reappearance:

Once again descending from the Palace of the Heavenly King to the Bodhi tree beneath which he sat in Jambudvīpa, [the Buddha] preached, for the sake of all sentient beings upon this earth—those ordinary people shrouded in the darkness of ignorance—the initial aspiration within the mind-ground of his original self, the Buddha Vairocana.
Within the mind, one should constantly recite this single precept: the Radiant Vajra Jewel Precept.
It is the source of all Buddhas, the source of all Bodhisattvas, and the seed of Buddha-nature. All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
all consciousness, form, and mind—whether emotional or mental—all enter into the precept of Buddha-nature.

Furthermore, descending from the celestial palace to the foot of the Bodhi tree, he preached for these sentient beings the precepts recited by Vairocana at his initial aspiration—namely, the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts. These are as taught in the *Avataṃsaka*;

the text has not yet been fully transmitted, consisting only of seven locations and eight assemblies. It mostly speaks of [the Buddha] not rising from his original seat, but does not mention him being in the Nirmāṇarati heaven.
The Dharma was preached by the Celestial Being (Devaputra). This sutra frequently describes rising from one’s seat and proceeding to other locations;

it was preached in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven regarding the ten dhyāna-concentrations. Furthermore, many of its stages do not correspond [to one another], and the preceding and succeeding sessions may be either identical or different.

This is truly because the traces of the Sage are inconceivable, and he provides diverse teachings according to the capacities of sentient beings. Among the three vehicles of teaching, this is the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao), which clarifies the Buddha...

The nature [of this teaching] eternally abides in the wondrous principle of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). Those for whom it is intended are solely the Mahāsattvas (Bodhisattvas), not those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas).

As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "When the followers of the Two Vehicles are seated there, they neither know nor perceive [it], because the stages and positions of a Mahāsattva are not within the sphere of practice of the Two Vehicles, and the gravity of the prohibitions and precepts is not that which is studied by the Lesser Vehicle.
Thus, the methods of regulation for the precepts of the Great and Lesser Vehicles are different.
The Bodhisattva simultaneously and instantaneously restrains fifty-eight matters, whereas the Śrāvaka awaits the commission of an offense before it is formally defined.

This is because the theoretical discussion pertains to the appropriate occasion. Regarding the practical application, there are generally three meanings: first, the Mahāsattva possesses deep faith and does not oppose what he hears instantaneously.

The first phrase concludes the provisional manifestation (traces), while the subsequent phrase concludes the fundamental reality (the original body). This clarifies that the thousands, hundreds, and ten-thousands of bodies all take Śākyamuni (Vairocana) as their basis.

[Commentary on the Hidden Meaning]: Although these are termed "original" and "traces," do not give rise to dualistic thoughts; the thousands, hundreds, and ten-thousands of bodies are none other than the single body of Śākyamuni.
