Because they have been healed, there is no confusion between them.
○ Second, Śākyamuni’s Transmission (three parts): First, an introduction to the causes and conditions of Śākyamuni’s transmission;
second, Śākyamuni’s bestowal upon the various bodhisattvas; third, an exhortation for the bodhisattvas to bestow it upon all sentient beings.
○ First Preface: The Account of Śākyamuni’s Transmission.
At that time, the thousands of millions [of emanations] returned to their original places of enlightenment;
each sat beneath a Bodhi tree and recited my Teacher’s precepts.
The third section clarifies that the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas each return to their original abode; yet, the Dharma-body has no fixed location.
Herein, first it is clarified that the provisional traces transmit the fundamental precepts: thus, the fundamental is the teacher of the provisional, because the provisional recites the fundamental.

*Fayi*: "The original site of practice (*daochang*) symbolizes the fundamental mind; the Bodhi tree symbolizes the essence of awakening. This means that by means of the fundamental mind and the essence of awakening, one maintains the fundamental precepts.
Although the Dharma-body has no fixed location, this means that although the Dharma-body is omnipresent, one recites the fundamental [precepts] based on its traces."
There is also that which exists.

○ Second, explaining Śākyamuni’s bestowal [of precepts] upon the various bodhisattvas (three parts): first, the essence of the precepts; second, the function of the precepts; third, the exhortation to uphold them.
○ First, the essence of the precepts:
the ten grave rules and forty-eight minor ones.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): This single phrase encompasses the entirety of the dharma of the precepts; the essential point for their observance truly lies herein. Therefore—
This refers to the essence of the precepts.
II. The Function of the Precepts:
The precepts are like the bright sun and moon, and are also like jeweled necklaces.
Maintaining these precepts can dispel the mist of transgressions; it is like the sun that brings about clarity and coolness.
It is comparable to the moon; it is rich in wholesome dharmas, like a jeweled necklace. Furthermore, just as the sun can cause all things to grow, so too are the precepts:
they can cause all manner of virtues to flourish. Moreover, just as a jeweled necklace can alleviate poverty, so too are the precepts: they can remedy the multitude of [defilements].

Born into poverty, one grows to possess the wealth of the sublime Dharma. Furthermore, just as the sun and moon adorn the heavens and all gaze up in reverence, so too do those who maintain the precepts within their being receive universal honor and veneration.

When the *śīla* (precepts) are upon the body, they constitute the foremost of adornments; through the observance of the precepts, one is freed from ugliness, becoming as upright and handsome as the most beautiful person.
*Fayi* (Unveiling the Hidden): To open the mist of karmic obstacles and extinguish the fire of afflictions is the benefit of cessation (*śīla*).

To possess the myriad dharmas and cause the myriad virtues to grow is the benefit of practice (*caryā*). Regarding "removing poverty, leaving ugliness," and even "returning to honor," there are two aspects to the intention of cessation and practice for leaving ugliness.
First, in terms of body, mind, and speech: because of this precept, one is inwardly free from deviant thoughts and thus leaves ugliness behind.
The mind is ugly; being free from external transgressions is to be free from the ugliness of the body. These two are spoken of in terms of cause and effect:
by observing the precepts in this life, one shall obtain the marks and signs of physical excellence in a future life; this is to be free from the ugliness of retribution.
III. Exhortation to Uphold (2) 1. The One Who Bestows [the Teaching]. 2. The One Who Receives [the Teaching].
1. The One Who Bestows [the Teaching]:
"By means of these, the multitude of bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust attain perfect enlightenment; this is that which Rocana recites."
I am also like this:
as when a person crossing the sea must rely on a ship or boat, so too, if one is to cross over birth and death, one must depend upon the precepts.
As a great sutra says, they are like relying on a raft or float, and are further likened to a life-preserving air bag.
*Fayi*: "Innumerable Bodhisattvas" refers to the fact that immeasurable worthies and sages attained Buddhahood by virtue of receiving these precepts;

how much more so for ordinary beings? Therefore, it says "exhorting to uphold. Upholding necessarily proceeds from being conferred. Who is able to confer them? Śākyamuni himself recited them, and I likewise recite them following him;
how much more so for all other Bodhisattvas? A boat, a raft, or a life-preserver are the tools for crossing a river; this serves as a metaphor for upholding [the precepts].
The precepts enable one to transcend the ocean of birth and death and reach the shore of nirvana. A life-preserving float may be made of leather, bladder, or wood;
being hollow within and buoyant on the outside, one who boards it to cross rivers and lakes will not sink.
Thus, there is the metaphor of the rākṣasa begging for a life-preserving float.
II. Those Who Receive [the Precepts].
You, newly initiated bodhisattvas, receive and uphold these precepts with the highest reverence.
Those who have first heard the precepts are all called "newly initiated. As stated above, it is by means of this that even bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust achieve [enlightenment].
If the Buddha is thus, then those who have newly begun their training can be known. If the Buddhas Vairocana and Śākyamuni recite [the mantra] themselves, then others can be known [to do so as well].
Third, the exhortation for Bodhisattvas to bestow [the teaching] upon all sentient beings.
Having received and upheld these precepts, one transmits them to all sentient beings—the Bodhisattvas of the thirty minds.
This refers to transmitting them to those outside the stage of the ordinary person (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) who have resolved to attain the Great Vehicle.

[Note on the hidden meaning: Regarding the "thirty minds," according to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), the stages of dwelling (*zhù*), practice (*xíng*), and direction (*xiàng*) constitute the internal ordinary persons (*neifán*), while the ten levels of faith (*shìxìn*) constitute the external ordinary persons.

Generally speaking, these "sentient beings" refer to those at the stage of faith (*śraddhā*). If one extends this principle to its ultimate limit—whereby those who have first heard the precepts pass them on to those who have not yet heard them—the succession will be inexhaustible.
III. Exhortation to Believe, Accept, and Uphold (2) 1. Revealing the Dharma Being Recited 2. Exhorting Others to Believe and Accept 1.
Revealing the Dharma Being Recited:
Listen attentively as I correctly recite The treasury of precepts within the Buddha-dharma, The Prātimokṣa.
This precept distinguishes [the Buddhist precepts] from those of non-Buddhists, such as the "chicken" or "dog" precepts. Pure morality (*śīla*) is the cause;
liberation (*prātimokṣa*) is the fruit. [To explain further: "Distinguishing" means to differentiate the precepts within the Buddha-dharma from those within non-Buddhist traditions.
*Prātimokṣa* is translated here as "protecting liberation. By guarding the three karmas, one attains liberation. It is also...

It is called "Prātimokṣa" (Individual Liberation) because by maintaining a single matter, one attains individual liberation; it is so named because each instance is distinct and not identical. Regarding cause and effect:
it is because one relies on the cause of the dharma of precepts to reach the fruit of liberation.
II. Exhorting Others to Believe and Accept (Three Parts) 1. Exhortation to Believe 2. Exhortation to Accept 3. Concluding Exhortation I.
Exhortation to Believe The great assembly believes with sincere hearts: "You are one who shall become a Buddha; I am one who has already become a Buddha."
Always maintain such faith, for the aggregate of precepts is already fully complete.
Why is this so? Faith is the initial gateway for entering the Path. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Faith is that which enables entry. [One thinks:
"By upholding these precepts, I shall attain perfect enlightenment; you, too, should do likewise."

*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): All Buddhas have already attained realization; all sentient beings shall attain it. Thus, from the very beginning, there is ultimately no difference between the Buddha and sentient beings.

One who maintains the precepts and practices meditative concentration can become a Buddha. You should believe this matter with earnest clarity and harbor no doubts. For one whose precepts are already fully perfected:
A single thought of faith dispels myriad delusions; guarding against wrongdoing and ceasing evil are entirely contained within this.

Why wait for the formal interrogation regarding impediments, or for the *karmavācanā* and the three proclamations, before one may receive the precepts? When the Buddha cried out "Welcome," the person immediately became a *śramaṇa*;
this is precisely that meaning. Thus we know that one who lays down the butcher’s knife is counted among the thousand Buddhas, solely because of the presence of faith.

Do not disparage or hold them in low esteem; for a thousand kalpas one will fall [into lower realms] due to a lack of faith. Faith is the gateway to entering the Way—how could this be mere empty words?
○ Second, the exhortation to accept [the teaching].
All who possess a mind should receive the Buddha’s precepts. When sentient beings receive the Buddha’s precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas.
Once their rank is equal to that of Great Enlightenment, they are truly the children of all Buddhas.
All who possess a mind may receive the Bodhisattva’s Mahāyāna [precepts] of permanence, bliss, and so forth; this clarifies that sentient beings possess a mind.
All who possess Buddha-nature must inevitably become Buddhas; they must receive the three precepts. To reveal this hidden intent:
those with a mind—meaning all except wood and stone which lack consciousness—should already receive them.

All sentient beings within the six realms of existence ought to receive the precepts. "To encompass" (*she*) means "to receive. Hearing them externally and internalizing them within, one should hold them forever without losing them. This is the stage of Buddhahood.

How distant it may seem! Yet how is it that upon receiving the precepts, one immediately enters? This is because these precepts are the mind-ground transmitted by the thousand Buddhas; every Buddha attains Buddhahood by means of them.
For one who receives the Buddha-precepts, would they not immediately enter the rank of a Buddha? Regarding "the permanence, bliss, self, and purity of the Mahāyāna":
this clarifies that the Buddha-precepts are the Great Precepts of the Mahāyāna’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity. The Three Precepts.
This refers to the three clusters of the great precepts (*trisaṃvara*). Those who possess the Buddha-nature shall all become Buddhas;

these three clusters of precepts are the direct cause for attaining Buddhahood—how could one not receive them? Therefore, there is no evil that is not eliminated and no good that is not perfected. One who saves all beings without exception is a Buddha.

The restraint of discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*), the gathering of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the benefiting of sentient beings (*sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla*) are the reasons for receiving the precepts.
This refers to entering the stage of a Buddha. Question: Since their stage is identical to that of a Buddha, why are they not called Buddhas, but are merely called "sons of the Buddha"? Answer:

Although their stage is identical to that of a Buddha, their merits are not yet perfected. They are like a crown prince who will certainly ascend to the throne, but for now remains in the Eastern Palace.

Thus, he is a consecrated prince; one named a prince will surely succeed to the royal throne, and one named a son of the Buddha will surely succeed to the Buddha’s position—how could this be a trivial matter?
III. The Triple Exhortation:
The entire assembly should listen with reverence and a sincere heart.

I shall now recite the preceding lines as an exhortation and the following lines as an injunction to listen. This collectively clarifies the transmission of the precepts by all Buddhas. The Prologue is concluded.

*Fayi*: Because the Buddha himself esteemed the precepts, he exhorted the great assembly to be single-minded. When we now recite the precepts thousands of years later, can we not do so as if facing the Buddha in person and hearing the Buddha’s own words?
Reverence (*gong*) means outward solemnity; respect (*jing*) means inward piety.

When both inner and outer sincerity are perfected, this is called being "single-minded. Regarding the category of the precepts for the mind-ground, if one is not single-minded, by what means could they be realized?
Attaining Entry. ○ Second, Śākyamuni’s Exhortation (in two parts): First, the narrator’s introductory account; second, Śākyamuni’s own discourse.

○ First, the narrator’s introductory account (in three parts): First, the Buddha’s desire to establish the precepts; second, the emission of light as an auspicious omen; third, [the assembly’s response].
May the great assembly listen! Section One:
The First Buddha’s Desire to Establish the Precepts (4). 1. Identifying the Teacher. 2. Indicating the Location. 3.
Clarifying the Attainment of the Way. 4. Proclaiming the Precepts.
First, the designation of the master of transformation:
"At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha" refers to the master of transformation,
the Great Sage, the Honored One of the Śākya clan.
*Fayi*: Regarding the "Master of Transformation" (*huazhu*), first the person is designated: "the Great Sage, the Honored One of the Śākyas. Next, his virtues are expressed:
he is called a "Great Sage" because he dwells in the ultimate fruit of the noble stages; he is called the "Honored One of the Śākyas" because he is the common patriarch of the sons of the Śākya clan.
As for the master who guides and transforms others, who else could it be but him?
Second, the location:
Initially, he sat beneath the Bodhi tree;
having attained the Way beneath the tree, it was therefore named the Tree of the Way (Dōju). It is also called "Contemplation" (Shisui); in Sanskrit, it is *Pippala*.

*Fayi*: Now, taking the first character [of the title] and joining it with the first character of the subsequent text forms the intended meaning. "First" refers to the initial attainment of the fruit of the Way;

this is the very first establishment of the precepts, the most urgent priority. *Bodhi* is here translated as "the Way. The Way is contemplation (*cintā*). As for "contemplation," it is the Sanskrit term *vaita*.
That the Way is contemplation means that when meditative reflection is undisturbed, that is the essence of the Way.
○ Having attained the Way through the three types of clear knowledge and realized unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,
he was immediately designated by the title of Samyaksaṃbuddha (the Perfectly All-Knowing One).
*Fayi*: That which is without deviation in the Dharma is called "correct" (*zheng*). That which is all-encompassing in wisdom is called "universal" (*bian*).

That which shatters the dream of birth and death is called "awakening" (*jue*). To synthesize these: that which is awakened to is both correct and universal. Now, regarding the term "Correct Awakening" (*Zhengjue*), within "correct" itself are inherently contained the two meanings of "correct" and "universal.
As for "unsurpassed": although this awakening is equally possessed by all sentient beings, it has not yet reached the state of a Buddha.
It is still considered "having a superior. When one attains the Buddha of Wondrous Enlightenment, whose wisdom is exhaustive and uniquely honored, it is called "having no superior.
IV. The Fourfold Exposition of the Precepts (4): 1. Designating the name of what is established; 2. The capacity to constitute the supreme cause;
3. The capacity to attain the supreme fruit; 4. Properly establishing the names [of the precepts].
○ First, the title of the precepts being established is indicated.
This is the initial establishment of the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa.
[The commentary] "Fayin" states: "The term 'Bodhisattva' is used to distinguish this from the Śrāvakas; it is the Prātimokṣa of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas."
[The previous section] ends here; see above for the beginning.
II. The Capable Causes for Accomplishment:
being filial and obedient toward one's parents, teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem.
The *Ratnakoṭi Sūtra* states: "If one serves one's parents with filial piety, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, will be in one's home.
Furthermore, if one can practice filiality, Mahābrahmā, the Honored Deva, will be in one's home. Moreover, if one can fulfill filial duty, Śākyamuni Buddha will be in one's home.
Śyāmaka Bodhisattva’s own illness was cured through filial service; the Wheel of Fire was swiftly extinguished by the Compassionate Child. Thus it is said.

Regarding its spiritual resonance: the *Erya* states, "To serve one's parents well is filiality (*xiao*). Filiality is thus obedience. Taishi Shuming interpreted filiality through the lens of obedience.
The *Xiaojing Gouming jue* states that the character for filiality (*xiao*) is defined as "ultimate" (*jiujing*), meaning the complete fulfillment of care and nourishment from beginning to end.
It may also be defined as "crossing over" (*du*). Crossing over refers to ritual propriety; it signifies being appropriately attuned to the seasonal warmth and cold.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden). Following the initial establishment of the Bodhisattva precepts, although these precepts encompass ten thousand practices, they take filial piety as their core;

hence it is said: "Be filial and obedient toward parents, teachers, monks, and the Three Jewels. As for the mention of Śakra and others, both the heavenly mind and the Buddha-mind desire nothing more than for people to be filial and obedient.
To serve one's parents well means that one provides for them in every way possible and attends to their needs with diligent devotion.
The beginning of the Way of Filial Piety is attended by Śakra Devānām Indra.
Those who can practice it further will carry out every act of filiality without exception. The middle of filial piety is attended by Brahmā.

Those who can fulfill it completely will repay the kindness of their parents in this life, their parents in previous lives, and their parents throughout all successive births, leaving none unrewarded. The culmination of filial piety is attended by Śākyamuni.
The heavens can hear the lowly, and the Buddha pervades all; that he is selected for his hidden grace is indeed a matter of principle.

Thus, when Śyāma cut out his own eyes to save his father, his chronic ailment was cured in a single morning; when one with a compassionate heart makes a vow to take on another’s suffering, the wheel of fire is extinguished in an instant.
That such actions move the heavens and such sincerity moves the Buddha is precisely like this. I fear that the world...
They did not believe it, asking, "How could the Buddha have been in such a household?
Therefore, he cited two matters to prove it. In the *Erya*, the "Shuming" chapter explains filial piety through obedience; the "Gouming" chapter explains filial piety by enumerating five meanings.

From these, he selected two: "investigation" (*jiu*) and "measurement" (*du*). However, in that book, "investigation" is assigned to the scholar-officials (*shi*), while "measurement" is assigned to the feudal lords (*zhuhou*). Now, taking the latter...
The text does not employ these meanings, but briefly outlines three senses. First is "conformity" (*shun*):
receiving the parents' countenance and nourishing their wills without any opposition or offense, as exemplified by figures such as Zeng Shen and Min Sun. Second is "ultimate fulfillment" (*jiujing*):

thoroughly understanding the beginning and the end, maintaining an uninterrupted single-mindedness, manifesting a gentle and mild countenance, and striving to please one's parents, as exemplified by the Great Shun and Lai Zi.

This is an example of such. Third, regarding "measures" (*dù*): this refers to the full observance of ritual protocols, such as settling the parents' beds at dusk and attending to them at dawn, providing coolness in summer and warmth in winter, as exemplified by King Wen and Xue Bao.
Regarding "the teacher-monk" (*shīsēng*): this refers to one's own *upādhyāya*, not a monk in general.

Following the principle of the "Precious Treasury," these may also be divided into three parts. First, "matters" (*shì*) refers to the service and nourishment of the teacher’s physical person. Second, "practice" (*xíng*) refers to... [the text continues with the instruction to follow].
To follow the teacher is to emulate his discipline. To "exhaust" [the purpose] means to propagate the teacher’s Way and universally benefit all sentient beings. It is the same for the Three Jewels.

As for "serving," it refers to making offerings to the Three Jewels, yet one may not necessarily be able to practice [their teachings]. As for "practicing," it refers to relying upon the Three Jewels, yet one may not necessarily be able to exhaust [the purpose].

One who "exhausts" [the purpose] succeeds and flourishes the Three Jewels; receiving the transmission above and transforming those below, their merit becomes all-pervasive and magnificent. The Sūtra cites these three...
Regarding the various causes for filial piety, the commentary states that "first" refers to parents, as they are the most immediate and proximate for human beings;
this one case is cited to serve as an analogy for the others. Furthermore, the teacher-monks and the Triple Gem are also called "parents":

the Dharma-body is born through the power of the preceptor’s instruction, and thus they are the parents of the Dharma-body; the life of wisdom is sustained through the power of cultivation under the Triple Gem.
Thus one attains it; this refers to the parents who are the life of wisdom.
Third, one is able to attain the supreme fruit:
the dharma of filial piety toward the Ultimate Way.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): The meaning of the precepts (*śīla*) fundamentally resides in filial piety and obedience.

Yet, those who practice such filial piety and obedience often regard it as merely the conduct of ordinary people, unaware that the method of filial piety is, in fact, the method of the Ultimate Way (*paramārtha*). This Ultimate Way is the most supreme path;
it is none other than Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). This Way is pure and vast, like empty space.
Emptiness: its essence is free from error and non-error; its function is without obstruction. To accord with this is the ultimate. A heart of filial piety perfectly accords with this Way;

therefore, it is called the Ultimate Way (*zhidao*). Furthermore, parents represent the meaning of Original Enlightenment (*benjue*), while teachers and monks represent the meaning of Prior Enlightenment (*xianjue*).
"Buddha" signifies the meaning of fulfilled awakening. "Dharma" signifies the meaning of manifesting awakening. "Sangha" signifies the meaning of harmonizing with awakening.
To accord with these, not turning away from them and not opposing them—is this not the sublime path of the unsurpassed, correct awakening realized by the Tathāgata?

That this path is called "ultimate" (zhì) distinguishes it from that which is merely extensive or shallow; thus it is termed the "supreme fruit. The *Lanpen Shu* states: "Śākyamuni is the Great Filial One."

Venerable One, you have requited the kindness of your parents through successive kalpas and attained perfect enlightenment by accumulating causes; this is what is meant by "superior cause and superior fruit.
Confucius praised filial piety, calling it the ultimate virtue and essential way, and further stated that the virtue of the sage cannot surpass that of filial piety.
Chengzi likewise held that the nature of life and filial fraternal duty are one and the same. He called filial piety the ultimate Way; its sincerity is such.
Is this so? One interpretation takes the three aforementioned types as examples to establish four objects.
To say that "one should practice filial piety according to this supreme Dharma" refers to the cause rather than the fruit; therefore, this [interpretation] is not accepted here.
Fourth, the formal conclusion of the names:
Filial piety is called the precept; it is also called restraint.
This refers to the establishment of the precepts.

*Fayi*: Following the preceding points on the excellence of the cause and the excellence of the fruit, this section concludes and resolves the matter by directly identifying filial piety (*xiao*) with the precepts (*jie*).

The *Fayuan zhulin* states: "The precepts are precisely filial piety; that is to say, all sentient beings are our parents. To refrain from killing and refrain from stealing is itself filial piety. The intent is exactly the same as this.
However, while these precepts may be named filial piety, it is not yet the case that filial piety is named the precepts.

Now, it is explained that filial piety and obedience inherently possess the meaning of the precepts. For instance, when being filial and obedient toward one's parents, one lowers their breath and softens their voice, ensuring their speech is free from harshness or contrariness;

this is called the precept of speech (*vāksaṃvara*). When attending to them with regularity and circumspection, ensuring that one’s actions do not cause offense or opposition, this is called the precept of body (*kāyasaṃvara*).

To love deeply and cherish [one's parents] until the end, with a mind free from discord or rebellion—this is called the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint). To follow the principle of ceasing evil out of fear of bringing shame upon one’s kin—this is called the *saṃvara-śīla*.
To follow the principle of practicing good in order to bring glory to one’s kin—this is called the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering wholesome dharmas).

To follow the principle of universal salvation—such as picking up mulberries to turn back a wild beast, sacrificing meat to awaken a ruler, or bestowing wealth upon all classes without exhaustion—this is called the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings). —The Master.
The Sangha and the Three Jewels are likewise so. To speak of it in brief: if one can simply be filial and obedient, one will naturally be complete in the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
It is precisely for this reason that the name "precept" (*śīla*) is established. Apart from filial piety, how could there be any precepts?
The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* says: "Having received and maintained the precepts, if one cannot make offerings to one's parents, teachers, or elders, one incurs [transgression]."

This is a transgression. To speak correctly, filial piety is itself the precept (*śīla*). It is also called "restraint" (*saṃvara*); that is to say, restraint is also designated by the name of filial piety.
To establish it as the dharma of the precepts in order to cease evil is what is termed "restraint. Now, if one simply practices filial obedience, one naturally does not commit evil;

how is this not restraint? The *Classic of Filial Piety* says: "One who is filial toward their parents does not speak unless it is according to the law, nor does he act unless it is according to the Way."

"Practice" (*xing*) also refers to the cessation of evil intentions. The character "precept" (*jie*) at the beginning generally refers to the essence of the precepts (*śīla-sarīra*), while "restraint" (*zhì*) at the end refers to the specific categories of precepts enumerated, such as the ten major and forty-eight minor precepts.
The single character "filiality" (*xiao*) alone can encompass the meaning of the precepts;
therefore, among the ten major precepts listed below, the first, second, third, fourth, and so on up to the... [text continues].
The ninth and tenth precepts are both called the "mind of filial piety.
The first light offense is likewise called the "mind of filial piety," as are the thirteenth, seventeenth, nineteenth, twenty-ninth, thirty-fifth, and forty-eighth.
Regarding the remaining precepts, they frequently cite parents as the primary example; thus, the principle of filial piety runs throughout the beginning and end of the ten major precepts.

This connects the beginning and end of the forty-eight minor precepts; once filial piety is established, all other precepts are fulfilled. Furthermore, filial piety is not merely called a "precept" (*śīla*);
it is also called "restraint" (*saṃvara*), and it is likewise termed the various teachings of the Tripiṭaka and all *dharmaparyāyas*.

There is nothing that is not encompassed within it. Question: The *dharmaparyāyas* are immeasurable and cannot easily be enumerated in their entirety. For instance, regarding rebirth in the Pure Land...
Birth is but a single dharma-gate. Within this sutra, it is beyond the reach of words. How is it that filial piety permeates all dharmas? Answer:
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations) states: "Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate the three kinds of merit. First:

filially supporting one's parents, serving teachers and elders, possessing a compassionate heart and refraining from killing, and practicing the ten wholesome actions. Second: receiving and upholding..."

The three refuges, the full observance of the various precepts, and the non-violation of dignified conduct, up to the third point of generating the bodhicitta and so forth—now, to nourish one’s parents, to serve one’s teachers and elders, and to receive the three refuges:
is this not filial piety toward one’s parents and reverence for the Sangha and the Triple Gem?
It is said: "Do not kill"; it is said: "the ten wholesome actions"; it is said: "the various precepts"; and it is said: "dignified conduct"—thus, there are no precepts that are not fully prepared.
Thus we know that precepts are not separate from filial piety. Various sutras state that by taking filial piety as the cause, one attains rebirth [in the Pure Land].
Therefore, this sutra truly encompasses the entire Dharma-gate of the Pure Land; it is simply that people themselves fail to perceive this.

For this reason, those who recite the Buddha's name and cultivate the Pure Land who do not accord with their parents cannot be called practitioners of Buddha-recitation. This is because the kindness of parents in giving birth to us is equal to the kindness of a Buddha.
To be disobedient to one's teachers and elders is not called "mindfulness of the Buddha," for they are identical with the Buddha’s transformation.
To be disobedient to the Three Jewels is not called "mindfulness of the Buddha"; although the Jewels are three, they are unified in the One Buddha.

Speaking according to the ultimate principle, to accord with the pure awakened mind and not oppose it with turbid defilement is what is called filial piety; to accord with the mind of compassionate benevolence and not... [the text continues].

To oppose stinginess and greed is what is called filial giving (*dāna*). To accord with a harmonious and gentle mind, rather than opposing it with anger and hatred, is what is called filial patience (*kṣānti*).
To accord with a firm and resolute mind, rather than opposing it with indolence, is what is called filial diligence (*vīrya*).
To accord with a tranquil mind, rather than opposing it with distraction, is what is called filial meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). To accord with spiritual awareness...
To have a mind that does not oppose [the parents] through folly—this is what is called "wisdom" within filial piety.

By extending this principle through analogy, if one does not oppose anything at all, then the myriad dharmas will all be perfected. How great is filial piety! How could it be merely designated as "precept" alone?
II. Emitting Light as an Auspicious Omen.
The Buddha immediately emitted immeasurable light from his mouth.
"Auspicious omen" (śakuna) means "faith. When one intends to expound a Great Matter, it is necessary to first emit light; therefore, it is called an auspicious omen. Light is form (*rūpa*).

The excellence of this image is such that it emits supreme radiance, summoning all those with karmic affinity to come together and hear the precepts. These precepts are the most supreme among all virtues;
they can extinguish evil and give rise to goodness. As for the light emitted from its mouth, it signifies that today the World-Honored One Śākyamuni proclaims the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva Precept Dharma.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden). As for the necessity of emitting light mentioned previously: it is truly because when a supreme matter is about to arise, auspicious omens manifest first.

How much more so in the case of these Mind-Ground Precepts, which transmit the Way through a thousand Buddhas and extend their transformation to all living beings—since no matter is greater than this, how could there not have been auspicious responses prior?
Regarding the excellence of their physical manifestations: on a small scale, they appear as sweet dew and limpid springs; on a large scale, they rain down [precious things].
The flowers shaking the earth, up to and including the emission of light, are all comprised within the category of material manifestations; they are auspicious omens possessing form.

Yet, among these, the emission of light alone is preeminent because it possesses the power to radiate brilliance and dispel darkness, and it embodies the principle of extinguishing evil and generating goodness.
Those who behold it give rise to the bodhicitta, and those who touch it are freed from the suffering of birth and death. Of all such omens...
Among these, this is the most supreme; it serves as a metaphor for how the precepts are the most supreme among all virtues. Regarding the phrase "emitted from the mouth," there are two meanings:
first, it signifies that this Dharma of the precepts was proclaimed by the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha];
second, it signifies that through hearing and receiving this Dharma of the precepts, Bodhisattvas achieve the supreme fruit, being thus "born from the mouth of the Buddha."
○ The Threefold Great Assembly’s Desire to Hear (3). First, a general description of the great assembly; second, a specific description of the fourfold assembly;
third, the assembly’s delight in hearing.
○ First, a general description of the great assembly.
At that time, a great assembly of hundreds of billions manifested;
humans and devas gathered together, and ordinary beings and sages were intermingled. Hence, it is called the "great assembly.
Second, the specific enumeration of the fourfold assembly.

The various bodhisattvas, the eighteen Brahmā deities, the sons of the six heavens of desire, and the sixteen great kings—namely, one bodhisattva, twenty-eight Brahmās, thirty-six sons of the heavens of desire, and forty-six kings.
Regarding the sixteen kingdoms, their names appear in the *Dīrgha Āgama*: first, Śākya; second, Magadha; third, Kāśi; fourth, Kośala.
1. Rāṣṭra; 2. Pañcāla; 3. Malla; 4. Cedi; 5. Vatsa; 6. Mālava;
7. Ceti; 8. Vatsa; 9. Nīla; 10. Vaṃśa; 11. Aśmaka; 12. Vatsa; 13. Sura; 14. Gandhāra.
Fifteenth is Kaṃboja; sixteenth is Aparāntaka. There are very many other kingdoms in the western lands; these have been mentioned only briefly.
Those with the capacity and response will naturally gather like clouds upon hearing this sound.
*Fayi*: The previous section described the general assembly; the present section highlights the preeminent. The Bodhisattvas are superior to the Śrāvakas;
the Brahmā heavens are superior to the Desire Realm heavens; the Desire Realm heavens are superior to the human realm; and the king is superior to his ministers and subjects.
This precept dharma is manifested as a supreme and sublime assembly for ordinary beings, sages, devas, and humans.
At these three times, the multitude joyfully desires to hear;
with palms joined and sincere hearts, they listen as the Buddha recites the Mahāyāna precepts of all Buddhas.
*Fayi*: "Joining the palms purifies the karma of the body. Single-mindedness purifies the karma of the mind. Listening with the ears focuses the mind and naturally quiets speech;
thus, it purifies the karma of the mouth. A listener of the Dharma should act in this manner."
II. Śākyamuni’s Own Explanation (3): 1. First, citing his own recitation; 2. Second, the causal conditions for emitting light;
3. Third, exhorting beings to practice and study.
I. First, citing his own recitation (2): 1. First, the introduction to his own recitation; 2. Second, exhorting others to recite.
The Initial Preface, Recited Personally.
The Buddha addressed the various bodhisattvas, saying: "I now, every half-month, personally recite the Dharma-precepts of all Buddhas.

[This is] revealed. This is the beginning of the establishment of the ritual for reciting the precepts that will endure for ten thousand generations. "Every half-month" refers to the day of the full moon.

The new moon day is the time for this. One should diligently recite it twice [each month], fearing forgetfulness. Furthermore, the waxing and waning phases of the moon serve as metaphors for wholesome and unwholesome karma;
one should examine oneself accordingly.
2. Encouraging Others to Recite:

"All of you bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds, as well as those in the ten stages of setting forth, the ten stages of nurturing, the ten vajra stages, and the various bodhisattvas of the ten bhūmis, should also recite this."
Generally speaking, there are five stages of persons: first, the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), which refers to bodhisattvas on the shared stages (*sādhāraṇabhūmi*);

second, the stage of application (*prasthāna*), which refers to the first ten mental states as listed in the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*: first, renunciation (*tyāga*); second, morality (*śīla*); third, patience (*kṣānti*); fourth, diligence (*vīrya*); fifth, concentration (*samādhi*); and sixth, wisdom (*prajñā*).
7. Aspiration; 8. Protection; 9. Joy; 10. The Crown of the Mind. 3. The Ten Minds of Cultivation (the ten intermediate minds):
1. Loving-kindness; 2. Compassion; 3. Joy; 4. Equanimity; 5. Giving; 6. Kind Speech; 7. Benefiting; 8. Commonality; 9. Concentration; 10. Wisdom. 4.
The Ten Minds Following the Vajra-like Samādhi: 1. Faith; 2. Mindfulness; 3. Dedication; 4. Penetration; 5. Perfection; 6. [The sixth is omitted in the source text].
1. Non-retrogression; 2. The Mahāyāna; 3. Signlessness; 4. Wisdom; 5. The indestructible mind; 6. The fifty stages (*bhūmi*), which refers to those from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward:
(1) the stage of the equality of essential nature; (2) the stage of skillful means of essential nature; (3) the stage of luminosity of essential nature; (4) the stage of suchness of essential nature;
(5) the stage of wisdom-illumination of essential nature; (6) the stage of flowers of essential nature... [and so forth].
7. The Ground of Radiance; 8. The Ground of the Fulfillment of Essential Nature; 9. The Ground of the Buddha’s Lion’s Roar of Essential Nature;
10. The Ground of Essential Nature Entering the Buddha-realm.

*Fayi*: "Bodhisattvas who share the same ground" refers to those who have resolved their minds through the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*), sharing the same ground as the Buddhas. One interpretation states that this refers to the ten grounds (*bhūmi*) shared by the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

From the initial arousal of the mind, through its cultivation and maturation, up to the adamantine stage (*vajra*), these stages are divided into beginning, middle, and end, and are termed the thirty minds (*triṃśaccitta*).

The first ten minds constitute the stage of abiding: first, the mind of equanimity, which relinquishes all internal and external phenomena; second, the mind of precept, which is the purity of the single path;
third, the mind of patience, which is the acceptance of all phenomena as they are, for their characteristics cannot be apprehended;
fourth, the mind of diligence, which enters the conventional truth through non-arising, being free from dualistic marks; fifth, the mind of concentration, in which every thought-moment is quiescent.
1. The Mind of Determination (*niścaya-citta*): All natures within the three realms arise through the power of meditative concentration and are extinguished therein.

2. The Mind of Wisdom (*prajñā-citta*): Cultivating the inconceivable contemplation, one enters the Middle Way of the Single Truth (*eka-satya*). 3. The Mind of Vow (*praṇidhāna-citta*): Because one seeks the fulfillment of vows through the intermediate path of cultivation upon first generating the mind of enlightenment, it is the source of all practices.
4. The Mind of Protection (*rakṣā-citta*): Protecting the Three Jewels and all meritorious deeds.

Virtue consists of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Ninth is the mind of joy (*muditā-citta*): seeing others obtain happiness, one constantly gives rise to gladness;
it does not enter into conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) that take all things as their object. Tenth is the crown mind (*mūrdhan-citta*): this single path is most supreme;

one does not undergo the fruits of the six realms and will certainly not regress from the lineage of the Buddha. These ten minds constitute the stage of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*). First is the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*): regarding selflessness...
The contemplation associated with joy within wisdom causes all sentient beings to attain the fruit of compassionate happiness. Second is compassion (*karuṇā*):
perceiving all phenomena as they truly are within emptiness, one bestows supreme happiness upon those in the three grades of enmity. Third is sympathetic joy (*muditā*):
rejoicing in non-arising, it causes sentient beings to enter right faith, abandon false views, and turn their backs on the suffering of the six realms. Therefore...
1. The mind of joy (*muditā*). 2. The mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*): the intrinsic nature of self and others is unapprehendable. 3. The mind of giving (*dāna*):

one's own body, the bodies of others, kingdoms, cities, men, and women are all the mark of suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*); neither recipient nor giver undergoes conjunction or dispersion. 4. The mind of eloquent speech (*priyavāditā*):
teaching all sentient beings with the words of the noble Dharma. 5. The mind of benefit (*arthacaryā*): manifesting within the six realms of existence.
One does not regard immeasurable sufferings as a calamity, but considers benefiting others as one's own profit. Eighth is the mind of sameness:
entering the six realms of existence, one views all phenomena as identical to emptiness, identical to non-arising, and identical to non-self. Ninth is the settled mind:
seeing that all seeds of self, others, and internal and external sentient beings are entirely devoid of conjunction, dispersion, accumulation, or production.

The ten wisdom-minds: one contemplates that all false views, fetters, and afflictions lack a determinate intrinsic nature. The subsequent ten minds constitute the stage of "heading toward" (the path).

First is the mind of faith: all phenomena are empty; because each moment of mind is empty, each act of faith is quiescent. This is called the "faith of non-attachment. Second is the mind of mindfulness:
through the six recollections, one is constantly aware and constantly practicing giving, remaining unattached to the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

There is no liberation. The marks of arising, abiding, and ceasing are unmoving, neither arriving nor departing, neither coming nor going. Third is the mind of dedication, which enters the Dharma-realm in eternal quiescence.
Fourth is the penetrating mind, which endures and accords with the true nature of all things; it is the penetration of phenomena and the penetration of their meaning.

The expression is thorough, and the transformation through teaching is thorough. The causes and effects of the three periods of time and the faculties and practices of all sentient beings are, in their suchness, neither joined nor dispersed.

Fifth is the perfect mind: it directly illuminates and enters the wisdom of non-arising, transforming and teaching the sentient beings of the ten directions so that they all enter *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Sixth is the non-regressing mind: it does not enter any stage of ordinary beings, does not give rise to various views, and does not...

1. Arising is the cause of accumulation. 2. The Mahāyāna mind: because it understands the single emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it enables all sentient beings to cross the river of the three realms and enter the ocean of Buddhahood.

3. The signless mind: regarding all fetters, karma, and phenomena of the three periods of time as suchness (*tathatā*) and the single truth, one practices within non-arising (*anutpāda*). All Buddhas are my teachers; all sages and saints are my companions.
All are equally non-arising. Ninth is the mind of wisdom: regarding all dharmas, whether spoken by Māras or spoken by Buddhas, one enters the locus of the two truths through discernment;
they are neither one nor two, and there are no aggregates, elements, or sense bases. Tenth is the indestructible mind:

entering the wisdom of the noble stages, approaching the state of liberation, attaining the cultivation of the correct gate, clarifying the bodhicitta, and remaining unmoved by the eight māras. The assembly...
The Sage strokes his head; all Buddhas exhort and inspire him. He attains the Vajra Samādhi and enters the gateway of all practices.

Regarding the ten stages (*bhūmi*): from the Stage of Equality to the Stage of Entry into the Buddha-realm—these refer to the ten stages beginning with the Joyful (*pramuditā*) and ending with the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*).

1. The Ground of Equality (*samatā-bhūmi*). This is the stage of entering immeasurable Buddha-lands from a single Buddha-land, entering immeasurable eons from a single eon, and constantly entering the two truths while remaining within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). 2. The Ground of Skillful Means (*upāya-kauśalya-bhūmi*).

This is the stage of being pure, clear, and penetrating regarding all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and dharmas such as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. 3. The Ground of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*). By means of the three... [text continues]

With the wisdom that clearly understands the profound, one knows the Dharma-gates of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. Manifesting bodies in the six realms of existence, one expounds immeasurable categories of Dharma within a single voice.
Fourth is the *Ārciṣmatī* (Blazing) Stage: neither interrupted nor eternal, arising, abiding, and ceasing simultaneously, one cultivates immeasurable merit.
Every practice is radiant, teaching and transforming all sentient beings so that they may see [the truth].

It is the Buddha-nature. In the fifth stage, the Ground of Illumination through Wisdom, one uses the wisdom of the ten powers to know the causes and effects of one’s own cultivation, and likewise knows the causes and effects of all sentient beings;
one regards pure lands as impure lands, and regards impure lands as pure lands.
In the sixth, the Ground of Flower Radiance, the clear wisdom of the ten supernormal powers manifests various [teachings] to all sentient beings.

The Stage of Transformation. The Seventh is the Stage of Fulfillment: fulfillment of desire, fulfillment of the mind of exertion, fulfillment of the mind of mindfulness, fulfillment of wisdom, fulfillment of liberation, and fulfillment of the six supernormal powers;
therein one manifests as a Buddha in all Buddha-lands. The Eighth is the Stage of the Buddha’s Roar.
He enters the Samādhi of the Stage of the Dharma King. His wisdom is like that of a Buddha.
He bestows the medicine of the Dharma upon all sentient beings, acting as a great Dharma Master and a great Guide.
Within hundreds of thousands of gates of dhāraṇī, samādhi, vajra, supernormal powers, and liberation—such hundreds of thousands of gates of space and gates of equality—he is great.
He is sovereign. He may speak of kalpas as non-kalpas, and speak of non-kalpas as kalpas; there is nothing he cannot accomplish as he intends. Ninth is the Flower Adornment Ground (Avataṃsaka-bhūmi).

By means of the Buddha’s majestic deportment and the Tathāgata’s samādhi, he enters and emerges from it at no fixed time. Simultaneously, he attains Buddhahood throughout ten billion four-continent worlds.
He manifests infinite bodies and speaks infinite Dharma-gates through body, speech, and mind, while being able to transform the realm of Māra.
Entering the Buddha-realm; the Buddha-realm enters the Mara-realm. Within a single thought-moment, infinite divine functions are manifested.
The ground of the ten Buddha-realms is empty, further empty, and yet again empty, like the nature of space. It is fully endowed with the ten qualities of the wisdom of equality.
Therein are unspeakably many wonderful and marvelous Dharma-gate chapters, and the *dhāraṇī* of the wonderful threefold gate of *samādhi*.
These gates of the *nirvedhabhāgīya* are not known by those of the lower stages; only the immeasurable body, speech, and mind of a Buddha can exhaust their source.
In the sūtras of each stage, it is stated that they possess immeasurable merit; for now, I shall briefly cite a small portion, which is like a mere hair’s breadth.
These thirty minds and ten stages differ slightly in name from those in the various *Avataṃsaka* sūtras, yet in reality—
This is identical. Furthermore, the phrase "even more so for the reciter" is a rhetorical expression used to draw a comparison. [The question asks:

"Regarding this statement that it is 'shared with the stage,' how does it differ from the *Śīla-sūtra* (Good Precepts), which divides the twelve abodes into seven stages—six being the bodhisattva stages and one being the stage shared by the bodhisattva and the Tathāgata?
[The answer is: That [text] focuses on the ultimate conclusion, speaking in terms of the fruit.
This means that when a bodhisattva’s practice reaches this stage, they become identical to a Tathāgata; this is its origin, spoken in terms of the cause.

It means that from the very first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*), one is already identical to a Tathāgata. Furthermore, this sutra takes the "mind-ground" (*citta-bhūmi*) as its central tenet.
These thirty minds are precisely the various dharma-gates of the mind-ground; the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts are all contained within these thirty minds.
The intermediate precepts arise from within the mind, as clarified in the section on the formulation of the precepts. Question: Why is it not said that the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are the mind?
Answer: The thirty minds are the causes of the ten stages; upon reaching the ten stages, the mind that was generated becomes fully perfected.
Above, it bears the Buddha-dharma; below, it carries sentient beings. Because it possesses the characteristics of earth, the mind is metaphorically called "earth.
In reality, there is no earth apart from the mind.
II. The Causes and Conditions for Emitting Light (2): 1. Directly explaining the conditions. 2. Enumerating the causes and conditions.
First, the conditions are stated directly.
Therefore, the light of the precepts issues from the mouth. [The commentary] explains:

"The mouth being able to emit light is called the condition (*pratyaya*); there must be a causal basis for this, which is called the cause (*hetu*). Now it is said that the light comes from the mouth.
[The text] proceeds. This directly explains the conditions (*pratyaya*) but has not yet explained the causes (*hetu*).
II. Listing the Causes and Conditions (in two parts): First, indicating the attainment of the fruit; second, indicating the practice of the cause.
I. Indicating the attainment of the fruit.
It has conditions but is not without cause; it is light. This light is neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor black; it is neither form nor mind.
It is neither existent nor non-existent, and it is not a phenomenon of cause and effect.

There are three aspects to attaining the fruit (*phala*): first, it is a mind that is neither blue nor yellow; second, it is neither existent nor non-existent; third, it is not a phenomenon of cause and effect.

[The commentary] *Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden) states: The meaning is that since there must be a cause for there to be conditions, "light" (*ābhāsa*) is the fruit that has been attained; there must necessarily be a cause that brings it about.
"A mind that is neither blue nor yellow" means it does not fall into deluded objects or deluded sentiments, nor into the [realms of] ordinary people or those of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
It is the fruit. It is neither existence nor non-existence; it is not the fruit of falling into the biased views of clinging to annihilationism or eternalism. It is not cause-and-effect;
it does not fall into the fruit of the provisional vehicles that involve cultivation and realization.

This mind-ground precept-text itself transcends the realm of objects and conditions, is free from annihilationism and eternalism, and cuts off cultivation and realization. Therefore, its attainment of the fruit is thus. Question: Since it is said there is a cause, [it is asked:]
One attains the fruit. Furthermore, it is asked: why is it said that this is neither cause nor effect? The answer is: there are two meanings to this.
First, it is not the cause and effect of the mundane world; second, it is neither cause nor effect. It is precisely because of this that it constitutes the true cause and the true fruit.
Second, the cause for manifesting practice:
this is the fundamental source of all Buddhas, the root of practicing the bodhisattva path, and the foundation for all the Buddha-sons of the great assembly.
The three causes of practice are: first, the source of all Buddhas; second, the root of Bodhisattvas; and third, the root of the great assembly.
Alternatively, it is said that these represent the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): The ocean of the Buddhas' perfect and universal knowledge is vast and inexhaustible; this precept of the mind-ground is its primary source.
The myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas blossom forth to achieve the wondrous fruit; this precept of the mind-ground is their very root.
All sentient beings, through their endless succession of births, even those who shall eventually become Buddhas, likewise [rely upon it].
The precepts of the mind-ground are their very foundation. They penetrate both the sages and the ordinary; all rely upon these precepts.
Because the precepts are pure, when purity reaches its ultimate limit, luminosity and penetration arise spontaneously. Some speak of the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional:
the Buddha is a supramundane phenomenon, the ultimate truth; sentient beings are mundane phenomena, the conventional truth. As for the Bodhisattva, they aspire to the higher realms...
The noble fruit follows downward to accord with the sentiments of ordinary beings, thus manifesting both the ultimate and conventional truths.
○ Third, Exhorting Others to Practice and Study (in two parts): First, the presentation of the four exhortations; second, the explanation of the four exhortations.
First, the four exhortations are set forth:
"Therefore, all you sons of the Buddha in the great assembly, you should receive and uphold it; you should read and recite it; you should study it well.
First is the exhortation to receive, second is the exhortation to uphold, third is the exhortation to read and recite, and fourth is the exhortation to study.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): "To receive" means to accept and not reject; "to uphold" means to grasp and not forget; "to read and recite" means to orally expound the text;
and "to learn well" means to practice its teachings with vigor. If one hears but does not receive, what was heard will not enter the mind.
If one receives but does not uphold, what has been grasped will be lost again. If one upholds but does not recite, one will remain mired in ignorance and fail to master the details."
To recite without studying results in empty words; in the end, what benefit could there be? Merit lies in the complete integration of both. Therefore, it is called the "Four Exhortations.
Nevertheless, the general heading states "four precepts and three exhortations," which refers merely to receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting, without mentioning "studying well.

In the old edition, the character "應" (yīng) does not appear above "善學" (shàn xué); instead, it is joined with the following phrase "佛子" (fó zǐ) to form a single sentence, which seems to be [an error].
This is secure. Why? Because within the text of the tenfold summary, there is the phrase "O virtuous learners," which perfectly accords with this.
Now, four exhortations are set forth; perhaps fearing that later generations might corrupt the text, these may not necessarily represent the primary intent of the commentator.
Let the reader examine this carefully.
II. Explanation of the Four Exhortations.
Son of the Buddha, listen attentively. Those who receive the Buddha’s precepts include kings, princes, high officials, and ministers; bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs;
the eighteen Brahmā heavens and the sons of the gods of the six heavens of desire; commoners, eunuchs, lecherous men and women, and slaves.
The eight classes of spirits, Vajra deities, animals, and even transformed humans— provided they understand the words of the Dharma Master—
all receive the precepts and are called the foremost pure ones.
This merely explains the single matter of encouraging acceptance; all else is omitted.
*Fayi*: "Eunuch" (*huanmen*) is a general term for an internal attendant. The Vajra Deities possess great majestic power.
They are able to repel external māras and protect the Buddha-dharma, like a diamond (vajra).

As for "transformed persons," they are like the magically created beings produced by non-humans; they must be those formed through the transformations of devas, nāgas, ghosts, or animals. To state it briefly:
Whether they belong to the class of kings, ministers, monks, nuns, devas, humans, ghosts, spirits, animals, or transformed beings—
even unto all possible categories— they may all serve as vessels for the precepts, provided that they are able to understand the Dharma Master.

It says simply, "If one understands. This distinguishes those who do not understand; however, anyone who understands the words may receive the precepts, and anyone who receives the precepts attains purity.
Before receiving the precepts, one may still possess either purity or defilement;

once the precepts have been received, one becomes a vessel of purity in every respect, just as the hundred rivers enter the sea and share the same salty taste. This passage corresponds with the fourth [section].

The ten minor [offenses] are largely the same; however, that text does not list animals, whereas this text does not list those without sexual organs (*aṇḍaja*) or those with dual sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*).
This is because in that text, animals are included within "all beings," while in this text, those without sexual organs and those with dual sexual organs are included among the eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*).

This passage merely explains the exhortation to receive [the precepts]. Since it is through receiving them that one is able to uphold and recite them, the explanation of the exhortation to receive them is intended to encompass the rest as well.

Question: The prohibitions regarding the grave and light offenses of the Śrāvaka precepts are exceptionally strict in their prevention. Yet, the Bodhisattva precepts allow for the inclusion of those who are licentious, low-born, ghosts, or animals without exception.
Is it not the case that those of the Lesser Vehicle (Śrāvakas) are all of noble capacity, while the Great Beings (Bodhisattvas), on the contrary, are a mixture of non-humans?
Yes. [The Buddha] replied: "Śrāvakas receive the tonsure and dye their robes from the Buddha; if they were not to exercise discernment, I fear it would damage the True Dharma.
Bodhisattvas specialize in benefiting sentient beings; if they were not to be inclusive, their capacity for transformation and deliverance would be limited.

However, even within this universal salvation there are distinctions, which are detailed in the forty-eight minor transgressions [of the Brahmā Net Sūtra]; I shall not trouble you with an elaborate explanation here."
