I have likewise recited all that the bodhisattvas of the past have studied, all that the bodhisattvas of the future shall study, and all that the bodhisattvas of the present are now studying.
Having thus briefly explained the characteristics of the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa, you should train yourselves in them, reverently accepting and upholding them.
Those who fail to manifest their hidden potential lose the name of "Mahāyāna Bodhisattva" in the present; those who are not of the Buddha-seed lose the fruit of the ultimate stage in the future.
As for "physical appearance" (*lakṣaṇa*): although the precepts have no form, they possess that which can be maintained and observed, and thus are also called "appearance."
II. Detailed Explanation (Ten Sections). First, the Precept Against Killing (up to the Tenth, the Precept Against Slandering the Triple Gem).
● First, the Precept Against Killing (Two Parts): 1. Brief Presentation; 2. Entry into the Text.
First, the brief introduction:
Regarding the beginning of the ten grave precepts, if unchaste conduct were placed first among the śrāvakas, it would be because many people commit such transgressions;

furthermore, as these afflictions are tied to the [sensual] realms, they are grave, and thus they are proscribed. Although killing is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), it is rare for renunciants to commit this sin. Moreover, [it is placed first]...
It is easy to prevent and sever [transgressions]. Since lust arises easily, it must be restrained at its inception. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"The precepts of the Śrāvakas gauge human sentiments and mostly prevent the side of arising [transgression]. Therefore, those that are minor tend to arise frequently; thus, they are strictly regulated. Those that are grave arise rarely;

yet even for minor offenses, regulations are established. Regarding lust, it is not an intrinsic offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), whereas killing is an intrinsic offense. When the Mahāyāna establishes its regulations, it should [be understood] in this way.

This is the first point. Now, regarding "killing": because it severs the life of another, and because there is a sentient being within the continuity of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), one now cuts off this continuity;
therefore, it is called "killing. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "To obstruct future continuity is what is termed 'killing'."

The rules for monastics and laypeople are the same, such as in the case of the five precepts and the eight precepts. Since the Mahāsattva takes compassion as his fundamental principle, he must sever [the roots of unwholesome action].
The seven classes of Bodhisattvas commit the same offenses; the five classes of Śrāvakas are largely the same but differ slightly.

What they share is the common prohibition against killing. The differences consist briefly of three matters: first, the difference between what is permitted and what is prohibited; second, the difference between matter and mind; third...

The differences in gravity and the differences in what is permitted or prohibited are as follows: A Mahāsattva may take life when he perceives the appropriate opportunity, whereas a Śrāvaka is not permitted to take life even if he perceives such an opportunity.
Regarding the difference between form and mind: a Mahāsattva disciplines the mind, while a Śrāvaka disciplines the body. Regarding the third difference in gravity:

if a Mahāsattva harms his teacher, he commits a pācittiya (an offense of immediate retribution), whereas for a Śrāvaka it is not a pācittiya; furthermore, the gravity for a Mahāsattva is even greater than the gravity for a Śrāvaka.

*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): "Non-Brahmacarya" refers to impure conduct. "Bound to the stages" (*dhi-baddha*) means that the afflictions of the stages to which one is attached are particularly heavy.
"To gauge" (*xiaoxi*) is synonymous with to deliberate or measure. Because one deliberates on human sentiments and finds that lust arises frequently, lust was the first to be regulated.
Furthermore, lust is the source of birth and death; Śrāvakas do not give rise to great compassion, as they fear only birth.

Because death follows from it, sexual misconduct comes first. Killing is the enemy of compassion; since Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) do not fear birth and death, but rather universally deliver others through great compassion, killing is placed first.

Regarding natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*): these are offenses by their very nature, as they are sinful within the fundamental nature of things, rather than being prohibited for the first time by the Vinaya.
Furthermore, the seven assemblies consist of: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, śikṣamāṇās, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
The five assemblies exclude the two lay groups and refer exclusively to those who have left the household life.

Regarding "killing when one perceives the appropriate occasion": if one perceives that there is a specific necessity for killing, then performing the act of killing incurs no harm; it is like killing one [to save many].
A person who saves many others severs their physical body to preserve their wisdom-life; this is the grand standard of the Mahāsattvas, beyond the capacity of the Śrāvakas.
Therefore, what is permitted for Bodhisattvas is prohibited for Śrāvakas. To restrain the mind is to sever the intent to kill altogether;
to restrain the physical form merely eliminates the act of killing. As for one who harms their teacher: the teacher is able to nurture the Dharma-body. This is...

Because he is the seed of the Buddha, a Great Being (Mahāsattva) who harms him commits a heinous crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*). A Śrāvaka, however, has no expectation of attaining Buddhahood, and thus [harming one] is considered light.
One interpretation states that even killing a mother while as an infant does not constitute a heinous crime, because such a child is ignorant and lacks conscious intent.
If a Śrāvaka, relying on this, were to intentionally harm his teacher, it would arise from a deliberate mind; he would certainly fall into the Avīci Hell and must therefore be cautious.
Furthermore, these three distinctions are frequently found in the various precepts that follow; they may be inferred by analogy and need not be cited in their entirety.
II. Entering the Text (three parts): First, identifying the person; second, setting forth the matter; third, concluding with the offense.
First, the person is identified.
The Buddha said: "O Sons of the Buddha!

To reveal the hidden meaning: having received the Great Precepts of the Buddha, you are born from the Buddha; your conduct must perpetuate and flourish the lineage of the Buddhas, for you possess the status of a son."

The Meaning. Do not disparage yourselves. ○ Second, the Exposition of the Matter (Three Parts): First, what is inappropriate; second, clarifying what is appropriate; third, concluding on what is inappropriate.
○ First, what is inappropriate (Three Parts): First, clarifying the act of killing; second, establishing the characteristics of the karma; third, citing a light case to illustrate a grave one.
First, clarifying the act of killing:
whether one kills by oneself, instructs another to kill, employs the means of killing, praises killing, rejoices upon seeing it being committed, or even kills through incantations.

First, killing by oneself: this refers to taking the life of another through one's own action. There are three types of objects: internal form (the body), external form (inanimate matter), and both internal and external form;
all constitute an offense. Second, inciting others: the other person’s act is also killing. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Verbal instruction constitutes the sin of killing."
It is not merely the act of inflicting a wound. The Vinaya section contains a vast number of detailed rules.

Regarding the three types of preparatory means for killing—such as commanding others or sending messengers—as well as the preliminary acts of killing, namely binding, tethering, and so forth, one incurs guilt.

Fourth, praising [the act] of killing also constitutes an offense. Fifth, rejoicing [in it], such as encouraging or exhorting another to take life, is likewise a violation. Sixth, killing by incantation refers to the *Vetāla*...
Although [the killing of] *dhāra* and others may depend on other conditions, they are all likewise offenses. The Vinaya clarifies fifteen types of killing, namely:
*utpāda*, *stūpa*, snares, strings, triggers, *vidhāra*, and so forth, as explained extensively in the Vinaya section, and so on.

*Fayi*: The *Xianshelun* (Treatise on Manifesting Colors) identifies internal color as consciousness (*vijñāna*) and external color as the sense organs (*indriya*). Now, to take away consciousness and destroy color constitutes the taking of life.
As for the mention of "internal and external colors," these collectively form three [elements]; all three together constitute the offense known as taking life.

One interpretation states that "internal and external colors" refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*); consciousness is internal, the organs are external, and the breath serves as their intermediate intersection.
Furthermore, it is not merely the act of inflicting a wound, nor is it limited to physical injury; it clarifies that [the victim] is already dead.
As for "praising," it means that although the other person has not necessarily killed, one nevertheless offers commendation to assist them in completing the act.

As for "rejoicing," it means that when the other person intends to commit a killing, one immediately complies with them to gratify their intent. As for "preparatory acts prior to killing," these consist of binding, fettering, and so forth.
Only then can one kill. *Vidhara* is the name for an evil incantation. Regarding "relying on other conditions":

although it does not involve killing entirely through incantations, the evil intent of sorcery and bewitchment takes the incantation as its primary means. Among the fifteen types of killing, I shall briefly cite one or two.
*Udaka* refers to a pit of fire. *Stunda* refers to things such as collapsing ground. *Kāla* refers to a wooden trap.
"Fraudulent taking" means to deceive and seize. "String" refers to a bow. "Fletching" refers to the stone of a crossbow. "Vetāla" refers to using a corpse to cast a spell that causes a person to die.
All of the above involve taking life; because the body subsequently dies, a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) is incurred.
II. The characteristic of the completion of the act (*karmalakṣaṇa*).
The cause of killing, the conditions for killing, the method of killing, and the act of killing—these constitute the characteristic of the completion of the act.
When the three types of action complete the act of killing, that which is performed by oneself is the primary bodily action (*kāyakarma*). Teaching others and...

Regarding incantations (*mantra*): when one performs a physical act through verbal karma and intends in the mind to kill, and a spirit or deity (*deva-gandharva*) spontaneously proclaims its fulfillment, this is the creation of physical karma through mental karma (*manas-karma*).

These three stages are all acts of karma (*karma-artha*) performed within the context of conditions (*pratyaya*). As for the "method of killing" (*vadha-dharma*), this refers to weapons such as swords and blades, pits, snares, and so forth;

because each possesses a functional essence (*dharma-svabhāva*), they are termed "methods. Regarding the causes and conditions of killing, there are two types: those involving close relatives and those involving distant ones.

[The factors are: the basis, the primary cause, the contributing conditions, and the karmic function. First, the basis: it is a sentient being. Second, the perception: the perception that it is a sentient being. Third, the act: the performance of killing. Fourth, the result: the severance of life. As for the contributing conditions, they consist of the mind of killing as the primary cause, with the remaining factors acting as supporting conditions.

As for the karmic function, it consists of producing the future fruit. Fourth [the four factors]: first, a sentient being; second, the perception of a sentient being; third, the act of killing; fourth, the severance of life.

First, regarding sentient beings: although sentient beings are numerous, they are broadly categorized into three grades. The first is the superior grade, which refers to the Buddhas, sages, parents, and the monastic community (śāstṛ-saṃgha).
To harm these constitutes a transgression of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*). Regarding those who have attained the three fruits [of the śramaṇa], there are two interpretations.

The first states that harming them is equivalent to a transgression of immediate retribution, because when one harms a śrāvaka, it is already a matter of the utmost gravity. The second states that it constitutes a grave offense (*guru-āpatti*), as stated in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.

This clarifies the three types of killing. Killing those who have attained the three fruits of the path constitutes only the intermediate category of killing; it does not fall under the highest category. Therefore, one should know that this is not a *ānantarya* (immediate) offense.

Regarding Bodhisattvas, from the stage of "practice through understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā*) upwards, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* refers to them as "Bodhisattvas of certain destiny" (*niyata-bhūmi*), which follows the same classification.

Here, we take those who do not turn toward the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) as being of the stage of certain destiny. Alternatively, one may take those from the seventh mental moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) onwards; both are acceptable.

This is for the purpose of severing [the continuity of life]. Regarding the mother who nurtures the fetus, one interpretation states there is no transgression, while the other states it constitutes a transgression of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).

For a Mahāsattva, this is a grave offense, more serious than for a Śrāvaka. The middle grade refers to humans and devas; harming them constitutes a grave offense. The lower grade refers to the four realms of existence (*catur-gati*). There are two interpretations:
first, some say they are equally grave because the Mahāsattva’s prevention of killing is particularly strict. As the text says: "All that have life..."

"Killing is permitted"—this is precisely the proof [of that]. Second, it is said that one merely commits a minor offense (*āpatti-laghu*), which is concurrently regulated within the context of the grave precepts (*guru-śīla*), because [the recipient] is not a suitable vessel for the Dharma.
The text states "one who possesses life," which cites a light case to illustrate the grave. Third, regarding the intent to kill, there are two types.

There are two types of intent for killing: first, the intent to kill by one's own hand; second, the intent to kill by instructing another. Regarding the intent to kill by one's own hand, there are two sub-types: pervasive intent (*sāmānya-citta*) and specific intent (*vyavacchinna-citta*).
Pervasive intent refers to actions such as indiscriminately digging pits or setting traps, or indiscriminately burning or boiling [living beings].

These constitute an offense regardless of the three moral natures (*tri-śīla*). If one intends for a certain being but harms another, or if one harbors a harmful mind toward all beings, these all belong to pervasive intent. This concludes the section on one’s own direct involvement.

Regarding the object (*viṣaya*): furthermore, if life is no longer sustained, even if the intended purpose was not achieved, it is entirely a formal offense (*sāpattika*). As for "separated by intention":

if one makes a pit specifically for this person, with no intent toward another, yet that other person dies, it is still an offense. If the other person’s side does not succeed [in their aim], it is a minor defilement (*dūṣaṇīya-āpatti*).
If this path was originally one used by many people for travel, and one now makes a pit specifically for this person, yet that person dies [as a result], [it is likewise].

It is also grave. Because this killing involves a specific entity that can cause harm, and because it possesses the causal conditions of the mind, it still pertains to the general category of the mind.

If one originally intends to strike an eastern person but mistakenly strikes a western person, and there is no intent to kill regarding the western person, this belongs to the category of the "separated mind.
There are two times when the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is severed: first, in this life; second, in future lives. In this life, there are two [types].

There are two points: first, committing a grave offense while possessing the precepts; second, severing [the precepts] when they no longer exist. When the precepts depart, the resulting offense is a minor defilement (*pāyattika*).

At the time of death, the resulting offense is the same as before. For a *śrāvaka* at the point of death who has not yet severed the *śrāvaka* abandonment of full ordination, it results in the binding of the five precepts and so forth.
After being reborn, the precepts are naturally restored in two ways: first, by one’s own recollection.

Second, not being conscious of it oneself. Regarding "being conscious of it oneself": if one dies by the force of prior circumstances, or if one further employs a means [of suicide], it constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), because one is conscious of it both before and after.
Regarding "not being conscious of it oneself": if one dies by the force of circumstances, it constitutes a grave offense, because at the time of death one still possesses the precepts.
If one employs a means, one should know that the previous wound does not cause death; rather, it is at the time of the subsequent means that death occurs.

I do not recall it; it was merely a minor transgression (*laghu-āpatti*). As for the term "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*), the Sāṃkhya school maintains that there is a distinct entity, neither material nor mental, which serves as the life-faculty.
However, according to the *Abhidharmakośa* and Mahāyāna teachings, there is no separate entity that is neither material nor mental to serve as the life-faculty.

It refers simply to the continuous succession and uninterrupted connection of matter and mind, which constitutes "life. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is likewise. [The same applies to] the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and the six...
The continuous arising of consciousness is conventionally designated as "life. [This is] the *Fayin* (Record of Hidden Meanings).
First, regarding the explanation of "karma": one version says it refers to past karma; another says it refers to the characteristics of karma being formed.

The underlying intent emphasizes the gravity of karma, which is why it is explained in this inverted manner. Regarding "the ghosts and spirits fulfill [the act]": when a person gives rise to a murderous thought in their mind, they kill...
The spirits follow along and act as intermediaries for that person, enabling them to carry out the killing. The "three stages of action" constitute the complete causal process of the act of killing.
As for "proximate and remote," the original arising of the murderous intent directly感召 (induces) the retribution of the future, just like a shadow follows a form.
Therefore, proximate conditions assist in its completion; this is also like the distinction between the principal and the accomplice in worldly law.
It distinguishes between light and heavy; therefore, it is called "sparse" (*shu*). Fourthly, there is also a textual omission in the two characters [following] "four.

The character "condition" (*yuan*) should follow "four," as an example below this precept details how many conditions must be met for it to constitute a grave offense. Regarding "committing a transgression and committing a grave offense": "grave" refers to a *pārājika*;
"transgression" (*ni*) further adds the crime of "great rebellion and unrighteousness" (*da ni bu dao*), which involves killing one's superior. The three fruits.

Regarding these two interpretations, each has its own validity. One holds that since harming a *śrāvaka* who has attained the third fruit is already considered an extremely grave offense, how much more so would it be for a Bodhisattva who compassionately seeks to save ordinary beings to instead harm a noble sage?
The other holds that those who have attained the third fruit are termed "perpetrators of immediate retribution" (*ānantarya*), and this extends even to the Tathāgata;
yet what crime could possibly be imputed [to one who harms such a person]? It is as the saying goes: "What further punishment can be added for taking a handful of earth from the Long Tomb?"

Regarding the Bodhisattva’s inclusion among the noble ones (*ārya*), there are generally three categories: some take those from the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) upward; some take those from the seventh mind upward;
and some maintain that anyone who does not turn toward the two vehicles is termed "fixed" (*niyata*). Being "fixed" means being determinedly non-retrogressive.

To kill any of these constitutes a transgression of the immediate offenses (*ānantarya*). As for "one who nurtures the womb," this refers to a wet-nurse; killing a wet-nurse is equivalent [to killing one's mother].
Regarding the three fruits [of karma]: there are two explanations concerning the killing of those in the four realms of existence—one being grave and one not grave.
When observing the Great Being’s (the Master) repeated emphasis on the śrāvakas in the *Vyākhyāyukti*, it appears his intention lies in asserting that the grave case is the correct one.

As for "separated mind" versus "penetrating mind," these refer to killing without intent and killing with intent. Regarding the three natures, one explanation holds that they may be motivated by greed, hatred, or [delusion].

It is due to delusion. One explanation [distinguishes] the three natures: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. Regarding "taking this as the object for that": although one takes this as the object, it is actually for the sake of that;

therefore, it is said that "one gives rise to a harmful mind toward that. As for "the object": the self is the agent of harm, and the other is the victim of harm. Regarding "the result not being as intended":
even though one has such a mind to harm a thing, the actual outcome does not accord with the intent.

If even the mind [intending] this constitutes a grave offense, how much more so when it accords with the mind? Regarding "one who employs such means of killing," this refers to someone who constructs a pit here;
although they have no intention to harm that specific individual, this pit and trap are inherently capable of harming all beings.
If one knows this and acts intentionally, then one's mind possesses the conditions for killing. How could there not be guilt? Therefore, this is also regulated as belonging to the universal mind.
If one were to strike the east by mistake and instead hit the center, only then could it be said that there was no intention.

Regarding "one who severs life when without precepts," this clearly demonstrates that severing life while possessing precepts constitutes a grave offense. How is it when one severs life while without precepts? As for "when without precepts":
When one is in the process of abandoning the precepts, at that time: if the act of killing has not yet been completed, it constitutes a minor offense (light defilement);

if the act of severing life has already been accomplished, it is the same as previously stated. Regarding the Śrāvakas, they speak only of "killing" and have not yet spoken of "severing. How, then, is the offense determined at the moment of death?
If it occurs at the very moment of relinquishing the precepts, that is what is meant by "the time when the precepts depart. [The offense is] determined.
The offense falls under the category of the five precepts. Regarding "recollection": it means knowing one's past lives.

If one knows that this person is an enemy and, acting upon the momentum of that prior enmity, kills them so as to cause death, or fails to kill them at first but subsequently employs further means to cause their death—because both the initial and subsequent acts were committed with recollection, it constitutes a grave offense.
Regarding "non-recollection": if there was awareness at the outset, yet one kills them by acting upon the momentum [of anger], it is likewise a grave offense.
Or, while not yet dead, when further expedient means are applied, one truly departs without being aware of it. This is because one remembers what precedes but does not remember what follows;
since there is no mindfulness, there is no mind, and thus [the offense] is light. Those of the Sāṃkhya school take that which is neither form nor mind to be the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

However, that which maintains the continuity of form and mind is the intersection of consciousness and breath; this is the true life-faculty. If separated from this maintenance, then form belongs merely to matter.
Obstruction: The mind belongs to the realm of the vast and indistinct; these two are unrelated. Where, then, can one find the "life-root" (*jīvitendriya*)?

Analyzing various explanations, it is clear that one must sever this continuity between matter and mind (*rūpa-citta*) for the act of killing to be established. Regarding the four factors of cause, condition, dharma, and karma:

the general meaning is that a single thought-moment of the original arising of the intent to kill constitutes the cause, while the various auxiliary factors that complete the act constitute the conditions. Within the act of killing...
The means and conditions constitute the dharma; its function is the accomplishment of the act of killing.
○ Third, using the light to illustrate the heavy:
one must not intentionally kill any living being whatsoever.
*Fayi*: "Up to and including" (*nàizhì*) is a term indicating from the highest down to the lowest.

From the Buddhas and sages down to even the most minute crawling insects and flowing creatures—among the four modes of birth and six realms of existence—if they possess the aforementioned physical form, mind, and life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), none may be killed.
The word "intentionally" (*gù*) serves to exclude accidental killing. To speak in the ultimate sense, the vast and great compassion of a Bodhisattva, although...
There are those who possess form but lack consciousness, yet they still possess the vital breath of life; even they cannot bear to be killed.
This is like one who binds grass to protect the precepts or bends willow branches to admonish a ruler. How much more so for those who possess life?
II. Explaining the Response:
This bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of constant compassion, a mind of filial obedience, and employ skillful means to rescue and protect all sentient beings.
There are two interpretations of "constantly abiding in a mind of compassion. First, one should learn to give rise to compassion by taking the Buddha as a constant model.
Second, the mind should always abide in the ground of compassion. Second, the "mind of filial obedience" means to uphold the teachings without troubling others.
Third, "skillful means of rescue and protection" means that it is not enough merely to avoid troubling others; rather, one must engage with affairs to provide salvation and resolution.
*Fayi*: There should be three [virtues] to be aroused: namely, compassion, filial piety, and the protection of others. To kill is to oppose Heaven and transgress the Way;
it is precisely a lack of filial piety and a lack of obedience. Furthermore, all sentient beings have frequently been one's parents in past lives; to harm them is therefore an act of cruelty.
This would immediately cause distress and harm to my parents. "Directly" means simply; if one can simply refrain from causing distress, one may be excused from transgression.
If one does not provide protection, how can one be called a Great Being (Mahāsattva)? Therefore, while not killing, one should still save life; while not stealing, one should still practice giving.
Hereafter, all cases shall follow this principle.
○ Third, regarding those who do not act according to the precepts yet, on the contrary, kill living beings with a mind of self-indulgence and pleasure:
because this is improper, it constitutes an offense. This also consists of three points: first, "self-indulgent mind" refers to killing with a mind of greed; second, "pleasure" refers to...
Killing with a mind of hatred constitutes the third type of killing. These are the three types of killing; because they exist, one falls into undesirable transgressions.
[Commentary: Killing out of greed refers to such acts as slaughtering livestock for market profit or seizing life for the sake of wealth.
This refers to those who kill out of anger, such as those with a heart of malice who harm living beings or inflict cruel punishments and oppression upon the people.
The delusion is not mentioned separately because the two minds of greed and anger arise from ignorance;
for when wisdom cannot block desire, greed arises, and when insight cannot restrain resentment, anger arises.
○ Third, the formal pronouncement of the offense:
This is a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
[The commentary] states: First, the designation "bodhisattva" indicates that this is a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva, not one for a śrāvaka.

*Pārājika*. *Pārājika* is translated here as "extremely evil" (*ji'e*) and also as "abandoned" (*qi*). This means that because the offense is extremely grave, one is forever cast out as a discarded object.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are three meanings: first, the meaning of "receding and sinking," because the fruits of the Path are lost;
second, the meaning of "not living together," because one is no longer tolerated by the Saṃgha; third, the meaning of "falling," because after death one enters hell. Based on this...
If one commits the act of killing, the seed of great compassion is severed; how then can the vow for universal deliverance be fulfilled?
One who is violent, evil, and cruel is a companion to the rākṣasas and a member of the executioners' guild; can such a person still be considered a bodhisattva? [The questioner asks:

"Śramaṇas devote themselves exclusively to the practice of compassion, whereas kings and ministers hold the authority over life and death. If those with guilt are not executed, how [can order be maintained]?"

Regarding the protection of the state, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: Suppose a bodhisattva sees a bandit who, out of greed for wealth, intends to kill many living beings or to harm a great and virtuous śrāvaka.
The bodhisattva reflects: "If I were to take the life of that evil person, I would fall into hell;
yet if I do not take his life, he will commit an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*). It would be better for me [to take his life]."
Entering hell, one shall never cause them to undergo the suffering of the Avīci Hell. Killing in such a manner constitutes no transgression and generates abundant merit;
this is precisely the meaning of killing after having perceived the [appropriate] opportunity (*tatkāla*). Thus, if there is a crime for which one kills, how could that killing be an offense?
The execution of the Four Wicked Ones by Yu Shun and the execution of the two rebels by the Duke of Zhou are instances of this very principle.

How much more so when, upon the execution of a death sentence, one must inevitably shed tears; and when the execution is carried out only after three verifications, this is precisely "killing that accomplishes compassion.
Although there is killing, it is not [true] killing. Thus, the law is not abandoned, yet benevolence remains unimpaired; state governance and the Buddha-mind are both without obstruction. Question:

Humans can be observed for their capacities (*māi*), but such considerations need not be applied to other creatures. Therefore, the "Great Sacrifice" (*tāiláo*) is offered to the Emperor, while the Great...
"Regarding the nourishing of the worthy: why do kings and ministers prohibit the killing of animals? Answer: "When a human commits an evil deed, they receive the highest punishment;
but what crime have these creatures truly committed that they must face the ground of death? Furthermore, the spirits enjoy sincerity; this does not preclude the *yue* sacrifice.

Confucius found sweetness in plain vegetables and water; why must there necessarily be sacrificial oxen? That feasts and offerings employ livestock is simply because the Buddha-dharma had not yet entered the Middle Kingdom."
These are merely provisional teachings (*upāya*). Is it appropriate to cling to provisional teachings as if they were eternal laws?
Therefore, we know that Emperor Wu of Liang’s practice of using flour for sacrificial victims completed the ritual for honoring ancestors while not violating the precept against killing;

this is a fine law for those who possess a state throughout ten thousand generations. Yet the ignorant condemn it. Furthermore, regarding the burial of a human-shaped effigy, Confucius said of it: [that it was a matter of expediency].
If there were no afterlife, then using elephants as sacrificial victims for worship would still leave the gentleman dissatisfied; yet now you consider such practices wrong.
This implies that those who wish to perform sacrifices must use genuine living victims, and by extension, those who wish to conduct burials must also use genuine living persons.
I hope you will not be bound by mere habit; I pray you will calm your mind and reflect upon this. May I ask whether it is permissible not to slaughter oxen, sheep, dogs, and pigs?
[Question: "When jackals and wolves block the road, and tigers and leopards devour humans, what should one do? [Answer:
"Fierce beasts will cross the river if they harbor virtue, and crocodiles will move far away if they are moved by sincerity. If one can truly act in this manner, what need is there for killing?
However, if it is otherwise, then capturing locusts and slaying dragons to eliminate harm for the sake of the people is equal to the state's regular penal codes and should not be prohibited."
● Regarding this precept: it arises from the mind of compassion, the mind of pity, and the mind of filial piety within the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground.
Question: For what reason are the precepts produced by means of the thirty minds? Answer: The Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground is inexhaustible;
these thirty are merely cited as a general outline. These thirty encompass and unify all myriad practices. Within the first ten [minds],...
Second is the correct cultivation of the mind of precepts (*śīlacitta*). This mind of precepts further comprises thirty items, as well as immeasurable others, because it is a virtuous mind.
For now, I shall cite those whose meaning is proximate and append them accordingly; in reality, however, the minds are mutually fused such that one is all.
Furthermore, the preceding text stated that this sutra briefly explains the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground (*cittabhūmi-dharmamukha*) like a hair-tip.
I agree. What is now grasped by the thirty mental factors is like taking a hair-tip upon a hair-tip;

yet as the grasping becomes ever more subtle, the benefit becomes ever more vast. A single remaining mouthful of fragrant rice satisfies ten thousand men; half a drop from the River of Heaven rains down to moisten the six realms.
How extensive is the benefit of this Dharma-gate of the mind-ground!
● Second Precept on Stealing (2): First, the brief introduction; second, entering the text.
○ First, the brief introduction: Taking what is not given.
Taking what is not given in an overt manner is called *kṣepa* (robbery); taking what is not given by stealth is called stealing (*steya*). Stealing...

That [offense] results in retribution for one's environment; this precept is equally violated by all seven classes of practitioners. Among the five classes of Śrāvakas, there are both similarities and differences.
The similarity is that none should commit theft. The differences are threefold:

first, the difference between what is permitted and what is prohibited, such as whether it is permissible or not to take [an object] upon seeing the opportunity (the *nimitta*), or the view that taking upon seeing the opportunity constitutes no theft because there is no intent to steal, as when a Mahāsattva acts for the sake of sentient beings through various means.
Both cases are permissible. Śrāvakas seek their own liberation and must necessarily rely on formal rules and regulations. Mahāsattvas do not fear transgressions;

provided it brings benefit to others, they will act accordingly. For a Śrāvaka, stealing the property of the Buddha after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa is considered a minor offense, whereas for a Bodhisattva, it is always grave.
Furthermore, one should originally bestow life upon others, yet here one takes it away instead—how could this be the mind of a Mahāsattva?

*Fayi*: The principles of what is permitted and what is prohibited are the same as before. Were it not for the Bodhisattva’s supreme impartiality, selflessness, great compassion, and benefitting of sentient beings, one could not grant exemptions upon perceiving the specific circumstances.

As for the fact that stealing the property of a Buddha is a minor offense for a Śrāvaka but a grave one for a Bodhisattva, it is truly because the Śrāvaka acts only for his own person, whereas the Bodhisattva succeeds and upholds the Triple Gem;
thus, regarding the property of a Buddha, he ought to protect and maintain all that belongs to it.
To increase what one does not possess and instead take it for oneself is to steal from one’s own stewardship; is this not twice as grave as the conduct of ordinary people?
That which is "external to life" refers to the fact that wealth and property are fundamentally intended to be relinquished to others;
yet, instead of doing so, one takes them to nourish one's own body—hence they are called "external to life."
II. Entering the Text (3): First, identifying the person; second, setting forth the matter; third, concluding with the offense.
○ First, identifying the person:
"If a disciple of the Buddha..."
II. The Introductory Matter (3): First, what is improper; second, clarifying what is proper; third, concluding with what is improper.
I. What is Improper (3): First, citing the act of stealing; second, establishing the characteristics of the karmic formation; third, citing a light case to illustrate a heavy one.
First, the matter of theft is raised:
stealing by oneself, inciting others to steal, stealing through expedient means, and stealing by means of incantations;

as well as uncovering what is hidden. Regarding "expedient means," these refer to the preliminary preparations for theft, such as tunneling through walls or picking locks. "Stealing by incantations" refers to...
As for this: there are malevolent sorcerers who can, through their arts, seize those objects. Regarding the omission of praise for sympathetic joy (*anumodana*):

matters of killing can generally be discussed openly, whereas plots for theft must necessarily be deliberated in secret; thus, instances of praising or rejoicing in such acts are rare, and therefore they are omitted here.
II. The characteristic of the accomplishment of karma.
The cause of stealing, the conditions for stealing, the method of stealing, and the karma of stealing—these four points are the same as before.
Moving the hand to take another's property and remove it from its original location constitutes the karma of stealing. Karma is volitional activity (*abhisamskāra*).
Regarding the meaning of "heavy object": it refers to five *kārsāpaṇa* coins. The Vinaya states that one large copper coin is equivalent to sixteen small coins;

among these, there are variations in value. The determination of the offense is based on the location from which the theft was committed. Some claim that for a Bodhisattva, the gravity of the offense exceeds that of a Śrāvaka, such that two coins or more constitutes a grave offense.
This view is not entirely accepted here; rather, the determination is made at five coins.
This is a grave matter. Since the karmic act of stealing by taking from another's place must be determined at this point, [the text] reveals its hidden meaning.
As the subsequent passage states that even a single needle or a single blade of grass constitutes theft, how can the commentary take "five coins" as the definitive criterion?
In general, the cutting of *śaṇa* grass is judged as theft; the value of five *kārsāpaṇas* is judged as a grave offense. Once the object has been moved from its place, the act of theft is completed;

while it has not yet been moved from its place, it still remains within the category of the preparatory stage of theft. The general meaning is that a single thought-moment in which the original intent to steal arises constitutes the cause (*hetu*);

the various factors that assist in accomplishing that theft constitute the conditions (*pratyaya*); the specific implements used for the theft constitute the method (*vidhi*); and the actual performance of the action that brings the theft to completion constitutes the [result].
This is karma.
○ Third, citing the light to illustrate the heavy:
even down to the property of ghosts and spirits, the goods of owners or robbers, and all manner of wealth—down to a single needle or a blade of grass—one must not take them intentionally.

Regarding "stealing" and "exposing what is hidden," the phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*) refers to the progression from the most serious to the least serious; thus, it is called an "illustrative comparison. [The objects are: first, the property of spirits and deities;
second, any object that has an owner; third, the property of bandits; and fourth, all other objects. Question: Regarding the taking of the property of bandits, it is said:

What constitutes the offense of theft? Answer: There are two meanings here. If the plundered object is my own property and I have already formed the perception that it is lost, or if the plundered object belongs to another and that other person has not given it to me—both cases constitute taking what is not given.
II. Clarifying the Response:
A bodhisattva should give rise to a filial mind toward the Buddha-nature, a mind of compassion, and should constantly assist all people so that they may produce merit and experience happiness.

This clarifies what should be practiced. It is largely the same as the preceding section, with only minor differences. Previously, it clarified that one should learn the constant practice of the Buddha’s compassion;
here, it states that one should practice compassion through filial piety. A Bodhisattva should learn these matters; therefore, it says "should.
As for "should not," this refers to such acts as stealing and killing. This constitutes both the gate of admonition and the gate of exhortation.

Furthermore, admonishing others not to commit killing or stealing, encouraging them to practice goodness, compassion, and filial piety, as well as studying the constant practices of the Buddha’s conduct—all such things constitute filial piety through wholesome dharmas.
As for "Buddha-nature," all sentient beings possess the nature that is their future fruition; "nature" simply has the meaning of being unchanging.
*Fayi*: To steal another's wealth out of filial piety or obedience, thereby causing them to fall into poverty, is to defy heaven and violate principle; all such acts are unrighteous.
Furthermore, since all sentient beings have been one’s parents in many past lives, to afflict or harm them is to harm one’s own parents.

As for the nature of the future fruition—the fruit of Buddhahood—its essence is fundamentally the same for all. Yet, by turning one’s back on this nature and habitually practicing evil, one destroys the very root of one’s own goodness. Thus it is said:

One should give rise to a heart of filial piety and compassion within the Buddha-nature; one must not commit theft or damage property, nor willingly endure the transgression of being rebellious or toxic toward others.
○ Third, the conclusion of what is improper.
As for those who, on the contrary, steal the property of others:
the manner of stealing the property of the Triple Gem is explained according to the Vinaya.

To reveal the hidden meaning: having already committed the offense of theft by stealing the property of others, it can be known that stealing the property of the Triple Gem is likewise theft; however, the classification of its gravity differs.
This is detailed fully in the Vinaya Piṭaka.
III. Conclusion on the Offense:
This constitutes a pārājika offense for a bodhisattva.

*Fayi*: The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "If a bodhisattva sees a robber or thief seizing another's property, they may give rise to a heart of compassion and forcibly take it away, so that the thief shall not enjoy such wealth and thereby undergo suffering for a long night.

Although this constitutes taking what was not given, there is no transgression; rather, much merit is generated. Furthermore, this [stolen property] may be returned to the original owner, or used to perform meritorious deeds."
If one acts accordingly, it truly constitutes merit; otherwise, one cannot avoid transgression and guilt.

According to this precept, it arises from the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, specifically from within the mind of precepts, the mind of compassion, the mind of pity, the mind of benefit, and the mind of filial obedience.
● Third Precept on Sexual Misconduct (2): Part One, Brief Introduction; Part Two, Entering the Text.
○ Part One, Brief Introduction:
"Sexual misconduct" (*abrahmacarya*) refers to base and vulgar acts; therefore, it is called "impure conduct. It is an offense common to all seven classes of followers.

Both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna prohibit [sexual misconduct], yet there are differences in the extent of these prohibitions. For the five classes of monastics, both improper and proper sexual relations are prohibited;

for the two classes [of nuns and male novices], only improper sexual conduct is prohibited. The general similarities and differences regarding this point are largely the same as previously described for the śrāvakas.
*Fayi*: Both the heterodox and the orthodox have many prohibitions, yet the prohibitions against sexual misconduct alone are few.

While the five groups of the ordained completely sever sexual desire, the two groups of the laity merely prohibit their heterodox forms. Those who can comply with these Buddha-prescribed rules are both termed practitioners of pure conduct.
II. Entering the Text (3): First, identifying the person; second, setting forth the matter; third, concluding with the offense.
○ First, identifying the person:
"If a disciple of the Buddha..."
II. The Introductory Matter (3): First, the inappropriate; second, the appropriate; third, the conclusion of the inappropriate. A. First, the Inappropriate (3):
First, citing the act of sexual misconduct; second, clarifying the formation of the karmic offense; third, citing a light case to illustrate the grave.
First, regarding sexual misconduct:
one must not intentionally engage in sexual acts oneself, nor incite others to do so, even with any woman whatsoever.
This is something an ordained person should not do.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden). "This up to... refers to all women, from one's own kin to those among others.

Regarding "those who should not [be approached] by the ordained," this means that for the ordained, it is a general prohibition; whereas for the laity, it distinguishes between what is improper and what is permissible. Question:

There are also instances of incantations used for sexual purposes, such as the *Mātangī* woman’s former *brahmā*-incantation. Why is this not prohibited now? Answer: Sexual matters are easy [to commit].
This is not comparable to killing or stealing; why wait for incantations? Therefore, these are omitted.
○ Second, explaining the formation of karma:
the cause of sexual misconduct, the conditions for sexual misconduct, the method of sexual misconduct, and the karma of sexual misconduct.
This precept becomes grave when three conditions are fulfilled: first, a sentient being; second, a lustful mind; and third, the completion of the act.
Alternatively, it may involve five conditions: first, a sentient being; second, the perception of that being as such, and so forth.

*Fayi*: It is fully prepared in five parts, as explained in detail later in the section on the precept against false speech. The general meaning is that a single thought of an originally arising lustful mind serves as the cause;
the various factors that assist and complete that lust serve as the conditions; and the implements and methods used within the act of lust serve as the constituent elements (*dharma*).
Its function is to accomplish sexual intercourse through correct application.
Third, using light cases to illustrate heavy ones:
this extends even to female animals, female deities, female ghosts or spirits, and engaging in sexual intercourse via improper orifices.

To cite inferior cases as faults: engaging with one’s own wife through improper means (*amārga*), at improper places (*adeśa*), or during periods such as after childbirth, while nursing an infant, or while pregnant—all these are termed "sexual misconduct" (*kāmamithyācāra*) in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* states that sexual misconduct is governed by six grave prohibitions; furthermore, within the precepts, it prohibits [intercourse] at improper times and in improper places.
Even with one’s own wife, engaging at an improper time constitutes a grave offense. This applies even when one instructs another to commit adultery.

There is no delusive defilement; one merely commits a minor offense (laghu-pāpaka). Some say that for a Bodhisattva it is grave, but here we explain that for both Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas it is the same;

this does not follow the same category as killing or stealing. Regarding humans, animals, ghosts, spirits, men, women, eunuchs, and those with dual sexual organs, if the three paths [of action] are all involved, it is grave.
All other acts such as praising, touching, or causing the emission of impurity are merely the preliminary stages (upāya) of this precept.
All constitute violations of the minor defilements (*laghu-mala*).
*Fayi* (Exposition of the Hidden) states: "This extends even to all women within the human realm and other realms of existence.
The six grave offenses, the three paths, and so forth—their vulgar details need not be fully enumerated."
II. Clarifying the Response.
The Bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of filial obedience, rescuing and delivering all sentient beings, and bestowing the pure Dharma upon others.
They should study the pure conduct of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, no differently than the gates of instruction previously taught.
*Fayi*: To observe that all sentient beings are one's parents and to extinguish deviant thoughts—this is called the mind of filial piety.
Furthermore, because sexual misconduct violates principle, it is likewise not in accord with filiality.

Third, though they ought not to form fetters, they instead give rise to lust for all people, making no distinction even among animals; they commit incest with their mothers, daughters, sisters, and other members of the six degrees of kinship.
Such persons possess no heart of compassion.
That which is prohibited herein should not be done in any case; to do so constitutes an offense. Therefore, it is concluded that these are improper.
*Fayi* (Unveiling the Hidden): "This even extends to" refers to those ranging from distant relatives to close kin.
○ Third, the formal confession of the offense:
this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.

Regarding the phrase "the manifestation of concealment," the fact that it does not say "having perceived the opportunity" implies that while the general outline is the same as previously stated, it is not identical in every respect. If...
The Buddha’s deliverance of the courtesan was merely the dispatching of a manifested being; he had not yet manifested his full transformative power.

To attempt to imitate him prematurely is to enter hell as swiftly as an arrow shot. Regarding this precept, it arises from the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, specifically from within the mind of precepts, the mind of concentration, the mind of protection, and the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, and filial piety.
● The Fourth Precept on False Speech (2): First, a brief introduction; second, entering the text.
○ First, the brief introduction:
"False" (*mṛṣā*) is a term for that which is unreal. It deceives ordinary people and deludes the sages, causing confusion in the human mind; therefore, it incurs transgression. This...

The precepts are transgressed by all seven groups [of the monastic community]. They are regulated by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. The general similarities and differences regarding their commonality with the Śrāvakas are largely the same as previously stated.
II. Entering the Text (three parts): 1. Identifying the person; 2. Sequencing the events; 3. Concluding the offense.
I. First, the designation of the person:
"If a Buddha’s disciple... II.
Second, the sequence of the matter (three parts): 1. That which is improper; 2. Clarifying that which is proper; 3. Concluding with that which is improper.
Section One: On False Speech (Three Parts) 1. Explaining false speech; 2. Establishing the characteristics of karma; 3. Providing an illustration by way of analogy.
1. Explaining False Speech This includes:
speaking falsely oneself, inciting others to speak falsely, and employing the means for false speech.

To speak directly is called "speech" (*vāc*); to proclaim and relate is called "discourse" (*bhāṣita*). To discuss and explain so as to clarify something, capable of expressing both principle (*dharma*) and phenomena (*artha*), is what is termed "discourse.
As for lying oneself: it is to claim one has attained the supreme Dharma. To teach another:
it is to instruct them to speak, or to instruct another to speak for oneself, employing skillful means to speak falsely—just as when honey is smeared on a tree, all the bees come flocking.

*Fayi*: There are two meanings to "instructing others": first, instructing them to say that one has attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*); second, instructing them to say that they themselves have attained superhuman states.
Regarding "honey-smeared": it refers to smearing honey to attract bees; [the practitioner] falsely claims, "I can summon bees," in order to deceive others.
II. The Characteristics of Completing the Karma.
The cause of false speech, the conditions for false speech, the nature of false speech, and the karma of false speech.
This precept constitutes a grave offense when five factors are present: first, a sentient being; second, the perception of that being as such; third, a deceptive intent.

Fourth, the declaration of the grave offense; fifth, the understanding by the person addressed. Regarding "the first being a sentient being": this refers to the objects of the three preceding categories, specifically within the superior category, [referring to] one's parents, teachers, or the Sangha.
To speak falsehood toward them constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). Regarding the Buddhas and noble ones (*ārya*), there are two interpretations:

first, it is said that [speaking to them] enters the cause for a grave offense; second, it is said that such persons are not deluded and can, moreover, use their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to obstruct others.

This prevents others from hearing it; however, one merely incurs a minor defilement. Among the noble ones (āryas), there are those of greater and lesser capacity: some possess the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), while others do not.
Following the general rule, for Arhats and those at the stage of "practice through understanding" (adhimukticaryā) and above, the offense is said to be light.

For those below this level, whether they possess the knowledge of others' minds or not, the offense is uniformly considered grave. This applies to objects of the middle grade, such as humans, devas, and so forth.

The gravity is the same. This is precisely the limit where delusion and understanding obstruct the Path. Regarding the objects of the lower grades, such as the four realms of rebirth (*cāturmahārājika* and so forth), some say the gravity is the same;
here, however, we explain them as light offenses. Second, regarding the perception of sentient beings, there may be cases of certainty, doubt, or perversion, which are generally the same as before.

Some say that the mind of false speech extends universally; this was originally stated with reference to this case: "This person does not hear it, but that person hears it," and so forth. Even when speaking...

The gravity [of the offense] is the same. In this current explanation, it is not considered grave because there is no intentionality (*cetanā*) therein. Third, a deceitful mind is the primary factor for the offense.

If one avoids danger or acts out of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), there is no transgression. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "A Bodhisattva who relishes meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) commits a defiled offense.
It should be understood that when a Bodhisattva gives rise to overweening pride, it is likewise a minor stain. Regarding the dispatching of a messenger, there are two interpretations. The first says:
It is also significant to instruct others to say that I am a sage. This is because our land lacks jade scepters and ceremonial vessels; the value of a person is determined by what others say of them.
When a bystander praises me more than I do myself, it is because they are teaching others that I am a sage. Since fame and profit do not enter into me, this is not something I hold as significant.

Second, it is said that the Noble Dharma is profound and subtle; its realization resides within oneself. It must necessarily be recounted by the person themselves to be considered weighty, for if told by another, it is deemed light.

There are four types of weighty accounts: namely, when one personally realizes and sees with one's own eyes. If one says they have attained the four fruits [of the śramaṇa], the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the eight dhyānas, or supernatural powers (*abhijñā*);
or if one says they have seen devas, nāgas, ghosts, or spirits—all these are weighty accounts. If one says they have ascended to the stage of *gotrabhū*, this is also a weighty account.

One view holds that since this is an ordinary dharma, the offense is light and defiling. Regarding the time of the conclusion of the offense (*āpatti-samāpanna*), there are two interpretations concerning its duration:
first, it follows the person; second, it concludes according to the speech. Since this precept restrains verbal karma, it logically should conclude according to the speech.

However, because it causes harm at a distance, it must necessarily apply to the person as well. As for the precept against minor false speech, it applies accordingly to both the person and the speech.

Furthermore, following the words [of the scriptures]: if one loses the precepts by committing an offense through predominant afflictions (*kleśa*), it is further stated that this applies only to the commission of a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

If there is no mutual understanding at the time of the face-to-face encounter, one first incurs the preliminary offense (*prayoga*). Later, if one reflects on the previous words and suddenly understands, then the light offense is sublated and a heavy one is incurred.
All ten grave offenses have their specific causes and conditions; here I shall first explain four of them, and the remainder may be understood by analogy.

*Fayi*: Regarding the majority of cases, this means that regardless of whether one has attained the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), [the offense] is light when directed toward an Arhat of the stage of practice (*śikṣamāṇa*) or above;
it is heavy for those below this level. Furthermore, those at these two stages or above possess spiritual power (*ṛddhi-bala*) and are not deluded.
This is because it is not otherwise. Regarding the "conceptions of sentient beings," there was no explanatory text in the previous commentary on the Threefold Precepts;
it is only now that this is presented, stating that one should suspect it of being obscure, as its meaning is not yet detailed.

My intention is that the Vinaya contains passages such as "an ordinary person conceives the conception of an Arhat" and "an Arhat conceives the conception of an ordinary person. Now, based on these three categories, we shall distinguish their relative gravity. Suppose, for instance...
Regarding those who speak falsely to an Arhat: if one thinks, "This person shall become an Arhat," and speaks a falsehood to him, the offense is light.
If one speaks falsely with doubt, thinking, "Is this an Arhat, or is he not an Arhat? the offense is somewhat heavier.
If one speaks falsely while harboring a biased view, thinking, "He is truly not an Arhat," and addresses him [with such words], the offense is even more serious.
Lying is an even more serious offense. If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) regarding someone else here forms the perception and says, "This must be an ordinary person," the offense is grave.
If one says, "Is this an ordinary person or not? the offense is somewhat lighter. If it is known for certain that they are not an ordinary person, the offense is even lighter.
The preceding three precepts should be understood by analogy with this. I am unsure whether this is correct; I await your esteemed judgment.
I shall clarify this further in detail. Regarding "the mind being pervasive": even false speech is categorized as either the mind being pervasive or the mind being obstructed.

Regarding "the master of the karma": speech is the sound of the mind; a deceitful mind is precisely the master of the karma of false speech. Subsequent precepts mostly follow this pattern. Regarding "defilement": this cites an example of a minor offense.
If one speaks of the flavor of dhyāna out of self-conceit, one commits a defiled offense; thus, one should know that [the gravity of the offense] increases.

One who gives rise to pride commits a minor offense. As for "arrogance" (adhimāna), it does not mean that one clearly knows oneself not to be a sage yet claims to be a sage to deceive sentient beings;
rather, it specifically refers to generating a sense of superiority based on having attained a small measure of realization, believing oneself to be a sage without self-awareness.
Thus, it is classified as a minor defilement. Regarding "ordinary ground" (pṛthagjanabhūmi), it means that the stage of nature (gotrabhūmi) still remains within the state of an ordinary person.

The Dharma is not something proven by one's own words alone; rather, it is realized through inference. Regarding the person who attains understanding, it is clarified that there are two ways in which the offense is incurred:
first, according to the number of people involved; second, according to the number of utterances. This is because the root of the precepts is established as being verbal.
One should simply follow the words; yet, where there are words that cease with a single phrase, how could their propagation be inexhaustible? Furthermore, one must be a person of broad understanding.

Regarding minor false speech, if the words do not involve a major transgression, one should follow the person concerned; for if the person was originally silent, from where would the fault arise? Moreover, it must also involve speech.
As for those who violate the precepts through the offense of the *adhi-citta* (higher mind), the loss of the precept pertains solely to their nature (*svabhāva*).
The aforementioned offenses are not covered by the present rule. Furthermore, if words are spoken that others do not understand, it does not yet constitute the full offense;
rather, it results in a minor defilement (*āpatti*). However, when the meaning is later understood, the minor offense is transformed into a grave one.

In essence, a single thought-moment of the original intention to speak falsely serves as the cause, while various contributing factors that facilitate the falsehood serve as the conditions. Among these, the requisites for speaking falsehood [are included].
That which is square is the *dharma*. Its primary function is to accomplish the karma of false speech.
○ Third, the illustration by way of analogy:
even to say one has seen what one has not seen, or to say one has not seen what one has seen—this is false speech of body and mind.
*Fayi*: "Not seeing yet claiming to see" and so forth constitute minor false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). To falsely claim to have realized the state of a sage is called major false speech;

therefore, this [minor case] is cited by way of analogy. False speech belongs to the mouth; why then are the body and mind mentioned? Internally one forms a thought, and externally one utters words; thus, both body and mind are spoken of together. Question:
When the Buddha saw the rabbit enter, why did he say he did not see it? Answer: It was for the sake of saving the rabbit.
Skillful means involve observing the opportune moment; this refers to that which involves no transgression and generates manifold merit.
Second, the explanation of the response:
the Bodhisattva constantly gives rise to right speech and right view, and likewise causes all sentient beings to give rise to right speech and right view.
*Fayi*: "Externally correct speech and internally correct view" correspond to the aforementioned non-falsehood of body and mind. This refers to not daring to speak what is wrong;
generally, not daring to speak of what is not holy constitutes both correct speech and correct view.
"Third, it is improper that, instead of [correcting them], one should rather give rise to the wrong speech, wrong views, and wrong actions of all sentient beings.
This is a hidden fault. A Bodhisattva ought to transform all sentient beings by rectifying their three karmas; yet now, instead, you lead them astray."
With a deviant mind one utters deviant speech, which eventually leads to the performance of deviant actions and the invitation of bitter retribution.
How could this be the essence of a Great Being? (3) Conclusion on the Offense.
This constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.

To harbor such concealment—pretending to possess the subtle wisdom known only to the heavens while claiming to be an ordinary person when one is actually a sage—causes beginners to wander in confusion and lose their hold on the precepts.
To be deluded and hesitant is precisely what is meant by deceiving the ordinary and overreaching toward the sages, causing people's minds to wander and be confused.
Above, it offends the Buddhas; below, it misleads sentient beings. Therefore, it constitutes a grave transgression.

Regarding this precept, it arises from the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, specifically from the mind of precepts, the mind of concentration, the mind of delighting in teaching, and the mind of uprightness.
● The Fifth Precept: Selling Alcohol (Part Two). I. Brief Introduction. II. Entering the Text.
○ I. Brief Introduction.
"Selling" (*ku*) is a term for trade or bartering; "alcohol" (*jiǔ*) is the commodity being traded. There are many kinds of commodities for sale, and alcohol is one such [commodity].

The medicine for ignorance causes people to become deluded, whereas the essence of a Mahāsattva bestows wisdom upon others. To give the medicine of ignorance to people is not the practice of a Bodhisattva.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that there are thirty-five faults associated with alcohol;

therefore, this [prohibition] is included among the ten grave precepts of a Bodhisattva. It is an offense common to all seven classes of followers, and it is regulated by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions. Great!

Regarding minor similarities and differences: [the prohibition on] buying and selling should not apply [equally]. For a Bodhisattva, because of the priority of benefiting sentient beings, it is weighty;

for a Śrāvaka, it simply should not be done. [If a Śrāvaka] violates the seven categories of offenses (*sapta-varga*), selling goods constitutes only an offense of the third category; this is what is regulated by the precept against trade.
If a Bodhisattva is in a brothel or sells meat, they commit a light secondary offense (*āpatti-laghu-mala*), as they cannot [properly] summon or attract [beings] through such means.
This is because of alcohol.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* lists thirty-five faults, beginning with destitution in the present life and ending with ignorance in future lives.
Furthermore, the *Fourfold Division* (*Sishen*) clarifies thirty-six faults, beginning with being unfilial toward one’s parents and disrespectful toward the Triple Gem.
In the end, they fall into water or encounter fire; they die of cold or perish of heat.

Thus one knows that alcohol, in its greatest consequence, destroys the life of wisdom, and in its lesser effects, injures and maims the physical body. How, then, can it be sold? Regarding the violation of the third article:
this refers to the violation of the third article among the seven groups of offenses in the Hīnayāna, which corresponds precisely to the precept against trafficking within these minor defilements.
II. Entering the Text (3): First, identifying the person; second, setting forth the matter; third, concluding with the offense.

"If a Buddha’s disciple..."

A. First, what is improper (3): First, citing the matter of selling; second, establishing the characteristics of the karmic act; third, providing a comparative illustration.
First, regarding the matter of selling intoxicants:

to sell alcohol oneself, to teach others to sell alcohol, or for one who sells it to seek profit—teaching others means causing them to sell alcohol on one's behalf; these are likewise grave offenses. Teaching others to [sell] themselves... [is likewise grave].
The offense of selling [a slave] is minor.

*Fayin* (Unveiling the Hidden) states: "If one instructs another to sell [a slave] for oneself, the profit accrues to oneself; if one instructs another to sell themselves, the profit accrues to the other.
Therefore, the gravity of the resulting offense is determined in accordance with the preceding text."

The causes of selling alcohol, the conditions for selling alcohol, the methods of selling alcohol, and the karma of selling alcohol.
Regarding the causes and conditions, five factors must be complete: first, a sentient being; second, the perception of a sentient being; third, the desire for profit through trade.
The four types of genuine liquor. Fifth, giving it to another sentient being—referring to the three aforementioned objects. For those who do not become intoxicated or deranged, the offense is light;
for those who do become intoxicated or deranged, it is heavy. Regarding the middle-grade object, namely humans and devas, this is precisely what is prohibited; therefore, it is heavy.
In the four lower realms, the principle of the path is weak and disorderly; the offense of selling [intoxicants] is light.

Regarding the perception of sentient beings, there may be correctness, doubt, or perversion, as previously stated. If the mind is separated [from the object], the offense is still grave. Selling for the sake of profit is also grave, because it leads to the accumulation of much desire.
"True liquor" refers to that which causes intoxication and confusion in people; medicinal wine, though sold for profit, does not cause confusion.
There is no offense regarding the person or the goods. One interpretation states that when it is time for drinking, one incurs a heavy offense according to the number of people;

for example, if a child comes to purchase [liquor] but ultimately does not drink it, against whom is the heavy offense incurred? "Dharma" refers to the method and application of the means for selling liquor.
The practitioner is the driver; the hidden [truth] is brought forth. Those who disrupt the meaning of the Way and are weak are like ghosts and beasts who drink [the nectar].

Compared to humans and devas, their delusion and the disruption of the mind’s intent regarding the Way are slight. Question: It is indeed true that humans and devas become disordered due to intoxication; how can this be considered a superior grade?

There are also those who become intoxicated. The answer is: there are two meanings to this. First, teachers, monks, and parents are not necessarily sages. Second, even minor sages may become intoxicated;
the meaning of this will be seen in the subsequent explanation, such as in the case of the *nāga*-subduing Arhat and others.

One should regard it lightly when the intoxication is caused by a separation of minds. As for why it is said here that it is also grave: although the drinking was done unintentionally, one becomes intoxicated.

This is equivalent to harming others; therefore, it is grave. Regarding the phrase "waiting for the time of drinking": this means that the grave offense (*pārājika*) is incurred at the very moment the alcohol is handed over to another.

If one must wait until the time of eating and then incur the offense according to each individual who consumes it, then even if a child buys the wine but does not drink it, with whom would the gravity of the offense be incurred?
The general meaning is that the primary cause is the single thought-moment of the initial intention to sell wine, which, through various contributing factors, brings it to completion.

Selling is the condition (*pratyaya*). The implements and means used within the act of selling liquor constitute the phenomenon (*dharma*). Its function (*karman*) is the accomplishment of the business of selling liquor through its primary activity.
○ Third, the illustration by analogy.
One must not sell any kind of intoxicant. Such intoxicants are the causes and conditions for giving rise to transgressions.

To reveal this further: "any kind of intoxicant" refers to the many varieties of intoxicants. First, those made from grain; second, those made from fruits, such as sugarcane, grapes, dates, and so forth;
third, those made from medicinal substances, such as the flowers, leaves, and bark of various fragrant trees. Furthermore, fermented milk may also be included.
In the production of wine, the strength of a person’s intoxication varies according to the type of wine; therefore, one must not sell any of them.
Thus, the phrase "taking the light to illustrate the heavy" indicates the underlying reason for the arising of transgression. The *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* states:

"The Buddha taught that among the evil deeds of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, alcohol alone is the root. As the root of evil conduct, it is precisely the causal condition for the arising of transgression."

Now, a bodhisattva should give rise to the wisdom of clear penetration regarding all sentient beings.

To reveal what is hidden, to distinguish the correct from the incorrect, and to be free from any obscuration is called "illumination. To advance toward what is right and turn away from what is wrong, without being hindered by anything, is also illumination.
Obstruction is called penetration. A bodhisattva should inspire sentient beings with such wisdom, causing them to abandon the path of delusion and ascend to the shore of enlightenment;
this is the very essence of a Mahāsattva.
"Third, it is improper;
yet, on the contrary, it gives rise to the deluded minds of all sentient beings. [Commentary: This reveals the hidden meaning.

Following the previous point regarding selling wine to others, it causes people to become deluded, unable to distinguish right from wrong, and thus they turn their backs on the truth and act in opposition to it.

○ Third, the determination of the offense:
this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.

*Fayi* (Unveiling the Hidden). Question: Drinking alcohol constitutes a minor offense; selling alcohol does not necessarily mean one drinks it. Why, then, is it a grave offense? Answer: It is because of selling that drinking occurs.
The harm of drinking has limits, whereas the calamity of selling is infinite. Thus, when Yi Di first created wine, Yu immediately banished him.
If a Bodhisattva commits this act, how could they avoid incurring the sin of expulsion? According to this precept, the Bodhisattva...

● Sixth: Explaining the Precepts on the Faults of the Fourfold Assembly (2). First, the brief introduction; second, entering the text.
The first section provides a brief explanation.
"Speaking" refers to the name for discussing the Way. "Assembly" refers to the fourfold assembly of fellow practitioners. "Transgressions" refers to the seven heinous acts and the ten grave offenses.

First, because one suppresses and eclipses those who came before, thereby harming the True Dharma, one incurs an offense. This precept is a common transgression for all seven assemblies and is regulated by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Since the Bodhisattva takes it as their core intention to conceal evil and promote good, the offense is grave. An upper-grade violation belongs to the second category (the *sthūlātyaya*);

a middle-grade violation belongs to the third category; and a lower-grade violation belongs to the seventh group (*pāyantika*). Such is the rule in the Śrāvaka-dharma. It is the same [for the Bodhisattva].
There is a distinction regarding Bodhisattvas. [The *Fayin* states:
"Śrāvakas distinguish between the lightness and gravity of offenses, whereas for Bodhisattvas all are grave. This is because Great Beings take compassion for all things as their core intention;
whatever they say must not wound that compassion. They praise but do not disparage; they do not exceed benevolence (*ren*) and do not overstep righteousness (*yi*')."
It is exactly like this.

If you are a Buddha’s disciple:

one personally speaks of the transgressions of lay and ordained bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, and bhikṣuṇīs; one instructs others to speak of their transgressions.
