"If a bodhisattva enters the assembly and sees unlawful joking or laughter, yet does not rebuke them, they incur an offense.

Based on this, even minor matters are taught to be repented of; how much more so for transgressing the precepts as in the aforementioned cases? The *Mingxiang ji* records that the śramaṇa Huída, at...
In the underworld, one may see Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. He says:

"Whether you be a śramaṇa or a layperson, if you recognize the transgressions of your current body as well as the karmic offenses and various evil deeds of your past lives, and if you can fully disclose them before the assembly and repent with diligent sincerity, your sins will be immediately extinguished.
Contemplating this, one knows that the merit of repentance is immeasurable. Thus the Bodhisattva [speaks] in the realm of darkness.
In both [the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*], it is taught that one should instruct others to repent for their offenses.
Third, regarding what is improper:
although a bodhisattva does not teach them to repent, they may dwell together with them, share the same monastic requisites and offerings, and perform the *poṣadha* together as a single community.
Regarding the precepts: if one does not expose another’s offense nor instruct them to repent, there should be three consequences:
first, one should not dwell together with them; second, one should not share benefits with them; third, one should not share the Dharma with them.
Generally, regarding what has been prescribed above, if one observes an offense and fails to expose it, this constitutes a transgression; this must not be permitted.
If one continues to dwell together with them in silence, one incurs another offense. If one continues to provide them with shared material benefits, one incurs another offense.
If one continues to appoint them to receive offerings and gains, one incurs another offense.
*Fayi*: *Posadha*. This is translated as "facing one another to confess transgressions. Every half-month, one raises [others'] offenses and performs repentance.

Those who abide in this manner all gather in pure clarity; therefore, it is called "Pure Abiding" (*Netzhu*). Furthermore, adding one more offense refers to not raising [another's] offense while living together and sharing benefits—these are the three offenses.
The *Maudgalyāyana-asks-the-Buddha Sūtra* states: During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who...
The disciple did not receive instruction or admonition; he frequently committed unrighteous acts and, at the end of his life, was reborn among the nāgas.

According to the nature of nāgas, every seven days they undergo a trial by fire, which burns their bodies until the flesh is consumed and only the bones remain. Immediately thereafter, the flesh is restored, only to be burned again.
Unable to endure such suffering, he then contemplated his past lives and saw that he had previously been a śramaṇa who failed to observe the prohibitions and precepts, and so too had his teacher.

He did not teach him, so the disciple became angry with his original teacher and thought of harming him. Later, when the teacher was crossing the sea with five hundred people, a dragon came and seized the ship.
The crowd asked, "Why have you seized our ship? It replied, "Disembark this bhikṣu, and I will release you and let you go.
They asked, "What concern is this bhikṣu of yours? Why do you seek no one else but specifically seek this one?"
He replied, "Originally he was my teacher; he did not instruct or admonish me. Now that I am suffering this pain, I am seeking him.

When the assembly saw that his resolve could not be turned back, they seized the bhikṣu and cast him into the water. The bhikṣu said, "I shall enter the water myself; there is no need for you to seize me.
By throwing himself into the water and sacrificing his life, the assembly was thereby preserved. From this evidence, it is clear that he was not instructed.
One must repent for one's transgressions; the harm [caused] is no small matter. Furthermore, the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states:
"It would be better to accept evil precepts and, within a single day, sever the life-faculties of immeasurable beings, than to harbor and nurture a base and wicked disciple who cannot be tamed.
The fourth fascicle of the *Bodhisattva-bhūmi-saṃvara Sūtra* says: "Even though those such as caṇḍālas and butchers perform evil deeds, they..."
One who can destroy the True Dharma of the Tathāgata does not necessarily fall into the three evil realms.
However, if a teacher is unable to instruct or admonish their disciples, they thereby destroy the Buddha-dharma and will certainly fall into hell.

Furthermore, the Sarvāstivāda school states that those who have received full ordination but are incapable of receiving instruction should be expelled. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "If a virtuous bhikṣu sees [the Dharma] being destroyed..."
Regarding the Dharma: to fail to reprimand, expel, or suspend such a person is to treat them as an enemy within the Buddha-Dharma.

If one can indeed reprimand and dismiss them, one is a true disciple of the Buddha. Examining the scriptural texts, it is truly impermissible for such a person to dwell indiscriminately among the pure assembly.
Let those who preside over the Dharma not yield to human sentiment, lest they incur grave blame themselves.
III. The Formal Confession of the Offense.
One commits a minor offense (light defilement).

*Fayin* asks: "If one has been instructed but does not reform, should they be exempt from punishment? Answer: Among the scholars of the world, there is a saying: "If instruction and teaching [fail...]"
"Strictness is the teacher's laziness; that learning achieves no success is the disciple's fault. If one is taught and does not reform, what cause for resentment can the teacher have?
According to this precept, it arises from the mind of compassion, the mind of pity, the mind of delight in teaching, and the mind of benefit within the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground."
● Sixth Precept: Not Providing for Those Who Request the Dharma (2). Part One: A Brief Introduction. Part Two: Entering the Text.
○ First, the Brief Introduction.

Because it deprives one of the benefits that nourish and sustain the spirit, this rule is established. It is an offense common to all seven groups of practitioners; however, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not share it entirely. In the Mahāyāna...
When a bhikṣu sees one who possesses understanding, he should always provide for them and request instruction, because his desire for what is wholesome is insatiable.

He should provide for a śrāvaka who understands the detailed or abbreviated *poṣadha* rules. For those within five years of ordination and those who do not yet understand the five dharmas, he should likewise request instruction according to the Dharma;
otherwise, he commits an offense of the seventh category (*saptama-varga*).

*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden) states: "If they are 'together,' they have committed the offense jointly. Furthermore, regarding those who are not 'fully together,' this refers to a lack of commonality in the gravity of the offense.
A Bodhisattva constantly provides offerings and makes invitations at all times; whereas for Śrāvakas, these cease after five years, as the detailed and abbreviated precepts explain.

This refers to those who should provide offerings and invitations. The five factors are: first, accomplishment through faith; second, accomplishment through precepts; third, accomplishment through learning... [and so forth].
1. Accomplishment through faith; 2. Accomplishment through precepts; 3. Accomplishment through giving; 4. Accomplishment through renunciation; 5. Accomplishment through wisdom. II.
Entering the Text (in three parts): 1. Identifying the person; 2. Narrating the events; 3. Summarizing the offense.
I. First, the designation of the person:
"If a Buddha’s disciple. II.
Second, the sequence of the matter (in two parts): A. First, the sequence of the arrival; B. Second, the clarification of what should be done.
First, regarding the arrival [of the teacher]:
one sees a Mahayana Dharma Master, a fellow student of the Mahayana, who shares the same views and the same practice, coming to the monasteries, residences, cities, and towns—
whether traveling from a hundred li or a thousand li away.
The phrase "those of the Mahāyāna who share the same view and the same practice" distinguishes them from those of the Hīnayāna.
Regarding the term "Dharma Master" (*fǎshī*): it does not necessarily refer to a teacher who lectures on the sūtras and śāstras;

rather, anyone who thoroughly understands the Mahāyāna Dharma and is able to transform and guide sentient beings so that they enter the stage of Buddhahood is such a master. As for "those who study the Mahāyāna together," first...
One should invite and serve both those called Mahāyāna masters and those called Mahāyāna friends.
(2) Second, clarifying what should be done, which has two parts: first, what should be offered in worship; second, what should be requested as the Dharma.
First, one should make offerings.
That is to say, one should rise to welcome them upon their arrival and see them off upon their departure; one should prostrate and make offerings, performing these services three times each day.

One should provide the Dharma Master with daily sustenance of three *liang* of gold, food and drink of a hundred flavors, bedding and seats, and medical requisites; all that is required shall be provided in full.
To speak of "three or two ounces of gold" is the height of hyperbole. If there were a request for such an amount, one ought to relinquish those three or two ounces of gold;
even if it meant sacrificing one's life for a single verse from the Snowy Mountains, how much more so for a small offering?
*Fayi*: These are merely empty words. When the Master took this medicine, his illness became even more severe.
2. Regarding the Practice of Requesting the Dharma:

One should regularly request a Dharma Master to preach the Dharma during the three periods of the day. One should perform prostrations three times every day, without giving rise to anger or resentment.
With a mind [devoted] to the Dharma, one should sacrifice the body for the sake of the Dharma and request the Dharma without weariness.
Regarding the "three times": these are the periods before noon, after noon, and the first watch of the night, during which one should seek further instruction and resolve hidden doubts.
"Before noon, at noon, and after noon" refers to the two time-divisions of *jia* (the sixth hour) and *wei* (the tenth hour). As for "a mind of anger," it means feeling resentment toward that Dharma.
The teacher will consequently give rise to a mind of retreat. Regarding "suffering from affliction": having already incurred excessive expenditure, one gives rise to a mind of retreat.
○ Third, the determination of the offense:
if one does not act thus, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "Those who do not incur an offense include those who encounter serious illness, or whose minds are deranged, or who are asleep;
or when another approaches with the intent to awaken them; or when one desires to employ skillful means to subdue them.
Examining this precept, it arises from the mind of faith and the mind of mindfulness within the *Cittabhūmi-dharmamukha-śīla* (The Precepts of the Mind-Ground Dharma Gate).
● Seventh Precept: Not Listening to the Dharma Due to Laziness (2). I. Brief Introduction; II. Entering the Text.
○ I. Brief Introduction.
The intent of the regulation is the same as before.

*Fayi*: The underlying intention is the same as before; however, previously it was when the Bodhisattva came to me and I requested him to preach the Dharma, whereas now it is when the Bodhisattva is there and I go to listen to the Dharma.
II. Entering the Text (3): First, identifying the person; second, setting forth the matter; third, concluding with the offense.
○ First, identifying the person:
"If a disciple of the Buddha..."
II. The Preliminary Matters (3): First, the location for preaching; second, what is appropriate; third, what is inappropriate.
First, the location for preaching:
There are places for preaching the Dharma, Vinaya, Sūtras, and Śāstras in all locations, including within large houses and residences.
Regarding what is called the *vinaya* of the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas: this refers to the Mahāyāna *vinaya* sūtras and vinayas, not the *vinaya* within the [Hinayāna] Tripiṭaka.
Because Mahāyāna sūtras possess the meaning of extinguishing evil, they are termed *vinaya*. Others had already requested that he lecture on them there.
One ought to go and listen to the Dharma; yet, through indolence, one does not go. Day by day, one's defilements increase.

If there is a place where the Dharma is being expounded, to fail to listen or to fail to go because of a mind of anger or pride constitutes an offense. According to the *Upāsaka-sūtra*, the distance need not exceed one *yojana*.
*Fayi*: When both the *sūtras* and the *vinaya* refer to *vinaya*, it is because the power of the Mahāyāna *sūtras* can extinguish evil, which is semantically identical to the *vinaya*.

Since the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śīla-sūtra* (*Dichi jing*) does not distinguish between distant and near, whereas the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* allows for non-offenses within a *yojana*, we know that the regulations for those who have left the household life apply to the distant, while the regulations for those remaining at home apply to the near.
This is likely because those who have left the household life take hearing the Dharma as their primary task, and thus find it burdensome to travel far.

He did not go. This was because of his pride regarding the Dharma. As for those living at home, their bodies are constrained by worldly laws; thus, they are unable to listen from afar, yet this is not due to pride.
II. Explaining the "Appropriate."
A newly initiated bodhisattva should take the scrolls of the sūtras and vinaya to the place where a Dharma teacher resides to listen, receive, and inquire about them.

Whether it be in mountain forests, beneath trees, on monastic grounds, within rooms, or at any other location where the Dharma is being preached, they should go to all such places to listen and receive the teachings.
*Fayi*: Question: Above it was said "in all places," and again "within a great house"; now it is further said "in all places such as mountain forests and beneath trees.
What is the distinction between these? Answer: The first "all places" refers generally to the locations of both monastics and laypeople.
The subsequent "great house" specifically refers to the residences of kings, officials, and those of powerful influence. The final [reference to] "mountain forests... [is as follows].
"Under a tree" refers in all cases specifically to the grounds of monasteries and *ārāmas*.
○ Third, what is improper:
if one does not go there to listen to, receive, or inquire about [the teachings].
*Fayi*: "The youth [Xuedou] traveled south to seek instruction across a hundred prefectures; the patch-robed monk [Dongshan] traversed a thousand mountains.

Even such figures as Touzi, who ascended three times, and Dongshan, who went up nine times—hiding themselves among commoners and wandering on pilgrimage for eighty years—were all those who fixed their wills on meeting masters and forgot their own bodies in seeking the Way.
This was the case everywhere. It is a pity that, despite taking this as a lesson, there are still those whose understanding of the Dharma remains confined within the span of a few inches."
To be within a foot's distance yet as if hearing nothing; that the traces of the Sage appear in one's very neighborhood yet one does not perceive them—how lamentable!
III. Summary of Offenses: One commits a minor secondary offense.

*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden). The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "There is no offense in not going [to hear the Dharma] in the following cases: if one is ill; if one lacks physical strength; if one knows that the teaching will be misstated;
if one knows that what is being said has already been heard many times before; if one is oneself widely learned and fully possesses the capacity for hearing and retention (*śruta-dhāraṇī*);
or if one is practicing meditative concentration and does not wish to interrupt it even briefly. Not going under such circumstances constitutes no transgression. Question:
The Sovereign has, above, the responsibility for the ancestral altars and the state, and, below, the trust of his ministers and subjects. If one cannot go to listen [to the teachings], what then?
Answer: Spiritual communion can still be established across a thousand ages; a message sent on one’s behalf will surely reach all quarters.
When Emperor Zhongzong issued his edict to Caoxi and King Injo wrote his letter to Mingjiao, though their bodies remained within the palace halls, their minds reached [the sages].
This is what is meant by "the site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) and "discourse within a thousand *li*. Does his listening to the Dharma not continue without end?
Regarding this precept: it arises from the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground—specifically from the mind of precept, the mind of progress, the mind of faith, and the mind of mindfulness.
● Eighth: The Precept of Turning Away from the Great and Toward the Small (2). I. Brief Introduction. II. Entering the Text.
○ I. Brief Introduction.
To directly prohibit hesitation and indecision is the expedient means for the inferior view of false attachment. If one decides that the Great is inferior and the Small is superior—

It is a grave offense (*pārājika*). If one calculates that the precept has been lost, it is so; if the mind was perverse and the drawing was not yet completed, one commits a minor defilement (*āpatti*), governed by the same rules as this precept.
Now, I shall speak in terms of turning away from the Great [Vehicle] and toward the Small, for ordinary bodhisattvas frequently engage in such matters.

If expressed in explicit terms, there are two types: if explained according to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), once the virtue of the precept has ceased, one is directly committing a fundamental transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). If...
To speak of the characteristics of what is not the Dharma constitutes the tenth grave offense.

*Fa-yin* (發隱) means "to give rise to concealment. *You-yu* (猶豫) is the name of a beast characterized by much doubt; if one merely turns away in hesitation without reaching a decision, it still belongs to the category of light offenses.

Once the turning away has been finalized, the precepts are lost. Regarding "ordinary persons and bodhisattvas," this clarifies that such things do not exist on the stages of the sages. [The text concludes with] "Dharma and non-Dharma."

The explanation is as found in the preceding text. Essentially, thoughts directed inward toward the mind result in loss that belongs solely to oneself; whereas words manifested outwardly cause harm that extends to others.
This is why [the latter] is considered grave.
II. Entering the Text (3): First, identifying the person; second, setting forth the matter; third, concluding with the offense.
○ First, identifying the person:
"If a Buddha’s disciple..."
II. The Introductory Matter (2): First, turning one’s back on the Great; second, turning toward the Small.
I. Turning One’s Back on the Great:
The mind turns its back on the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas that teach eternal abiding, declaring them not to be the Buddha’s teaching.
*Fayi*: To claim that the Mahāyāna is not the word of the Buddha is a grave offense. Why, then, is it categorized as a "light defilement"?
It is because the mind rejects it while the mouth has not yet proclaimed it; these words and characters are merely internal deliberations.
If there were the sound of slander, it would belong to the tenth grave offense.

Second, those who lean toward the Lesser Vehicle and yet uphold the teachings of the two vehicles of the śrāvakas, the evil views of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), and all the prohibitions, heterodox views, sūtras, and vinayas. Regarding "upholding the two vehicles," there are two interpretations of this:

first, it refers to the desire to receive [the teachings of] the two vehicles; as for the evil views of the non-Buddhists, there are two explanations. One says that the two vehicles, when compared to...

The Mahāyāna is entirely [the teaching of] non-Buddhists. Second, it is said: if one turns one's back on the Mahāyāna and desires to receive the dharma of the six masters, yet their calculations have not yet been completed, this is a skillful means of wrong view and constitutes a minor offense. This precept prohibits such conduct.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden). "Wishing to receive" refers to the preceding phrase "the mind turns its back," meaning the mind wishes to receive.

There are two interpretations: first, turning one's back on the Great [Vehicle] while wishing to receive the Two Vehicles; second, turning one's back on the Great [Vehicle] while wishing to receive the Six Teachers. These calculations have not yet been finalized; it simply means "wishing to receive.
Formerly, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed the *Pañcakaśata-śāstra*, clarifying the Small Vehicle and disparaging the Great. Later, he encountered...
Asanga repented of his own faults and wished to cut out his own tongue. Asanga instructed him to use that very tongue to further praise the Mahāyāna.
Vasubandhu accepted this instruction; he resolved his mind toward the Great Vehicle, propagated and expounded it widely, and ultimately attained the fruit of sainthood.
To reform one's errors without regret is truly a law for all ages.
III. The Formal Confession of the Offense.
This constitutes a minor transgression (light defilement).

[Commentary on the Origin: The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states that there is no offense for reading secular texts, prose, verse, commentaries, or sub-commentaries, provided that [one does so] for the sake of...
It is for the purpose of destroying false views; it is for the purpose of knowing that external scriptures are false and illusory while the Buddha-dharma is true and real;
it is for the purpose of understanding worldly affairs so as not to be treated with contempt by worldly people. Regarding this precept:

it arises from the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground—specifically from the mind of precepts, the mind of vows, the mind of the crown, the mind of faith, the mind of mindfulness, the mind of orientation, and the Mahāyāna mind.
● Ninth Precept: Not Tending to the Sick (2) I. Brief Introduction. II. Entering the Text.
○ I. Brief Introduction.

This precept was established because failing to do so violates compassion. It is an offense for all seven classes of followers. While it is not entirely shared between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, a Bodhisattva should observe it in its entirety.
Observe this: for śrāvakas, the regulations apply only to their teachers and friends, those living together, those sharing a room, as well as fellow monks and nuns;
beyond these, no restrictions are imposed, because they fundamentally do not involve others.
*Fayi*: "Teachers and friends" refers to one's primary teacher and companions; "monks and nuns" refers to all members of the monastic community.

"Roommates" refers to close associates living nearby; "co-residents" refers to those who share the same hearth and kitchen. By citing these four types, it is made clear that the scope of observation is limited.
II. Entering the Text (3): First, identifying the person; second, setting forth the matter; third, concluding with the offense.
○ First, identifying the person:
"If a disciple of the Buddha..."
II. The Preliminary Matters (3): First, the presentation of the sick person; second, what is appropriate; third, what is inappropriate. I.
Presentation of the Sick Person:
Upon seeing anyone who is afflicted by illness.
This is the supreme field of merit.
"To reveal" means to bring forth what was hidden. "All" refers to including both the near and the distant, as well as both monastics and laypeople. "Supreme" is a term for that which is foremost.
II. Clarifying the Duty of Response:
One should always provide offerings as if to the Buddha, without distinction. Among the eight fields of merit, the field of merit consisting of tending to the sick is the foremost field of merit.
If one's parents, teachers, monks, or disciples are ill, lacking in their sensory faculties, or afflicted by the hundred kinds of sickness and suffering, one should provide for them all.
Nurture them until they recover.
To say that one should serve a sick person as if they were the Buddha is spoken with the utmost reverence; this clarifies that it lies in the mind, not in the field [of merit].
For example, when Ānanda divided his rice and gave it to a starving dog, because this mind was pure and excellent, it was equal to that of the Buddha. Thus, a bodhisattva...
Upon seeing any sick person, one should attend to them according to one's own capacity.

In the text, the mention of parents, teachers, disciples, and so forth begins with those who are closest. The conclusion states that one should rescue all who are ill, whether in cities or wildernesses;
from this, it is known that the principle applies universally to all.
*Fayi* (Unveiling the Hidden). Question: Among the eight fields of merit, the Buddhas are the most venerable; why then is nursing the sick considered the foremost? Answer:

The Buddha is a field of veneration (*kṣetra*), which does not encompass compassion (*karuṇā*) alone. It is precisely for the sake of these sick people that the Buddha entrusted me [with this task] after his parinirvāṇa.
One should provide excellent offerings to them, for within them dwell many Buddhas and holy sages; thus they are the field of respect (*gurutva-kṣetra*).
When the hundred bones suffer pain and the four elements are in turmoil, such that one has no means to move and depends on others for life, they are the field of compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*).

Moreover, the Way of the Buddhas is most honored, and humans and devas offer universal support. Among all forms of suffering, none exceeds the suffering of the sick; among all forms of merit, none surpasses [the merit of serving] the sick.
"It is fitting that we return to attend to the sick. Master Yan personally stayed in the infirmary for lepers, suckling and washing them without hesitation;
Master Kuan carried the patients back home, making no distinction between monastics and laypeople. They may truly be called those who provide offerings as if to a Buddha.
Third, it is improper.

Yet, if a bodhisattva, out of a mind of resentment and anger, fails to look after others—even when encountering the sick within monasteries, cities, towns, wildernesses, mountain forests, or on roads—and does not provide them with relief or assistance; [this is a transgression].

If one sets [the matter] aside out of a mind of anger, one incurs a light secondary offense (*āpatti-dūṣaṇa*) according to the person involved. If one is physically incapable, there is no offense provided one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
The minor details are as found in the Vinaya section.

*Fayi*: The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "When traveling on a road, if one sees a sick person and does not stop to look after them, provide skillful means, or entrust them to someone else before departing, one incurs an offense.
This means that if one has the capacity, one should personally provide medical care;
if one lacks the capacity, one should transfer the responsibility to another. To remain indifferent as if one had neither seen nor heard of the person is contrary to compassion.

Where is the [proper] mind? Therefore, one incurs an offense. Regarding "a mind of anger," it means to harbor resentment and jealousy toward the sick person and fail to give rise to thoughts of compassion.
If one’s strength is insufficient to provide care, yet one maintains a compassionate mind, then there is no offense. As for "trifling matters":
As stated in the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*: "If one has an illness oneself, or lacks the personal strength to attend to it, one should extensively exhort those who possess such strength.
If that patient has many kinsmen, one should instead urgently cultivate the unsurpassed wholesome dharmas oneself."
In all these cases, there is no offense.
III. Conclusion on the Offense: One commits a minor secondary offense (light dust offense).
*Fayi*: The previous commentary distinguished between the mind of anger and the inability [to act]. Thus, this formulation of the offense specifically refers to the mind of anger;
it does not include the inability [to act] as well. An offense is committed only when one is unable to act yet fails to give rise to thoughts of loving-kindness.
● Regarding this precept: it arises from the mind of compassion, the mind of pity, and the mind of filial obedience within the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground Precepts.
● Tenth: The Precept Against Possessing Instruments for Killing Sentient Beings (2). First, the brief introduction; second, entering the text.
I. Brief Introduction.
This was established because of injury to compassion; it is an offense common to all seven assemblies, and it is regulated for both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
II. Entering the Text (three parts): 1. Identifying the person. 2. Sequencing the events. 3. Summary conclusion of the first section.
I. First, the designation of the person:
"If you, O sons of the Buddha. II.
Second, the sequence of the matter (in three parts): A. First, what is not permitted; B. Second, citing analogies; C. Third, citing transgressions to conclude with the faults.
At the outset, this is not permissible:
one must not possess any weapons for combat, such as swords, staves, bows and arrows, spears, or axes;
nor any evil nets, snares, or instruments for killing living beings. Nothing of this kind may be possessed.
*Fayin*: A "máo" (spear) is a long pike. A "juàn" (snare) is a device for binding the feet to capture birds and beasts.
Instruments of combat wound people; tools for killing living beings wound creatures.
Second, the citation of an analogy:
Even when a bodhisattva is killed by their own parents, they do not seek retribution; how much less so when it concerns killing all sentient beings?
One must not keep any instruments for killing sentient beings.
If one does not even think of avenging the enmity of one's parents, how much less would one wish to harm sentient beings by using instruments of slaughter?

Fishing nets, birdlime, and snares are prohibited for both the laity and the clergy. As for blades, spears, bows, and arrows, these were formerly permitted for kings, princes, and others of such rank.

*Fayi* (Unveiling the Hidden): "The vengeance for one's parents' enemies is not requited"—a detailed explanation of this appears below. *Jiao* (Lasso/Catcher): This refers to shooting arrows with raw silk cords attached.
Nets, lassos, and snares are all implements for fishing and hunting. As for *shuo* (lance), it is a type of spear;

those who possess blades, spears, bows, and arrows—namely kings and princes—are exempt from restrictions because they maintain the state with military forces. Others, having no state, are not so exempt.

This is improper. Regarding the prohibition against nets, birdlime, and the like: it is unsuitable for both the clergy and the laity, whether noble or humble, to inflict injury or kill birds and beasts that commit no offense.
To untie the encircling net and to unstring the bow aimed at the startled deer—therein lies the way to achieve governance and transcendence;
this too possesses its own path.
Third, raising the point of non-restraint to expose the fault:
if one intentionally keeps [such weapons], one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
*Fayi* (Exposition of the Hidden) asks: "Regarding Deshan’s staff and Shigong’s bow, would these not constitute a violation of the precepts? Answer: These are for the protection of life.
"Excellent staff! It is the divine bow that rescues from death. Where could a lethal weapon exist?

If one lacks realization within while practicing the empty head-games of external studies, wielding a blind staff recklessly and brandishing a deluded bow at random, one falsely discourses on Prajñā, misleading and confusing future generations.
According to the explicit texts of the Vinaya, such offenses incur immeasurable guilt. Examining this precept, it is the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground."
The precepts arise from a mind of equanimity, a mind of loving-kindness, and a mind of compassion.
○ Third, the summary of the first section:
These ten precepts should be studied; one should reverently uphold them. They are explained in detail in the following six chapters.
This is a summary of the ten precepts, as elucidated in the six chapters below.

[Commentary on the Hidden Meaning]: In the *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Extensive Version), the aforementioned ten precepts are explained in detail across six chapters; here they are abbreviated. Subsequent sections shall follow this pattern.
● Chapter Eleven: The Precepts on Serving as an Envoy to a Foreign State (Part Two). I. Brief Introduction. II. Entering the Text.
○ I. Brief Introduction.
Now, one who serves as an envoy to an enemy state must necessarily scout for strengths and weaknesses, employ deceptive strategies, and seek to coordinate with battle formations.

To harbor thoughts of victory and defeat violates fundamental compassion. As the text states, such individuals are "enemies of the state"; this offense applies equally to all seven assemblies and is prohibited for both Mahayana and Hinayana practitioners.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden) explains: "To spy" means to watch for opportunities; "to deceive" means to act with treacherous fraud. One spies upon the reality or falsehood [of others]...
They act according to their own whims; they carry out their affairs only after devising schemes of deceit and fraud. As for those called "thieves," Mencius said:

"I can enter into treaties with your state's allies for you, and ensure that in battle you shall surely be victorious. Those who are called "good ministers" today were what the ancients called "thieves of the people."
II. Entering the Text (in two parts): First, identifying the person; second, citing the event.
I. Identifying the Person:
O Disciples of the Buddha!
II. Citing Specific Instances (3): 1. What is improper; 2. Drawing an analogy; 3. Citing the improper to conclude with the fault.
I. What is Improper:

One must not, out of a malicious mind for the sake of gain and offerings, serve as a messenger between nations, attend military parades and assemblies, or join in the mobilization of armies for mutual warfare.
They slaughter immeasurable sentient beings.
Driven by an evil mind for their own profit, they disrupt harmony and incite hidden turmoil.

There are two types of emissaries: those who cause strife, which damages the state and brings calamity upon the people; and those who promote harmony, which stabilizes the nation and provides relief to the populace.

Therefore, they must be distinguished. Question: If that is so, then as for the schools of Yan, Yi, Qin, and Zhong—who each excelled in their own systems of "conformity" (cong) and "balance" (heng)—were one truly good and the other evil?

Answer: According to their original intent, those who followed [Yan] certainly committed the offense of raising armies, and those who practiced "balance" (Zhong) likewise lacked benevolent intentions;
both ultimately result in nothing but transgression. To distinguish them more precisely, the harm caused by "balance" (heng) is specifically defined as follows:

It is merely a matter of being frugal. Surely, one should discuss benevolence and righteousness to bring an end to the wars between Qin and Chu, and decline gifts and tributes to establish peace between the north and south.
Is such a state envoy what is meant by "one who has performed many meritorious deeds"?
II. The Citation of an Analogy:
Even a bodhisattva may not enter an army to come and go; how much less so one who intentionally acts as a traitor to the state?
One must not enter an army, for an army is a place of clamor and disorder, not a place where the sons of the Buddha should frequent. It is a place where armies are raised and mutual slaughter occurs.
To give rise to killing is to violate compassion; it is something that should not be done. This [rule] was established because such missions serve as causes and conditions for mutual harm.
Thus, the *Fayi* (Exposition of the Hidden) states: "Thief" means to harm. Because they harm one another, the rule was established; it clarifies that where there is no harm, there is no prohibition.

When Huiyong flew his alms-bowl to stop the soldiers and Fotudeng divined from the bell to end the calamity—when these two elders were within the military camps, what was there that was not permissible?
Third, the raising of the transgression to expose the fault:
If one acts intentionally, one commits a minor offense (light垢罪).
[Commentary on the Hidden Meaning: A Mahāsattva should act as an envoy of the Tathāgata to bring universal peace to all sentient beings within the three realms; yet, if...
Thus, one becomes a traitor to the state; how could one not commit an offense? Regarding this precept:
it arises from the mind of compassion and the mind of pity within the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground.
● The Twelfth Precept on Selling (2): Part One, the Brief Statement; Part Two, the Textual Explanation.
○ Part One, the Brief Statement:

This precept was established because seeking profit and damaging objects contravene loving-kindness (*maitrī*). It constitutes an offense for both the Great and Small Vehicles. While it applies to all seven classes of practitioners, it does not apply in its entirety to all of them simultaneously.
*Fayi*: "If my benefit is another's harm, it is called 'contrary to compassion. Regarding the fact that the seven groups [of practitioners] do not fully share [in certain matters]:
this is the common practice of worldly trade; those at home should not prohibit it."
II. Entering the Text (in two parts). First, identifying the person; second, introducing the matter.
○ First, identifying the person:
"If you, O Sons of the Buddha..."
II. The Introductory Matter (3): First, what is improper; second, providing an illustration by contrast; third, citing an example of misconduct to conclude with the fault.
I. What is Improper:

Therefore, one should not engage in the buying and selling of free persons, male or female slaves, or domestic animals; nor should one trade in coffins, planks, wood, or other implements used for containing the dead.

As for those who engage in trade, this refers to the selling of living beings, such as domestic animals, or the trafficking of free persons, which often involves the suffering of being separated from one's kin.
If one trades in coffins, it is done with a malicious intent to seek profit; therefore, both monastics and laypeople alike refrain from such practices.
*Fayi*: To say that people keep coffins [as a means of livelihood] clarifies that this is severed for both monastics and laypeople alike;
it distinguishes this from ordinary trade, which is not severed for either monastics or laypeople.
○ Third, the illustration by analogy.
One should not do this oneself, much less teach others to do so.
Whether one acts on one's own, instructs another to act for oneself, or instructs another to act for themselves, all constitute a minor transgression (*laghu-āpatti*).
Furthermore, it includes stealing living beings for sale, selling livestock for slaughter, using incantations to cause death, or desiring to sell coffins. This...
This separately constitutes the offenses of theft and killing.
[The following] reveals the hidden meaning. There are two types of instructing others: first, instructing another to act on one's behalf; second, instructing another to act for themselves.
Smuggling living beings across [a border] is distinguished from openly selling them—it is not theft—as in the case of purchasing female slaves and the like.

Ordering the slaughter of livestock is distinguished from selling them for trade—it is not mere sale—as in the case of draft oxen and the like. Using incantations to cause death and then selling the coffins.

This distinguishes [this case] from the previous instance of waiting for death while preparing a coffin; it is not a matter of killing through incantations. If one commits these three matters, they constitute the two *pārājika* offenses of intentional killing and stealing, and are not subsumed under minor impurities (*āpatti*).
3. To raise the issue of transgression and its consequences:
if one intentionally acts [in such a manner] oneself or instructs another to do so, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
[Commentary]: Question: In ancient times, the dead were abandoned in the wild; later sages changed this to using coffins. The ritual for sending off the deceased is called the "Great Matter."
Question: Why is it that even coffins and outer cases are prohibited? Answer: This prohibition is intended to restrain those with malicious intentions who seek profit;

it does not mean that coffins and outer cases are forbidden for general use. Just as one who manages a livelihood must rely on trade and sales, the admonitions against shamans and carpenters become clearly evident.
If one prepares [offerings] and bestows them upon the poor, then the merit will naturally be immeasurable.
According to this precept, the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground arises from within the mind of morality, the mind of loving-kindness, and the mind of compassion.
● Thirteenth: Slandering the Precepts (2). Part One: A Brief Introduction. Part Two: Entering the Text.
○ First, the Brief Introduction:

This was established because [the act] causes others to fall into ruin and harms compassion; it is prohibited in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and all seven classes of followers commit this offense. [The following is] an abridged selection.

For those above the rank of devas who equally possess the Bodhisattva precepts, it is said that they commit either a grave transgression or incur punishment for the seven inversions and ten heavy offenses, regardless of whether the basis for the offense exists or not;
provided only that they speak to a person of a different dharma, all such acts constitute a grave violation.

The transgressions of the fourfold assembly have already been explained above. If one speaks of these to a fellow practitioner—regardless of whether that person’s status is superior or inferior, or whether they possess the precepts or not—and thereby causes them to fall into ruin, this constitutes a violation of the same minor defilement (laghu-āpatti).

*Fayi*: "To 'delete and select' (*shanchu*) means to excise. One must excise those who slander or defame those above the rank of *tianren* (celestial beings), for they all equally possess the Great Precepts.
Whether their reputation is ruined or their person is punished, it matters not whether the basis for the slander exists or not;
yet, if one directs such words toward those of a different dharma, the calamity will be broadcast and endless. But if directed toward those of the same dharma..."
This is because [the offense] was concealed and the harm was not yet widespread; therefore, one case belongs to the heavy category and the other to the light.
○ Second, entering the text (three parts): first, identifying the person; second, narrating the events; third, concluding with the offense.
I. First, the designation of the person:
"If a disciple of the Buddha. II.
Second, the sequence of the matter (in three parts): 1. First, citing the act of slandering; 2. Second, clarifying what should be done; 3. Third, clarifying what should not be done.
First, the matter of slander is raised:
out of an evil mind, one slanders a virtuous person, a good person, a Dharma master, or a preceptor without any basis,
claiming that they have committed the seven heinous offenses or the ten grave transgressions— such as a king, a nobleman, or others of high status.
*Fayi*: "Evil mind" refers to either greed or anger; it is groundless, for there is originally no reality [to the offense]. Question:

The previous statement that self-praise and disparaging others, as well as slandering the Triple Gem, both constitute the ten grave offenses—how is it that the current instance of slander and disparagement falls into a lighter category? Answer:

To disparage others while simultaneously praising oneself constitutes a grave offense; now, there is no self-praise. To disparage the Three Jewels while simultaneously praising the Buddha and Dharma constitutes a grave offense;

now, one merely slanders the Sangha. Furthermore, in the commentary (*shu*), the author himself distinguishes between "different dharmas" and "identical dharmas"; this likely refers to identical dharmas.
II. Clarifying the Response:
Among parents, siblings, and the six classes of kinsmen, one should give rise to a mind of filial obedience and a mind of compassion.
Regarding the mention of "parents and siblings," this illustrates the mind of a Great Being (Mahāsattva); such a mind constantly regards all beings as its own parents.
Regarding the six types of kin: one should give rise to a mind of filial piety, obedience, compassion, and kindness.
The *Fanyi* (Explanatory Commentary) details two meanings: first, regarding one’s own actual six types of kin; second, regarding all sentient beings, conceiving of them as one’s own six types of kin.
One who is filial and obedient does not dare to slander [them]; one who is compassionate and kind cannot bear to slander [them]. [As for] those who are unfilial...
Compassion! What has one to fear or avoid?
Third, those who instead of desisting commit even greater acts of hostility and harm, thereby falling into undesirable states of existence.

Now, conversely, one who slanders and harms another—whether a śrāvaka, a candidate for the fruit, or one who shares the same precepts, views, and community—if the four grave offenses (*catur-uttara-pārājika*) are groundless, it constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
The remainder is as explained extensively in the Vinaya section.
*Fayi*: Following the previous point, instead of giving rise to filial piety and obedience, one instead commits acts of rebellion; instead of giving rise to compassion, one instead inflicts harm.
One inevitably injures and oppresses the other, depriving them of their proper place; therefore, it is said that they "fall into an undesirable state.

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, if a śrāvaka speaks falsely, claiming that a bhikṣu has committed the four pārājika offenses when he has not, it constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. It does not yet say that [the case] is the same.
Regarding the Dharma: because the Bodhisattva’s wisdom is profound and free from delusion, the offense committed toward one of equal status is light;

because the Śrāvaka’s wisdom is not yet profound, the offense committed toward one of equal status is somewhat heavier. "Without root" means that while there are branches and leaves, there is no fundamental basis.
○ Third, the pronouncement of the offense:
one commits a light secondary offense (*āpatti*).

[This concludes] the "Manifestation of the Arising. ● Regarding this precept: within the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, it concerns guarding the mind and rejoicing in the mind within the heart of the precepts.
It arises from a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and filial piety (*śuśrūṣā*).
● The Fourteenth Precept: Against Setting Fire to Burn (2). Part One: A Brief Introduction. Part Two: Entering the Text.
First, the brief summary:
This precept was established because it causes injury to sentient beings; thus, all seven classes of followers commit this offense, and it is proscribed for both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. *Fayi*:

"Sentient beings" (you-shi) distinguishes them from insentient things such as grasses and trees. Although one’s original intention may have been to burn a mountain, if there is no conscious intent to harm living creatures, [the offense is not incurred].
Yet things will inevitably suffer injury; this is what is meant by the saying, "When a fire breaks out at the city gate, the calamity reaches the fish in the pond.
○ Second, entering the text (in two parts): First, identifying the person; second, narrating the events.
I. First, the designation of the person:
"If you, O sons of the Buddha. II.
Second, the sequence of the matter (in three parts): 1. First, clarifying the act of setting fire; 2. Second, the remote consequence of burning; 3. Third, citing the transgression.
The Section on the Transgression.
○ First, the account of setting fire.
Out of an evil mind, he set a great fire to burn mountain forests and wildernesses. He set fires from the fourth month through the ninth month.
There are masters who say that killing spirits or animals constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*), as this was already prohibited by the first precept;

they claim that this present precept merely prohibits burning forest trees, based on the sense of causing distant harm. Now, it is explained that since killing spirits or animals does not constitute a grave offense, the case of one who dies from burning forest trees is governed by the same regulation as this precept.
From the fourth month to the ninth month, many types of insects and creatures are born; at this time, when traveling...

The secular regulations are the same: one must not burn forest trees, as this carries the implication of causing harm at a distance. For a lay bodhisattva whose occupation involves burning, there is no prohibition;
for a monastic bodhisattva, however, even for the sake of preventing obstacles to communal affairs, it should likewise be permitted [only under specific conditions].
If one burns without careful heed, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

*Fayi*: The previous ten sections clarified that one incurs no grave offense for killing when it is not intentional. Now, the statement that killing ghosts or animals does not constitute a grave offense is because there was no intent to kill.
Even when burning forest trees and thereby harming living beings, the intention is directed toward the trees themselves.
Therefore, this follows the same regulations as before. For those living at home, it concerns their livelihood; for those who have left the home life, it concerns the removal of harm.
These are not prohibited, but one should exercise careful protection and act with thorough diligence to bring matters to completion. Otherwise, an offense is committed.

Fearing that this prohibition might be disregarded and people would burn [things] at will, the commentary says "be cautious. Question: Since the prohibition here applies from the fourth month to the ninth month, what about the tenth month?

It is clear that by the third month, [the insects] have not yet been suppressed; yet in the tenth month, when they have not yet finished [their life cycle], there are no insects. Furthermore, the second month is precisely when creatures emerge from hibernation;
if one were to burn [the fields] at such a time, how could it be without harm? Answer: This is said with reference to regions of bitter cold.
If it were the warm and mild regions of the southeast, it would likely be unsuitable. It is only appropriate for the freezing intensity of the twelfth month, when frost and snow fall repeatedly.

This is the latter interpretation. One who skillfully understands the text should naturally grasp its intended meaning. Some say that ghosts and animals do not commit a grave offense (*pārājika*), taking this to mean they lack the capacity for the Dharma among the ten types of grave offenses mentioned above.
This follows the commentary (*śāstra*), but it does not accord with the meaning of the sutra.
Second, regarding distant burning:
if one burns the houses, dwellings, cities, towns, monasteries, fields, or timber of others, or the property of spirits, deities, or officials—
nor any other living beings— one must not burn them intentionally.
"All living beings" refers to those possessing life; it is an error to say "living beings," and one should rather say "possessions belonging to others.
If one burns possessions belonging to others, why would it be restricted only to the fourth and ninth months? One should know that this constitutes the taking of life.
*Fayi*: The preceding text spoke only of mountain forests; now it includes cities and towns as well as all other places. Therefore, it says, "In the distance there is burning.
[This concludes the section. Three:
Raising objections to conclude the refutation.
If one intentionally sets fire [to them], one commits a minor offense (light impurity).

*Fayi* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) states: "Intentional burning is of two kinds: setting cities and towns ablaze while giving rein to greed and anger; or burning mountains and forests beyond the prescribed time limit. Both are 'intentional' (*hugu*).
The term 'intentional' serves to distinguish this from unintentional acts. Regarding this precept, it is the Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground.
The gate of precepts arises from guarding the mind with a compassionate heart.
● Fifteenth: Precepts against Deviant Teachings (2). First, the brief introduction; second, entering the text.
First, the brief introduction:

This was established because it causes people to lose the right path; it is an offense common to all seven assemblies, yet it is not shared between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as their respective trainings differ.
*Fayi* (Unveiling the Hidden): "Perversion" means partiality; it means deviance. Both the followers of the Two Vehicles and externalists fall into this category.
II. Entering the Text (in three parts): 1. Identifying the person. 2. Narrating the events. 3. Summarizing the offense.
I. First, the designation of the person:
"If a Buddha’s disciple. II.
Second, the sequence of the matter (in three parts): 1. First, citing that which is taught; 2. Second, clarifying what should be done; 3. Third, clarifying what should not be done.
First, the objects of instruction are set forth:
from the Buddha’s disciples to non-Buddhist heretics and evil persons, and to all six types of relatives and virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
"The Buddha’s disciples" refers to the internal assembly; "non-Buddhists" refers to the external assembly; and the "six types of relatives and virtuous spiritual friends" pertain to both.

"External. [From] *Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): "From" means following. In contrast to "and" (*ji*), those who study the Buddha-dharma are called the internal assembly; those who practice other teachings are called the external assembly.
As for "evil persons," they are those who oppose the right path; they are precisely what are called unwholesome people. "Virtuous friends" (*śāstrī*) refers to those whose realization is matured.
Regarding the category of "associates": these are not necessarily spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) who have attained the Way.

As for those who "pervade both the internal and external," among these six types of relatives and acquaintances, some study Buddhism while others study non-Buddhist paths; therefore, they are said to "pervade."
II. Clarifying the Response:

One should instruct each individual to receive and uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas. One should teach them to understand the principles and meanings, causing them to give rise to the bodhicitta, the ten *cittotpāda* (aspiration) minds, the ten *paripuṣṭi* (nurturing) minds, and the ten *vajra* minds. Within these thirty minds, one should cause them to understand each one individually.
Regarding the sequential application of the Dharma:

one should instruct them in the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, causing them to resolve upon bodhicitta. As for the "ten minds," these are the ten minds of initial aspiration (*daśa-prasthāna-citta*) that arise;

they are the ten adamantine minds (*daśa-vajra*). This refers briefly to the ten adamantine [minds] and does not mention the ten nurturing [minds]. These thirty [minds] constitute the stage of the beginner.
This is urgent; it must be elucidated for the sake of providing instruction.

Regarding the "unveiling of the hidden": one who understands the meaning and one who resolves their mind [on awakening]—neither of these two may be neglected. If one does not understand the principles of the meaning, that which is resolved upon will be a deviant mind;
if one does not resolve upon the Great Mind, then what is known will be a mere empty understanding. Therefore, both must be practiced together. (Text)
Among these, there are ten stages of nourishment (*puṣṭi*). The commentary states that they are not mentioned, perhaps because they were absent from other versions;
however, we now take their presence as correct, since the ten stages of nourishment appear in both the preceding and subsequent texts. As for "the initial practice":

this refers to the thirty minds of the stages of abiding, advancing, and heading toward [enlightenment], which constitute the initial practice of the Buddha-way. Since these are not secondary or urgent matters, they ought to be revealed and cannot be postponed.
Third, it is improper: yet a bodhisattva,
out of a malicious mind or a mind of anger, arbitrarily teaches the sūtras and vinayas of the two vehicles— the śrāvakas— as well as the heterodox treatises of external paths and false views.
One should not, with an evil mind, instruct those of the Two Vehicles in non-Buddhist texts and the like. There is no offense if one perceives an opportunity to benefit sentient beings.
[The *Fayi* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) states: "An 'evil mind' refers to one who originally forms an unwholesome resolve, desiring only that people enter into partiality and heterodoxy."
"One with a mind of anger" refers to one who gives rise to affliction upon being provoked; therefore, such a person is taught to enter into partiality and deviance. "Arbitrarily" means unjustly;

it refers to teaching what should not be taught. "Discerning the occasion" means perceiving what is appropriate for the specific circumstances, employing skillful means to teach and benefit sentient beings.
It is clear that this was not done with an evil mind or a mind of anger, but rather through indirect persuasion and inducement; what offense could there be?
Third, the conclusion of the offense:
one commits a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*).

*Fayi*: According to this precept, it arises from the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground Dharma-Gate—the precept-mind, the mind of excellence, the mind of penetration, the mind of perfection, and the Mahāyāna mind.
● The sixteenth: Misrepresenting the Precepts for the Sake of Gain (2). Part One: A Brief Introduction; Part Two: Entering the Text.
○ First, the brief introduction:

Because it violates the way of instruction and transmission, this rule was established. It is an offense common to all seven assemblies; it is regulated by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. The preceding precept was concealed.

To show the great while acting small: although one now preaches the Great [Vehicle] for the sake of others, if one is stingy regarding gain and profit, concealing and suppressing the essential meaning so as not to reveal it, or if a śrāvaka suppresses the principles when instructing others, they commit a minor secondary offense (āpatti).

*Fayin* (Unveiling the Hidden): "Jin" means to begrudge; "xi" means to cherish; "gu" means to be firm; and "mi" means to be secretive. To begrudge, cherish, be firm, and remain secretive is not to provide the correct teaching; it is because of the desire for profit.
To withhold the True Dharma due to private bribery, yet only exhaustively reveal what one knows once something has been obtained—this is the way of a merchant.
How could this be the mind of a Mahāsattva intent on great salvation? When speaking of those who transgress as Śrāvakas, it clarifies the Great [Vehicle].
Because it is a minor offense (duṣkṛta).
○ Second, entering the text (three parts): First, identifying the person; second, setting forth the matter; third, concluding with the offense.
○ First, identifying the person.
If you are a Buddha’s disciple:
(2) Second, the sequence of matters (3): First, one should first learn it for oneself; second, one should explain it for others later; third, one should not conceal or suppress it.
First, one should initially study for oneself.
One should, with a sincere mind, first study the Mahāyāna Vinaya-sūtras on dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), extensively elucidating their meanings and flavors, and revealing what is hidden.

Regarding "with a sincere mind": this clarifies the beginning of initial study; it means that from the very start, one generates the aspiration to seek the supreme [enlightenment] above and to transform sentient beings below, severing [all worldly attachments].
Because of the desire for profit. Now that you have merely begun to study the Buddha-dharma, you already harbor thoughts of gain; this is not a sincere heart.
As the former sages said, "When people of today read books, they go wrong from the very beginning. The meaning is precisely like this.

Regarding the *Vinaya* and the *Sūtras* on majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*), one is the model for the Mahāyāna transformation and guidance of others, and the other is the Mahāyāna practice of self-cultivation and progress.
The gateways of these [teachings] all possess their own principles and aesthetic flavor; one should first achieve understanding of them before being able to guide sentient beings.
Second, it is for the sake of those who come later.
Seeing new students of the Bodhisattva path who have traveled from hundreds or thousands of *li* to seek the Mahayana sutras and vinayas, one should—like [the previous example]—[respond accordingly].
The Dharma teaches that all ascetic practices involve either burning the body, the arms, or the fingers, or failing to burn the body, arms, and fingers as offerings to the Buddhas;
such a person is not a renunciant bodhisattva, even if they [offer themselves] to hungry tigers, wolves, lions, or any hungry ghosts.

One should, in every case, sacrifice one's own body, flesh, hands, and feet to make offerings to them. Thereafter, one should explain the True Dharma to each person in turn, causing their minds to open and their intentions to be resolved.
A master says that the ascetic practices listed here are intended to compel one to save sentient beings; otherwise, it constitutes a minor offense. Furthermore, he explains:
This is a statement of comparison. A Great Being (mahāsattva) ought to sacrifice his own body to give to others before fully expounding the Dharma for them;

how much more so now, when he merely expounds the Dharma while seeking profit and remaining concealed? The subsequent section demonstrates three points, the textual structure of which is easy to discern.
*Fayi* (Unveiling the Hidden): First, the ascetic practices are clarified in order to broaden the mind’s resolve and strengthen its vows;
only then does the sequential teaching of the Dharma proceed, such as the thirty stages of mind (*triṃśaccitta*) and so forth. This clarifies that the teaching is direct, orderly, and non-perverted.
The commentary lists two interpretations, the former of which is correct. The passage states, "teaching all ascetic practices according to the Dharma," which serves as an illustration.

This was taught for the sake of instructing others, showing that the conduct of a bodhisattva should be as described; it does not necessarily mean that one must sacrifice one's body to provide for them.
Third, one should not remain hidden.

Yet, for the sake of gain and honor, a bodhisattva may fail to answer when they ought to answer; they may explain the words of the sūtras and vinaya in a distorted manner, lacking proper sequence, and they may slander those who preach the Three Jewels.
*Fayin* (Unfolding the Hidden): This should not be included among the three [cases] for the middle and latter stages.

First, for the sake of gain and honor, one fails to answer according to correct principle and instead provides a separate answer; this constitutes "stinginess in speech" (*matsaravāda*) and "concealment" (*antardhāpana*). Second, for the sake of gain and honor...
To arbitrarily alter the sequence of the scriptural meaning is a concealment through inverted exposition.

Third, to answer by contravening the Buddha’s original intention, turning one's back on the fundamental meaning of the Dharma, and violating the primary tenets of all the worthy and holy ones, is a concealment through slanderous exposition. None of these are appropriate.
III. Determining the Offense: One commits a light secondary offense (*āpatti*).

[From] the *Fayin*: Question: Regarding the statement that slandering the Triple Gem is not included among the ten grave offenses, why is this so? Answer: The ten grave offenses refer exclusively to the act of slandering.

This [offense] is grave because it involves the total repudiation of the Triple Gem. This, however, is a case of erroneous interpretation and false discourse, termed "slanderous speech" (*pāpa-vāda*);

it is not a case of actual repudiation, and is therefore light. According to this precept, it arises from the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, specifically from within the mind of morality, the mind of compassion, the mind of fondness for teaching, and the mind of penetration.
● The Seventeenth Precept: Begging by Exploiting One’s Power (2). I. Brief Introduction. II. Entering the Text.
○ I. Brief Introduction.
This precept was established because it causes distress to others. It is a violation for all seven classes of followers. It is proscribed in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
II. Entering the Text (in two parts): First, identifying the person; second, setting forth the events.
○ First, identifying the person:
"If you, O Son of the Buddha..."
II. The Introductory Matter (2): 1. Approaching for the sake of profit; 2. Unreasonable begging; 3.
Pointing out the fault and concluding the transgression. I. Approaching for the sake of profit.
For the sake of food, drink, wealth, gain, and reputation, one approaches kings, princes, ministers, and officials.
One reveals secrets for the sake of food and such; this excludes those who act for the sake of the Path. "For oneself" excludes those who act for the sake of the community. [End of excerpt]
That our family may not have been able to draw close to royal ministers was precisely because of people such as these.

Had they been willing to forget their own bodies for the sake of the multitude, and forget profit for the sake of the Way, then even the noble favor of three successive courts and the veneration of seven emperors—who could have said it would not be possible?
Second, begging through improper means:
relying on the use of forceful postures to solicit, beating, or dragging others; taking money and goods by force; seeking profit in every way—this is called evil seeking and excessive seeking.
Teaching others to seek in such a manner is likewise included.

To use one’s influence to solicit the placement [of a request] in writing, or to solicit through threats and beatings—whether acting on one’s own initiative or instructing others to do so for one’s sake—one violates this precept.

*Fayi* (Exposition of the Hidden) states: "To solicit the placement [of a request] in writing" means to rely on one’s powerful influence to borrow the weight of a written edict to entrust someone with a particular arrangement or disposition.
"Beating and striking" refers to using force to intimidate. "Begging for wealth" means to solicit material goods. "Dragging and pulling" means to bind, pull, and haul away;
these are all methods of taking by intimidation and force. All such seeking of profit is called "evil seeking" (*akuśala-paryeṣaṇā*) and "excessive seeking" (*bahu-paryeṣaṇā*).
"Evil" is contrasted with "virtuous" seeking, and "excessive" is contrasted with "moderate" seeking. Intimidation is termed "evil," while lack of contentment is termed "excessive."
Third, the accusation of failing to rectify faults:
To be entirely devoid of a compassionate heart and a heart of filial piety constitutes a minor offense. [Commentary:

Compassion consists of constantly contemplating how to provide relief and succor, taking concern for the poverty of others. Filial piety consists of making offerings to sentient beings as if they were one's own parents.
How could one possibly bear to take them away by force from one’s own parents?
According to this precept, it arises from the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, specifically from the mind of compassion, the mind of filial piety, and the mind free from seeking.
● The Eighteenth Precept: Not Ordaining Those Lacking Competence (2). Part One: A Brief Summary. Entering the Text.
○ First, the Brief Summary.

To ordain someone who lacks understanding is to commit the error of misleading others; therefore, this rule was established. Both monastic communities (the two assemblies) incur this offense equally, whether they belong to the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna.

Both [the monastic and lay] vehicles are governed by these prohibitions. For the three assemblies and the laity, there is no principle of having a formal preceptor (*ācārya*); thus, it has not yet been established.

Regarding the Śrāvaka, the qualities of a teacher are contained within the seven rules, as prescribed in the recitation of the *Śīla-dharma*. As for the Bodhisattva’s teacher-disciple relationship, one must necessarily be ten years senior; the five dharmas are as explained at the beginning.
*Fayi*: "The three groups" refers to śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās.

Because śrāmaṇeras have not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*), and śikṣamāṇās—women training in the precepts—lack the status of being teachers of others, they were not subject to [this rule]. As for the "seven dharmas of the śrāvakas": [text continues]

In the Vinaya, it is said there are seven categories of dharma: first, the dharma of receiving full ordination; second, the dharma of the *poṣadha*; third, the dharma of the *pravāraṇā*; fourth, the dharma of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*);

fifth, the dharma of leather; sixth, the dharma of medicine; and seventh, the dharma of robes. Furthermore, one should thoroughly master both the recitation of the precepts and the ritual for receiving them.
Regarding the five dharmas of a bodhisattva, according to the commentary, they are explained as being the same as the aforementioned five virtues. However, when explained separately:
First, faith; second, precepts; third, learning; fourth, relinquishment; fifth, wisdom. Furthermore: first, ten years [of age]; second, being endowed with the precepts;
third, extensive learning; fourth, the ability to remove sorrow; fifth, the ability to uproot the heterodox. These are also roughly similar to the five virtues.
II. Entering the Text (in two parts): First, identifying the person; second, setting forth the matter.
○ First, identifying the person:
"If you, O Sons of the Buddha..."
II. The Preliminary Matters (3). First, one should recite and explain; second, if one does not understand, one should not recite; third, to cite the fault and conclude with the transgression.
I. First, one should recite and explain.
One should study the twelve divisions of the scriptures. As for those who recite the precepts, they should uphold the Bodhisattva precepts at six periods every day.
They should understand the principles of the Buddha-nature.
At six periods daily—three during the day and three during the night—one interpretation states that if the recitation has not yet been mastered, one must necessarily practice at these six periods.
[The text] is clear and fluent. It is not necessarily always so; the second [interpretation] says it should always be during the six periods [of the day].

*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden) states: "One who acts as a precept master should first extensively study the various sutras, recite the Vinaya from memory, and understand the principles explained within the precepts.
Furthermore, one must exhaust the source and reach the root, attaining a subtle awakening to the essential doctrine of nature—that is, the nature of Buddha-nature."
This [term] "nature" (xing) distinguishes this nature as the nature of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), and not the nature as conceived by the Śrāvakas or non-Buddhists.

It is precisely the "ground of the mind" (*cittabhūmi*) of the Bodhisattva. Regarding the presentation of two meanings during the six periods of the day: it clarifies that although one has already attained thorough mastery, practicing during these six periods is likewise not excessive.
Second, not understanding and not reciting:
if a bodhisattva does not understand even a single phrase or a single verse, nor the causal conditions of the precepts, yet falsely claims to understand them,
they are deceiving themselves and also deceiving others.
To act contrary to one's own mind is to deceive oneself; to mislead those before one is to deceive others.
*Fayi*: "One sentence, one verse"—this refers to not understanding the twelve divisions of the scriptures mentioned above. It does not say "reciting."
Within the section on the causes and conditions for upholding the precepts:
3. Raising an instance of transgression to expose the fault.
If one does not understand each and every point and lacks knowledge of all dharmas, yet acts as a teacher for others by bestowing the precepts, this constitutes a minor offense.
"Stains and offenses. "Revealing what was hidden. Each of these refers to the Vinaya; "all dharmas" refers to the various sūtras. Question:

To act as a master who bestows the precepts is truly difficult to find such a person. Yet, the world is named after the Vinaya—does such a master exist today? Answer: Regarding the ancient interpretations of the Vinaya masters...
These could all be enumerated; I shall cite just one or two examples. First was the compilation of the *Vinaya*, for which Upāli was its patriarch.
During the Jiaping era of the Wei dynasty, Dharmakāla from Western India produced the *Mahāsāṃghika-śīla-mūla*.

During the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, Buddhajīva from Central India produced the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya). Following this, there were the Vinaya masters Daocong of the Wei and Faguang of the Song.

The masters were: Vinaya Master Yunhui, Vinaya Master Leqi, Vinaya Master Suiqi, Vinaya Master Zun, Vinaya Master Zhishou, Vinaya Master Xuanchao of the Tang, Vinaya Master Wengang, Vinaya Master Dao’an, and Vinaya Master Daliang. Furthermore, there was Vinaya Master Tanyi.
Daocheng Vinaya Master, Huichin Vinaya Master, and even Song Yunkan Vinaya Master and Lingzhi Vinaya Master—
some were venerated by sovereigns, some were supported by devas and humans, and some elucidated the commentaries on the Vinaya.
Alternatively, one may establish a precept platform (kai-dan), which shall serve as a model for ten thousand generations; how could one not revere it?
According to this precept, it arises from within the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground—the mind of precepts, the mind of wisdom, the mind of faith, and the mind of penetration.
● Nineteenth Precept: Divisive Speech (2) I. Brief Introduction. II. Entry into the Text.
○ I. Brief Introduction:
This precept was established because inciting discord between parties destroys harmony; it is an offense for all seven classes of followers, and is regulated by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
II. Entering the Text (3): First, identifying the person; second, setting forth the matter; third, concluding with the offense.
○ First, identifying the person:
"If a disciple of the Buddha..."
II. Introduction to the Matter (2). First, citing those with whom one engages in conflict; second, the impropriety of such conflict.
I. Citing Those with Whom One Engages in Conflict.
Because of an evil mind, upon seeing a precept-observing bhikṣu holding an incense burner and practicing the bodhisattva path...
This refers to a Bodhisattva Bhikṣu who upholds the precepts and carries an incense burner in his hand; let us briefly cite one instance of his virtuous conduct.
Second, he must not engage in strife.
To engage in strife at both ends—slandering and deceiving worthy sages and committing every kind of evil—is forbidden.

To take these faults and speak of them to the other party is why it is called "two-headed. To slander and deceive a worthy person by claiming they have committed every kind of evil is the speech of double-tonguedness (*paiśunya*).

Even speaking the truth constitutes a violation of this precept; however, this rule specifically addresses the act of fabricating and meeting [the two sides] in speech, which is why it is termed "slandering and deceiving.
The character *gòu* (構) may also be written as *yù* (遇). The text explains that through such divisive words, one encounters both sides in conflict. Both are...
Exegesis of the Text: Some say that the character should be written as "gòu" (遇), but this is an error in the text. This precept is named the "Precept Against Envy of the Virtuous.

It refers specifically to hating and envying virtuous people and proclaiming their conduct to be evil. The phrasing "at both ends" is slightly awkward; thus, it is now stated as "envy of the virtuous."
This precept also governs [this case], because it involves instigating a quarrel between this person and that. *Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden) states:
"To commit no evil" refers to slandering a virtuous person by accusing them of committing evil. Even speaking the truth constitutes an offense here;
if one instigates a conflict between two parties, one commits an offense even if what is said is true, let alone when it is a lie. "Gou" (instigate) is sometimes written as "yu" (encounter).
Regarding this, the meaning of the words in the text may also be explained as follows: by using the term "quarreling over words," one encounters both extremes;
thus, both meanings are obtained, and it is said that "both aspects are resolved in the text. To speak only of "envy of the good" lacks the sense of both ends.

Now, it is clear that within the context of "strife and contention" (*dòugòu*), the suppression of envy toward the virtuous is also included. This is truly because using this to fight against that causes those of good character to be unsettled;
this is precisely the meaning of envy. This precept does not merely concern monks who engage in strife;

by extension, those who slander and cause disorder between sovereign and minister, or create estrangement between kinsmen, all belong to this same category. Only now do we understand that the factions of the East and the factions of the North were not [merely political].
This was the original intent of Cheng and Su; yet there are still those who discuss Yuanwu and Gaoyuan as forming a faction.
