Having left the household life out of faith and received the Buddha’s true realization, one who conceives the thought of violating the noble precepts shall not receive the offerings of any donors,
nor shall they walk upon the ground of the king, nor drink the water of the king.
Bearing guilt without shame, one may not receive offerings. Kings originally grant land and water to those of virtuous conduct;
one who lacks virtuous conduct should not enjoy them.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden). "Earth and water" is used as a metaphor. If this is so even for earth and water, how much more so for other things?

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Regarding one who has committed a root offense, the Buddha did not permit such a person to eat even a single morsel of food or to tread upon even a single heel's breadth of ground within the great assembly or the dwelling place.
Observing this, one knows that [the gravity of] breaking the precepts is such.
"O Bhikṣus, though heaven and earth are vast, there is nowhere for [the unrepentant] to dwell; though the offerings of the donors are many, even a drop of water is difficult to digest.
How can one not be afraid?
These two types of people are destroyed by ghosts."
Five thousand great ghosts constantly block his path ahead. These ghosts cry out, "Great thief! Whenever he enters a room, a city, or a house, the ghosts further sweep away his footprints.
All people of the world revile him, saying, "A thief within the Buddha-dharma.
No sentient being wishes to see him with their eyes; such a person who violates the precepts is no different from a beast, no different from a block of wood.
To carry on with one's offenses without shame is to be reviled by both humans and spirits.
To reveal what is hidden: those who uphold the precepts have benevolent deities guarding their bodies; those who break the precepts have malevolent ghosts following them.
Why is this? It is because the essences of good and evil naturally resonate with one another, just as the carriage, horses, and servants attend upon a person of high station in the world.
"Guarding and protecting" refers to how, in the world, one who has committed an offense is restrained and forbidden by cangues, shackles, and soldiers.
These various evil spirits obstruct their path while they are still alive; therefore, their majestic virtue daily diminishes and whatever they do becomes unfavorable.

At the time of death, they are led into hell, and thus their body and mind suffer pain while their consciousness becomes deluded and confused. Furthermore, regarding "sweeping away their footprints," the Sūtra says:
Where the noble sages recite the sutras and practice the Way, that ground is entirely composed of vajra.
Now, where these evil people travel, that ground is entirely defiled. How could the ghosts not sweep away their footprints?

Those who are thieves within the Buddha-dharma are evil persons who violate the precepts—namely, those who steal the robes of the Buddha and pilfer the food of the Buddha while remaining within the Buddha-dharma.
To inwardly subvert the Buddha-dharma—how could this not be a great thief?
Third, raising the error to conclude the fault:
If one intentionally destroys the right precepts, one commits a minor offense (light垢罪).

*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden). The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "To knowingly accept the offerings of the faithful while being aware that one has violated the precepts is called the fourth subtle affliction.
A renunciant who possesses this affliction is like one carrying a heavy burden into hell.
Regarding this precept, within the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, it concerns the mind of morality, the mind of faith, the mind of mindfulness, as well as shame and remorse.
It arises from the mind.
● Forty-fourth: The Precept of Not Failing to Make Offerings to the Scriptures (2). I. Brief Introduction. II. Entering the Text.
○ I. Brief Introduction.
The Triple Gem should all be honored with offerings. For those who do not practice [these], the rule was established out of a spirit of reverence;

it applies equally to the seven classes of followers, though the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions do not entirely coincide. A Bodhisattva should cultivate five matters, while a Śrāvaka should recite and uphold the light and heavy rules of the five categories (*pañca-varga*);
other matters are not prescribed.
*Fayi*: Following the five matters of the Bodhisattva, the five categories for Śrāvakas are: first, the four grave offenses (*pārājika*);
second, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; third, the combined *niḥsargika-pāyattika*; fourth, the *pratikarmanīya* (or *pratideśanīya*); and fifth, the *duṣkṛta*.
II. Entering the Text (in two parts): First, identifying the person; second, setting forth the matter.
○ First, identifying the person:
"If you, O sons of the Buddha..."

II. The Introductory Matter (3): First, the heading that exhorts one to receive and uphold [the precepts]; second, the specific enumeration of the matters for exhortation; third, citing what is improper to conclude with the faults [of non-compliance]. I.
The Heading that Exhorts One to Receive and Uphold.
One should always maintain a single mind.
To "arouse the hidden" means that a single mind is one without a second mind. Only when there is no distraction in this single mind can it be called the practice of recitation.

According to this, the single-minded recollection of the Buddha has both an aspect of phenomena (*dharma*) and an aspect of principle (*li*); this case should be understood in the same way. As for the single-mindedness of phenomena, it consists of guarding the mind with the mind.
Regarding the precepts: to uphold them is not easy; to recite them is not to forget. There is no intention of contravention, nor any intention of distraction.

When the mind does not oppose the precepts and the precepts do not oppose the mind, this is called "single-mindedness" (*ekacitta*). As for single-mindedness in principle, the mind merges with the precepts:
one upholds them without upholding, yet there is no mark of upholding; one recites them without reciting, yet there is no mark of reciting. Thus, the mind itself is the precept.

The precepts are themselves the mind. Not perceiving that which upholds [the precepts] nor that which is upheld, the two—transgression and non-transgression—are fused as one; this is called "one-mind.
○ Second, the specific enumeration of exhortations.

They receive, uphold, read, and recite the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas; they even flay their own skin to make paper, draw blood for ink, use marrow as water, and split their bones to make pens to transcribe the Buddha’s precepts.
They likewise write and maintain them upon tree bark, rice-husk paper, silk, and bamboo slips.
One should always use the seven treasures, priceless incense and flowers, and various miscellaneous jewels to make caskets and bags for containing the volumes of the Sūtras and Vinaya.
There are five kinds of exhortations regarding these matters: first, receiving and upholding; second, reading; third, reciting; fourth, transcribing; and fifth, making offerings.
The explanation of these has already been provided above within the thirty-ninth section.
*Fayin* (Unfolding the Hidden). Regarding the acts of flaying the skin and piercing the blood, there are two meanings.

First, the flesh and blood of one’s physical form are related to the life-root (*jīvitendriya*), which is the most precious thing in the world; thus, by relinquishing this body and life, one causes the "wisdom-life" (*prajñājīvita*) to circulate.

Second, the four elements (*mahābhūta*) are false and provisional, ultimately destined for decay and ruin, and are therefore the most useless things in the world; thus, one relinquishes that which is useless.
To "use" means to bring about great utility. The character for *gǔ* (grain) is composed of *qiào* (husk) and *mù* (wood).
Those who write it with *hé* (rice/awn) instead are incorrect; *gǔ* refers to the grain of a crop. The present *gǔ* (mulberry paper) is the *chǔ* tree, which can be used to make paper.

Below are listed the three types upon which one may write: first, paper; second, silk; third, bamboo. In antiquity, bamboo was used, hence the terms *jiǎn* (slip) and *zhí* (bundle), as well as *hànqīng* (the green-rotted bamboo).
In the Han dynasty, vermilion-soled paper first appeared; later, Cai Lun further produced paper from fish nets and tree bark.

From this point on, the recording and circulation [of texts] became inexhaustible. As for the mention of "five kinds," the intention is to emulate the five types of Dharma-preachers described in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Third, raising the point of error to expose the fault:
If one makes offerings that are not in accordance with the Dharma, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
The scriptures are the mother of the Buddhas; they should be venerated. To fail to do so constitutes an offense.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): All Buddhas of the three periods of time emerge from within the sutras; therefore, they are called the "Mother of Buddhas.
To treat one's parents with negligence or contempt and fail to provide them with offerings is unfilial. How could such a person still be said to possess the precepts?

According to this precept, the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground consists of the precept-mind, the vow-mind, the protective mind, the faith-mind, the mindfulness-mind, and the mind of reverence.
It arises from the mind.
● Forty-fifth: The Precept of Not Transforming Sentient Beings (2). Part One: A Brief Introduction. Part Two: Entering the Text.
○ First, the Brief Introduction.
The Bodhisattva resolves to benefit sentient beings; seeing those with consciousness, they ought to instruct and transform them so that they may attain awakening and understanding.

If one is unable to do so, it deviates from the conduct of a Mahāsattva; therefore, this is prescribed as a transgression for all seven classes of followers alike, though the precepts of the Great and Small Vehicles are not shared.
The Great Being (Mahāsattva) transforming sentient beings is the correct practice; the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) seeks only its own deliverance.

Not transforming others does not constitute a transgression for them. *Fayi* (Unveiling the Hidden) states: Regarding why a transgression constitutes one for a Great Being but not for the Small Vehicle—it is like this:

when a single person is left behind, one who takes the whole world as their own responsibility says, "This is my fault. But what fault could there be for those such as the cowherd or the man carrying a *kuei*-basket?
II. Entering the Text (in two parts): First, identifying the person; second, setting forth the matter.
○ First, identifying the person:
"If you, O sons of the Buddha..."
II. Introduction to the Matter (3): First, exhorting the arousal of compassion; second, enumerating the matters of compassion; third, citing what is contrary to it to conclude with the faults.
I. Exhorting the Arousal of Compassion.
One should constantly give rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

It does not arise as a simultaneous restraint (*sahagata-saṃvara*). Compassion is able to extract one from suffering; the Great Being (*mahāsattva*) constantly vows that sentient beings shall be free from suffering.

[This is] the revelation of the underlying intent. The "simultaneous restraint" follows the previous example. Regarding the statement "arising," the simultaneous restraint of non-arising refers to the transgression of a fault. The term "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*) is not mentioned.

"Maitrī" (loving-kindness) bestows happiness; "karuṇā" (compassion) uproots suffering. Uprooting suffering is more urgent than bestowing happiness. Furthermore, when suffering departs, happiness immediately follows; thus, compassion encompasses loving-kindness.
For this reason, the Buddha is praised as the "World-Honored One of Great Compassion," and Avalokiteśvara is praised as the "Bodhisattva of Great Compassion.
Indeed, the very basis for distinguishing between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna lies precisely here. Those who study the Bodhisattva path...
One must not forget this mind for even a moment; therefore, it is said that one should "constantly arouse" it.
II. Listing the Matters of Compassion (3): 1. Seeing humans and causing them to arouse the resolve. 2. Seeing animals and causing them to arouse the resolve. 3.
According to direction and whatever is seen, causing [beings] to arouse the resolve.
Upon first seeing people, one should cause them to resolve their minds [on enlightenment].
When entering any city, town, or house, upon seeing any sentient beings, one should proclaim:
"All you sentient beings, you should all receive the three refuges and the ten precepts."

*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): Although sentient beings encompass the six realms of existence, the present discussion is specifically concerned with those among humans who resolve to generate the bodhicitta.
This is because the subsequent text mentions cattle, horses, pigs, sheep, and so forth; for now, we shall speak only of human beings. According to the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, it says:
When a Bodhisattva goes to the home of a layperson, if they fail to preach the Dharma and provide instruction so that the person may offer worship to the Triple Gem, they incur an offense.
The *Luefu luohan jing* (Sūtra on the Subjugation of Arhats) states: "At the end of his life, Prince Lili was destined to receive the body of a pig."
He went to the Buddha to seek salvation. The Buddha instructed him to take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.

Thereupon, for seven days and seven nights, he diligently practiced the Three Refuges and was thus spared from rebirth in a pig’s womb, becoming instead the son of an elder. Furthermore, the *Mukhaṇḍika-sūtra* states that the Buddha told King Virūḍhaka:
"By stringing beads of *mukhaṇḍika* wood and reciting the names of the Triple Gem, one shall sever the bonds of karma and attain the unsurpassed fruit."
Thus, we know that the Three Jewels are the place of refuge for all sentient beings. It is not called the five precepts but rather the ten precepts;
for while the five precepts are the cause for rebirth as humans or devas, the ten precepts are the path of the Bodhisattva.
2. Seeing Livestock and Inspiring Resolve:
If you see oxen, horses, pigs, sheep, or any other kind of livestock, you should mentally reflect and verbally say: "You are an animal;
arouse the bodhicitta."
*Fayi*: "You are an animal" first reveals the name of its retributive fruit;
"one who has resolved on Bodhicitta" subsequently teaches the essentials for transcendence. Bodhicitta is the vast, pure, and inherently luminous essence of awakening;
it is precisely the self-nature Three Refuges, the Mind-Ground, and the Ten Precepts. Because one is deluded regarding this mind, it remains hidden and unmanifest.
[The cycle] begins. One revolves through the three miserable realms without end. When this mind is aroused, spiritual awakening becomes clear and penetrating;
darkness, obscurations, and folly are instantly extinguished. How could there be such a thing as an "animal"?
Third, causing [beings] to resolve their minds toward enlightenment according to their location and their perception:
when a bodhisattva enters all places— mountains, forests, rivers, and fields— they cause all sentient beings therein to generate the bodhicitta.

To cause all to resolve their minds [for enlightenment] is the urgent necessity for deliverance; therefore, these three [methods] must be employed. They universally regulate both monastics and laypeople.
First, to reveal the hidden and cause people to resolve their minds. Second, to cause those who harbor [doubts] to resolve their minds.

Third, to cause them to resolve their minds according to their circumstances and perspectives. Bodhisattvas, whether ordained or lay, should all act in this manner; hence it is said they are "universally regulated."
Third, raising the objection to point out the fault:
If this bodhisattva does not give rise to the mind to teach and transform sentient beings, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
[Commentary]: Question: When preaching the Dharma to humans, if the people do not yet believe, one may direct the mind toward animals; but how can animals know?
Answer: The nature [of awakening] resides within all sentient beings and is inconceivable. To presume that animal species will never possess a mind of enlightenment is incorrect.
Consider the clam reborn in heaven, the Peng bird who revered the Vinaya, the tiger who lowered its ears to avoid the area, and the python who shed tears to reform its heart.
There was the sea fish who, in a subsequent life, rose to honor the Dharma-gate, and the flying bird who, in its next birth, returned as a disciple.
Examples such as these are too numerous to enumerate exhaustively. Even if those beings are burdened by heavy karma and lack understanding, the practitioner shall naturally obtain merit.
Therefore, one should teach and transform those in the Avīci hell, as well as humans and animals. Regarding this precept, it arises from the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground:
specifically, from the mind of precepts, the mind of vows, the mind of loving-kindness, the mind of compassion, the mind of benefit, and the Mahāyāna mind.
● Forty-sixth Precept: Teaching the Dharma Unlawfully (2). I. Brief Introduction. II. Entering the Text.
○ I. Brief Introduction.

To explain forcefully [without regard for the listener's capacity] results in the fault of mutual arrogance regarding the Dharma; therefore, this rule is established. It applies equally to all five groups of renunciants. Great.

The Minor Collective Prohibition (*khuddaka-saṃghādisesa*). If one who is a layperson does not act as a master of the Dharma, and even speaks but a single sentence or a single verse that is not in accordance with the Dharma, one also commits an offense.
*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden) states: "Both parties" means that both the speaker and the listener incur guilt. "Not acting as [a master] completely" also refers to certain occasions.
Regarding the preaching of the Dharma: although the verses may not constitute the full text, to fail to accord with the formal protocols for preaching the Dharma also constitutes an offense.

Preaching the Dharma while living as a layperson includes such instances as Vimalakīrti’s discourse on non-duality at Vaiśālī and the lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* beneath the twin śāla trees in the palace hall of Liang.
However, these were great *mahopāya-kauśalya* bodhisattvas who skillfully manifested in the bodies of laymen; they were not [ordinary persons].

Nowadays, non-Buddhists and laypeople have erroneously assumed the responsibility of preaching the Dharma; some falsely claim to be the patriarchs of the Three Teachings, while others fabricate scriptures of the Five Sections.
Some secretly transmit the "Scripture of Sixteen Characters," and others clandestinely pass down the "Buddha of Seven Characters.
Some practice internal circulation of qi and mental visualization, calling these "public cases" (gong'an), while others claim to hear voices or see objects in the dead of night.
They manifest strange portents; some, having no genuine realization, deceitfully claim to belong to the Chan school, while others deny cause and effect and slander the True Dharma.
Their myriad methods and paths cannot be fully recounted. They occupy seats and call themselves teachers without the slightest humility;
though they are laymen by status, they vainly seek to oppose the monastic community. Like one blind man leading a crowd of the blind, they all head toward the same abyss of ruin.
Thus it is said: these are but momentary masters of the Dharma; their half-syllable, heterodox words are all seeds of hell.
I pray that when the lecturer reaches this point, they will not begrudge their compassion, but will exert themselves to rescue [the listeners].
II. Entering the Text (2): First, identifying the person; second, setting forth the matter.
○ First, identifying the person:
"If you, O Sons of the Buddha..."
II. The Introductory Matters (3): First, a general explanation for all; second, specific instructions for the fourfold assembly; third, citing deviations to clarify errors.
I. General Explanation for All.
One should always teach and transform others by giving rise to the mind of great compassion.
When entering the home of a wealthy patron or among any assembly, one must not stand while preaching the Dharma to laypeople; rather, one should occupy a high seat before the assembly of laypeople.

One should always teach and transform others through great compassion; this also serves as a restraint. One must not stand when teaching the Dharma, thereby demonstrating the proper ritual for preaching.
When speaking to laypeople, one must not lean or stand; the rule is that both should sit together. However, if both are standing, it is not an offense.

In this context, "standing" is what is being established as the rule. If a person is lying down while one preaches the Dharma while sitting or standing, or if one covers one's head or holds a staff, none of these are permitted.

Regarding the manifestation of hidden faults, if one stands together with another and preaches the Dharma while both are standing, there is no offense. In this context, "standing" is what is being established.
This is merely cited as a solitary example. "Sitting on a high seat" (gāozuòshàngzuò) does not mean sitting upon the top of a high seat;
rather, these are two types of seats: either a "high seat" (gāozuò) or an "upper seat" (shàngzuò). "High seat" refers to its height, while "upper seat" refers to its relative position.
Regarding lying down and covering one's head, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) provides an exemption for those who are ill, such that there is no offense. This...
It should also be so. A Bodhisattva’s great compassion benefits all beings; for the sake of the sick, how could one adhere strictly to conventional rules?
○ Second, specific provisions for the fourfold assembly:
A Dharma-preacher bhikṣu must not stand on the ground while preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly. When preaching the Dharma, the Dharma-preacher should be elevated.

They took their seats and made offerings of incense and flowers. The fourfold assembly of listeners sat on lower seats, listening with filial devotion as toward parents and respectful obedience as toward a teacher’s instruction, just as fire-worshipping Brahmins attend to their sacred fires.

When preaching to the fourfold assembly, one must likewise not stand. Do not say that because monks and nuns possess the Way, it is permissible to preach while leaning against something while standing;
this too is a violation due to treating the Dharma lightly.

*Fayi*: The previous section was specifically for laypeople; the present section includes all four assemblies. In one manuscript, the phrase "the fourfold assembly" is followed by "laypeople" (*baiyi*).
The two characters [for "lay"] refer to the fourfold assembly; since this already includes the two lay assemblies, why is it necessary to further mention "white-robed ones" (*avadātavasana*)?
As for "those who serve fire": because Brahmins serve fire and pay their respects with the utmost ritual propriety, this is used as a metaphor.

It is intended that they apply the same mind they use to serve heterodox teachings toward the True Teaching. Do not say that monks and nuns are those who possess the Way; even if they were to possess the Way...

It is honorable that, in the end, it is difficult to abandon the Dharma for the sake of the Way. The regulations governing the high seat and the lower seat must not be discarded or left unpracticed merely because of monks and nuns.

All sentient beings were individually filled with joy and each practiced accordingly.
○ Second, regarding other locations:
if one wishes to extensively explain the characteristics of the mind-ground, it is as described in the "Seven Practices" chapter of the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-rāja-sūtra*.
The "Chapter on the Buddha Flower-Light King" must have been part of the Great Version [of the sutra], as the original texts differ.

Regarding the "three thousands," this refers to the three thousand modes of dignified conduct that a bodhisattva should study. Regarding the "three years," while śrāvakas require five years, bodhisattvas require only three.
Regarding the "three matters," these are simply morality, concentration, and wisdom.

*Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): Briefly stated, there are ten billion as mentioned above; if explained extensively in other places, it would be as in the "Chapter on King of Light" (*Guangwang pin*), yet this chapter is not present here now, hence it is said that this must be from the *Daben* (Great Original Text).
Regarding "each and every mark" (*xiangxiang*): the precepts are the marks of the mind-ground.
The marks of the precepts—both general and specific—are layered and inexhaustible; thus they are called "each and every mark. What is clarified in the present chapter raises [these points].
This is merely a general summary. It fundamentally differs from the subsequent commentary that traces back to the preceding text. Regarding the statement "fundamentally different":

among the three thousand scholars, there are those who read it as "three thousand," "three years," or "three matters. Each interpretation according to the text has its own meaning, and all meanings are equally valid.

The characters for "thousand" (qian), "year" (nian), and "matter" (shi) are easily corrupted through transcription—like the confusion between "wu," "an," and "ma"—therefore [the text] says "five years" (wunian).
Three years: this is the period for training in the precepts. III.
General Praise for the Propagation (in three parts): 1. Praising the benefits of upholding the precepts; 2. Setting forth the matter of training in the precepts;
3. Vowing to deliver sentient beings.
I. First, Praising the Benefits of Upholding the Precepts (in two parts): A. General Praise; B. The Fivefold [Benefits]. A. General Praise:
The person of wisdom, possessing strong endurance and insight, is able to uphold such a Dharma. Until they attain the Way of Buddhahood, they will securely obtain five kinds of benefits.
*Fayi*: "Those who are enlightened" means that this Great Precept cannot be maintained by the ignorant.

They are called "enlightened" because they possess patience (*kṣānti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Patience is the mind’s steadfastness; when that patience reaches the utmost firmness, it is called "strong patience.

Wisdom is the mind’s spiritual penetration; when that wisdom reaches the utmost sharpness, it is called "strong wisdom. One with strong patience is able to maintain [the precept] forever, and in the end...

From the beginning, there is no shifting. When wisdom is strong, one is able to maintain it well, remaining perfectly integrated and unimpeded. A person such as this is brilliant, acute, and exceptionally outstanding;
they transcend ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles—how could they be anyone other than a person of clarity? This refers to one who has not yet achieved the attainment of profit.
One who is able to uphold this Dharma will certainly attain Buddhahood; yet, without waiting for that attainment, they will first obtain five benefits during the interim.
These are praised as the supreme advantages of upholding the precepts, intended to encourage others to do so.
As for "attaining with ease," these five kinds of benefits are acquired spontaneously and naturally, rather than through strenuous seeking.
II. Five kinds [of benefits]:
First, the Buddhas of the ten directions take pity on one and constantly protect them. Second, at the time of death, one possesses right view and the mind is joyful.
Third, in every place of rebirth, one becomes a friend to all bodhisattvas. Fourth, the accumulation of merit—the perfection of the pāramitā of ethical discipline—is fully accomplished.
Fifth, regarding future lives: when the precepts of nature (*śīla*), merit, and wisdom are fulfilled, these are the sons of the Buddhas.
This is the single benefit protected and sustained by all Buddhas. These precepts are the very heart-ground of all Buddhas.
When sentient beings uphold the precepts, the Buddha-dharma flourishes; when sentient beings violate the precepts, the Buddha-dharma perishes. [The power of] upholding the precepts—
O people! How could the Buddha not, out of compassion and pity, bestow his majestic spiritual protection so that what they undertake is ultimately accomplished?
Second, regarding the benefit of joy at the time of death: those who have violated the precepts fall into evil realms at death and their hearts are filled with fear;
whereas those who maintain the precepts until the end possess radiant right view and know for themselves that after death they will certainly be born before the Buddha—how could this not be so?
Rejoice! This is the benefit for the three types of bodhisattva companions. This precept is upheld by all bodhisattvas; those who uphold the precepts are the very peers of the bodhisattvas.
In birth after birth and in every place, will they not walk together with Avalokiteśvara and dwell together with Samantabhadra?
Within the state of Bodhi, they shall be fellow members of the same retinue. Thus, the fourfold assembly shall achieve excellence.
Benefit. The precepts are the foundation of all virtuous merits. By upholding the precepts, all merits are gathered together without exception.
Just as there are immeasurable gates of *pāramitā* regarding merit, let us cite one example: the *śīla-pāramitā* transcends transgression.
Thus, the perfection of the precepts has now been accomplished; the accomplishment of the remaining perfections may be understood by analogy. These are the five blessings.

The wisdom of the dual cultivation of merit and insight is the precept of the mind-ground, which is itself Buddha-nature. The essential substance of Buddha-nature is free from transgression and devoid of fault;
therefore, it is called "inherent precept" (*prakṛti-śīla*). Within this inherent precept, both merit and wisdom are fully present.

Because it is inherently good, the myriad practices are cultivated simultaneously; because it is inherently luminous, all phenomena are clearly manifest. This is what is meant by the fulfillment of merit and wisdom. Question: When merit is sufficient, is wisdom...?
The title "Worthy among Two-Legged Beings" refers to the fruit of Buddhahood. Since he has not yet attained Buddhahood, how can it be said that [the perfections] are fulfilled? Answer:
The text states, "In this life and in future lives. This means that in this present life one plants the superior causes, and in future lives one realizes the ultimate fruit.
One who thus maintains the precepts and attains these five benefits is truly a son of the Buddha and shall succeed to the Buddha’s position;
this is precisely the meaning of receiving the Buddha’s precepts and entering the Buddha’s rank as described above.
II. The Second Section: On the Matter of Training in the Precepts (in two parts). First, observing the causes of the precepts; second, maintaining the characteristics of the precepts.
I. Observing the Causes of the Precepts. The wise person reflects skillfully:
"Those who calculate based on a self and cling to signs cannot give rise to this Dharma. Those who seek realization by extinguishing the life-faculty [cannot give rise to it either]."
Nor is it a place for sowing seeds. Those who wish to grow the sprouts of Bodhi and have their radiance illuminate the world should calmly observe the true nature of all phenomena:
that they are neither born nor extinguished, neither eternal nor annihilated, neither identical nor different.
Neither coming nor going—within such a single mind, one should diligently adorn it through skillful means. This is what a bodhisattva ought to do;
one should train in this according to the sequence. Regarding those in training and those beyond training, do not give rise to discriminatory thoughts. This is called the foremost path.
It is also called Mahāyāna. All evil conceptual proliferations are extinguished from this source;
the sarvajñā (omniscience) of all Buddhas emerges entirely from this source.

*Fayi*: "This Dharma" refers precisely to this precept-Dharma. Because this precept is the fundamental ground of the mind of all sentient beings, and because this ground of the mind belongs neither to existence nor non-existence:
those who calculate their own bodies and become attached to illusory appearances are those who cling to existence;
those who extinguish the life-span and seek to realize quiescent extinction are those who cling to non-existence. Both of these are like withered sprouts and rotten seeds.
From what source does the sublime and excellent dharma of the precepts arise? Therefore, let the wise contemplate this well. "The wise" refers to the person previously explained.
There are two kinds of thorough contemplation: first, correct contemplation; second, careful contemplation. Through these, one gives rise to true and correct wisdom.
Furthermore, examine with careful attention: know that all previous false conceptualizations are not the seeds of Bodhi.
If you truly desire to nurture the sprouts of the Way so that its radiance may shine forth brilliantly and illuminate all directions without limit, you need not seek outward;

it lies solely in the quiet contemplation of the true, non-illusory, and eternally abiding nature of all phenomena. As for what is called "quiet contemplation," it is like seeking a pearl [from within].
When the waves are stilled, it is difficult to obtain a response from the moving water.

As for what is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), marks such as arising and ceasing, or annihilation and permanence, are all illusory and unreal, false and insubstantial. This true reality is originally without any thing;
it does not arise. Since it does not arise, it does not cease, yet it is clearly and constantly known. It does not cease, yet it dwells nowhere for even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
It is not permanent; yet if it were not permanent, it would be subject to annihilation, whereas it remains eternally as it is throughout the ten thousand ages—thus it is not annihilated.

Its manifestations are distinct and difficult to reconcile—thus it is not one; yet if it were not one, it would be disparate, whereas its essence is identical and difficult to divide—thus it is not disparate.
One meets it but knows not whence it comes—thus it does not come; yet if it did not come, it would depart, and even if one pursues it, one knows not whither it goes.
That which one aspires toward does not depart. Such single-mindedness is profound, subtle, and inconceivable;
it should be adorned with skillful wisdom and expedient means. This adornment is what a bodhisattva ought to perform.
It is indeed appropriate that one should train in the stages in succession; yet, regarding training and non-training, do not make any distinctions.

Why is this? Speaking in terms of training, although the myriad practices are manifold, not a single thought can be grasped, for there is no increase whatsoever in the ground of the true mark (*bhūtatathatā*).
Speaking in terms of non-training, when not a single thought arises, the whole is fully present, for there is no decrease whatsoever in the ground of the true mark.
Because they are absent, within this mind-ground there are merely no signs of arising and ceasing, or of annihilation and permanence;

this itself is adornment, and this itself is study. Therefore, whether one is a learner (*śaikṣa*) or one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), even if one wishes to distinguish between them, there is nothing to be distinguished.
In the state of non-discrimination, the Middle Way is perfectly manifest; this is called the primary path. For as soon as discrimination arises, it constitutes duality. Furthermore—
It is named Mahāyāna because even the slightest conceptual differentiation constitutes the Two Vehicles. Furthermore, this ground of the mind of true reality is like a great mass of fire;
it utterly consumes all the myriad categories and thousands of families of worldly views—namely, the clinging to existence and non-existence, and the reckoning of "that" and "self."
Because all the firewood of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is extinguished here without remainder;

and because this ground of the mind of true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa-citta-bhūmi*) is like a vast ocean, wherein all the Tathāgata’s wisdom, eloquence, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), samādhis, and the wealth of the qualities of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) arise inexhaustibly. Upon reaching this, it is by virtue of the Bodhi...

Sowing the seeds, one binds the fruit of Bodhi. The radiance of wisdom and the flames of insight shine universally and without end upon all sentient beings of the three periods of time, throughout the ten directions, across all worlds and ages.
There is none who does not become like one who regains sight after being blind, or like one who finds a lamp in the darkness.
Therefore, it is said that "the light illuminates the world. Were it not for one of great illumination, how could one well contemplate within the ground of the mind?
This is the wondrous meaning.
II. The Characteristics of Guarding and Maintaining the Precepts:
For this reason, O sons of the Buddha, you should arouse great courage and vigor; regarding the pure precepts of all Buddhas, guard and maintain them as if they were bright pearls.
All bodhisattvas of the past have already trained in this; those of the future shall train in it; and those of the present are training in it now.
This is the sphere of practice of the Buddhas, praised by the Holy Lord.
*Fayi*: Following from the above, since pure precepts emerge from this very ground of the true mark (*bhūtatathatā*), they must be maintained.
Yet, because the categories of precepts are difficult to uphold and easy to lose, one must maintain them with vigor. Regarding the three meanings of the "bright pearl": first, the meaning of purity;
one must protect and maintain it so as not to allow it to be defiled. Second, the meaning of perfection; one must protect and maintain...

Do not allow it to become impaired or deficient. Third is the meaning of radiance: to protect and maintain it so that it does not fall into obscurity. Pure and perfect radiance is precisely Vairocana;
when evil is exhausted and goodness is perfected, there is nothing that is not saved. This is not merely what all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time study together;
it is also the common practice of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Thus the Holy Lord proclaims:
How could this be merely a matter of coincidence? The "Holy Lord" (Shengzhu) is none other than the Buddha. He is the most holy among the holy; thus he is called the Holy Lord.
○ Third, the vow to deliver sentient beings.
I have expounded this in accordance with the truth; may this immeasurable mass of merit be dedicated to all sentient beings so that we may together proceed toward omniscience.
May all who hear this Dharma attain the path to Buddhahood.
*Fayi*: "To follow" means not to turn one's back; "to accord with" means not to oppose. All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past have revered these great precepts of the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*).
I, too, shall speak of these precepts in accordance with them. The merit thus accumulated will be vast and immeasurable.
Yet, this merit is not sought for oneself; it is entirely dedicated and bestowed upon all sentient beings. And so it is.
This dedication of merit is not directed toward the Two Vehicles; it is dedicated entirely toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
Furthermore, may there be not a single person who hears this Dharma who does not attain Buddhahood. May it once pass through the faculty of hearing and forever become a seed for the Path.
By practicing in accordance with the Dharma, may they ultimately achieve perfect enlightenment. At this point, whether grave or light, the immeasurable and boundless precepts—
In this chapter, we realize the source of the mind together. Whether mundane or supramundane, all infinite and inexhaustible sentient beings return to the single nature.
Only then do we know that I, now as Vairocana, am not a Buddha who has come from elsewhere; the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground reaches its ultimate point here. Question:
The text states, "one immediately enters the rank of all Buddhas," yet it also says, "in the interval before attaining the Buddha-way. How can these two statements be reconciled?

It is further stated: "All shall attain the Buddha-way. "Immediately" (*ji*) means attaining the causes of Buddhahood all at once; "not yet" (*wei*) means eventually tending toward the fruit of Buddhahood;
"all" (*xi*) means that everyone universally becomes a Buddha. The merit of upholding the precepts is manifest in this way.

Alas, why do those who lecture on the sutras and those who practice Chan still insert their tongues [to dispute this]? The lecturers say: "The intent of the Buddha is profound and mysterious; it resides in the *Sūtras*, such as the *Śūraṅgama*."
This means that upholding and violating the precepts merely restrain the body; if there were no body, there would be nothing to restrain. Therefore, one should know that one must study the teachings.

Is it not the case that the Vinaya rules are shallow and superficial, and thus insufficient for study? Answer: The *Lengyan Lun* (Śūraṅgama-sūtra Commentary) treats the four fundamental precepts with great earnestness, using such metaphors as "steaming sand" and "a leaking cup.
This demonstrates that the teaching itself is the precept. The Vinaya states: "Commit no evil; perform all good..."

"Practice it. Purify your own minds; this is the teaching of all Buddhas. Thus, the precepts are themselves the teaching. Furthermore, it is said that until one has completed five summer retreats (*pañca-varṣa*), one should focus exclusively on the Vinaya;
only after five summers should one listen to the teachings and engage in Zen meditation. Therefore, the precepts should come first and the teachings later.
To discuss the teachings while violating the precepts is like having a body bound by the five wooden stocks while reciting the six [perfections] with one's mouth.
[Sutra]: "Though one may escape from guilt and punishment, if one has not yet attained [liberation], what is there to say of mere literary arts? Question:
A Chan practitioner says, "The ancient masters said that 'being urgent about the precepts and slow about the vehicle' is not as good as 'being slow about the precepts and urgent about the vehicle.

Thus we know that the vehicle is the primary task; the precepts are trivial matters and not worth studying. Is this so, or is it not? Answer: You claim to know that one should be urgent about the vehicle and lax about the precepts. Why do you suffer such hardship?

Yet, one does not choose that which is urgent in both vehicle and precepts. It is like the eyes and ears: why suffer by choosing one with clear vision but deaf ears, rather than choosing one who possesses both eyes and ears intact?
In the past, Caoxi said that when the mind-ground is free from transgression, it is the precept of self-nature;
thus, the vehicle is itself the precept. The First Patriarch said that the mind must be like a wall or a screen to enter the Way; thus...

The precepts are themselves the vehicle. Master Guishan remarked that he had never had the honor of attending a formal assembly on the *vinaya*, and how could he possibly have mastered the ultimate teachings of the Supreme Vehicle?
This implies that the precepts come first and the vehicle comes later.

To abandon the precepts while speaking of the vehicle is like someone who starts out as a lowly peddler and suddenly mounts a ceremonial imperial carriage; before his feet have even turned, he faces execution—what more need be said?
This is indeed glorious and honored. Now, as for the precepts (*śīla*), they are the fundamental ground of the mind of both the Buddha and sentient beings.

It is for the purpose of clarifying this that the teachings exist. Throughout his entire career of preaching, the World-Honored One taught the ground of the mind. The vehicles (*yāna*) serve to realize this.

When Bodhidharma came from the West to transmit the Dharma, he transmitted the ground of the mind. Since it is called the "ground of the mind," its profundity and shallowness, its urgency and leisure, and its priority and sequence are all contained therein.
Neither can be apprehended. The characteristics of precepts, the characteristics of teachings, and the characteristics of dhyāna likewise cannot be apprehended.
Even that which is called the "ground of the mind" cannot be apprehended. How, then, could there be any dispute?
The Exegesis on the Meaning of the Bodhisattva Precepts from the "Mind-Ground Chapter" of the Brahmajāla Sūtra, Volume Five (End)
